concepts/spice-trade-line-of-demarcation.title: The Spice Trade and the Line of Demarcation
concepts/spice-trade-line-of-demarcation.content:
The Spice Trade and the Line of Demarcation

The value of spices in 16th-century Europe, the Venetian/Arab monopoly, the fall of Constantinople, Portugal’s Cape Route, the papal division of the world, Magellan’s westward end-run around Portuguese control, and the treaties that finally settled the Moluccas dispute. Drawn primarily from Bergreen’s Over the Edge of the World (Prologue and Chapter I).


The Value of Spices in 16th-Century Europe
Spices were the most precious commodity of the Age of Discovery. Bergreen likens their economic role in the 16th century to that of oil in the modern era: they drove the world’s economy, influenced global politics, and became inextricably intertwined with exploration, conquest, and imperialism. The mere mention of their names — white and black pepper, myrrh, frankincense, nutmeg, cinnamon, cassia, mace, and cloves — evoked the wonders of the Orient.^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
The economic stakes were enormous. A sailor who returned from the Spice Islands with even a small sack of cloves or nutmeg could sell it for enough to buy a small house and live off the proceeds for the rest of his life. A captain could expect not only vast riches and fame, but titles to pass on to his heirs and foreign lands to rule. Successful expeditions could yield profits of 250–400 percent.^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
The European climate could not sustain these tropical spices. The Iberian peninsula during the 16th century was in the grip of the Little Ice Age — too cold and too dry to cultivate cinnamon, cloves, or pepper. An Indonesian ruler was said to have boasted to a trader who wanted to grow spices in Europe: “You may be able to take our plants, but you will never be able to take our rain.”^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]

The Venetian/Arab Monopoly
Arab merchants traded in spices across land routes reaching across Asia and became adept at boosting prices by concealing the origins of cinnamon, pepper, cloves, and nutmeg. They maintained a virtual monopoly by insisting these precious items came from Africa, when in fact they grew in India, China, and especially throughout Southeast Asia. Europeans came to believe that spices came from Africa, when they only changed hands there. To protect their monopoly, Arab merchants invented monsters and myths to conceal the ordinary process of harvesting spices, making it sound impossibly dangerous to acquire them.^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
The spice trade was central to Arab life. Muhammad himself belonged to a family of prominent merchants and traded in myrrh and frankincense. Arabs developed sophisticated methods of extracting essential oils from aromatic spices for medical and therapeutic purposes, formulating elixirs and syrups including julab (from which the word “julap” derives). During the Middle Ages, Arab knowledge of spices spread across western Europe, where apothecaries developed a brisk trade in concoctions made from cloves, pepper, nutmeg, and mace.^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Under the traditional system, spices reached Europe by slow, costly, and indirect routes over land and sea — across China and the Indian Ocean, through the Middle East and Persian Gulf. Merchants received them in Italy or southern France and shipped them overland to their final destination. Spices passed through as many as twelve different hands, each transaction driving the price higher. They were the ultimate cash crop.^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]

The Fall of Constantinople (1453)
The global spice trade underwent an upheaval in 1453, when Constantinople fell to the Ottoman Turks. The time-honoured overland spice routes between Asia and Europe were severed. This disruption opened up new economic possibilities for any European nation able to master the seas. For those willing to assume the risks, the rewards of an oceanic spice trade — combined with control over the world’s economy — were irresistible.^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]

Columbus’s Search for Spices (1492–1504)
While Columbus’s voyages are remembered for the discovery of the New World, Columbus himself believed to his dying day that he had reached the eastern edge of Asia — and that the Spice Islands lay just beyond the lands he had found. The search for spices was the explicit economic motive of all four of his voyages, and its repeated failure was one of his greatest disappointments.
The Promise of the First Voyage
Columbus’s contract with Ferdinand and Isabella (the Capitulations of Santa Fe, April 1492) specifically empowered him to “discover and acquire” islands and mainland in the Ocean Sea, with the explicit expectation of finding spices, gold, and precious stones. On his first voyage, every native report of gold was eagerly interpreted; every new island was scanned for cinnamon, pepper, and other spices. ^[source: irving_columbus_full.txt]
When Columbus reached Cuba in October 1492, he sent an embassy inland specifically to find the Grand Khan of Asia and the spice markets of the Orient. The embassy found a village of forty huts and a population that fled in terror — no spices, no gold, no Grand Khan. ^[source: irving_columbus_full.txt]
The False Spices
Throughout the first voyage, Columbus and his men collected bark, berries, and leaves they believed were valuable spices. Irving records that Columbus identified “cinnamon” from the bark of a local tree (likely Canella winterana or a similar species native to the Caribbean, unrelated to true Asian cinnamon). He found “pepper” in the form of allspice (Pimenta dioica) and chili peppers — pungent but commercially valueless in the European spice market. ^[source: irving_columbus_full.txt]
On the second voyage, Columbus brought seeds and cuttings of plants he believed were nutmeg and ginger. None survived the crossing. The Caribbean simply did not produce the high-value spices of the Indian Ocean. The only tropical products Columbus could ship back in quantity — cassava bread, sweet potatoes, cotton, and dyewood — were too bulky and low-value to pay the costs of a transatlantic voyage. ^[source: irving_columbus_carvill_v2.txt]
Why Columbus Failed to Find Spices
The fundamental problem was geographical. Columbus had not reached Asia — he had stumbled upon a New World whose spice profile was entirely different from that of the Indian Ocean. The Caribbean pepper (Capsicum) was novel but competed with black pepper only as a curiosity. The “cinnamon” was a local substitute, not the true Cinnamomum of Ceylon. The profitable spice trade ran from the Moluccas (cloves, nutmeg), Ceylon (cinnamon), and the Malabar Coast (pepper) — all of which lay on the opposite side of the world from Columbus’s discoveries.
Vasco da Gama’s success in reaching Calicut in 1498 made this abundantly clear. While Columbus returned to Spain in chains in 1500, his claims of reaching Asia increasingly disbelieved, Gama’s pepper-laden ships were arriving in Lisbon to enormous profits. Columbus never accepted this. On his fourth voyage (1502–1504), he still believed he was approaching the Spice Islands from the east — a geographical delusion that motivated his desperate search for a strait through Central America.
Columbus’s Spice Legacy
Columbus brought back no significant spice cargo in any of his four voyages. The gold and pearls he found were real, and the Taíno people he enslaved made a political point, but the commercial driver of his expeditions — the spice trade — remained wholly out of reach. It was the Portuguese who reaped what Columbus had sown, sailing the route Columbus’s navigational techniques had helped pioneer, but reaching the real spice sources that Columbus’s geography had so fundamentally mislocated.

Portugal’s Cape Route (Vasco da Gama, 1498)
Portugal was the first European nation to exploit the sea for spices and the global empire that went with them. The quest began as early as 1419, when Prince Henry the Navigator established his court at Sagres, an outcropping of rock at the southern edge of Portugal. He attracted navigators, shipwrights, astronomers, pilots, cosmographers, and cartographers — both Christians and Jews — who designed the caravel, a small manoeuvrable vessel with triangular lateen sails borrowed from Arab vessels. By 1434, Gil Eannes had sailed past Cape Bojador, opening the African coast to exploration.^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
In 1488, Bartolomeu Dias rounded the southern tip of Africa (the Cape of Good Hope). Ten years later, Vasco da Gama retraced Dias’s route, reached Mozambique, and sailed east to establish an ocean route to India. King Manuel I of Portugal anointed himself “Lord of Guinea and of the navigation and commerce of Ethiopia, Arabia, Persia, and India.” Other European monarchs disparaged him as “The Grocer King.”^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Gama’s Impact on the Spice Trade
Vasco da Gama’s arrival in Calicut on May 20, 1498, broke the Venetian-Arab monopoly on the spice trade that had endured for centuries. Calicut was the hub of the pepper trade on the Malabar Coast — a bustling emporium where Arab, Gujarati, and Chinese merchants exchanged goods from across Asia. The Portuguese, under Gama and subsequent commanders, systematically redirected the flow of spices around Africa, bypassing the Red Sea and Levant routes that had funnelled Asian spices through Arab middlemen to Venice and the Mediterranean markets.^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart]
The economic consequences were profound. Pepper (pimenta), cinnamon, ginger, cloves, and nutmeg — previously subject to the markups of twelve or more intermediaries between the Moluccas and a European kitchen — could now be shipped directly from India to Lisbon. Portuguese carracks arriving in the Tagus estuary with their holds full of spices could realise profits of 250–400%. This fundamentally shifted the economic centre of gravity from the Mediterranean to the Atlantic. Venice’s share of the spice trade collapsed from virtual monopoly to a fraction of its former volume within decades; Lisbon replaced Alexandria and Venice as the spice capital of Europe.^[source: career-legend-vasco-da-gama-subrahmanyam]

Pope Alexander VI’s Inter Caetera (1493) and the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494)
On June 7, 1494, Pope Alexander VI — a Spaniard born Rodrigo de Borja, of the Borgia family — divided the world in half, bestowing the western portion on Spain and the eastern on Portugal. Responding to appeals from King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella (the “Catholic Monarchs”), the pope issued papal bulls establishing a line of demarcation between Spanish and Portuguese territories. The line extended from the North Pole to the South Pole, located one hundred leagues (about four hundred miles) west of the Cape Verde Islands. Spain received exclusive rights to lands west of the line; Portugal was to keep to the east.^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Rather than settling disputes, this arrangement touched off a furious race between the two nations to claim new lands and control trade routes. The bickering continued as diplomats convened at Tordesillas in northwestern Spain. The Portuguese prevailed on the Spanish to move the line 270 leagues further west, so that it now lay 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands (approximately 46° 30’ W by modern reckoning). This placed the boundary in the middle of the Atlantic, roughly halfway between the Cape Verde Islands and Hispaniola, and — critically — allowed Portugal to claim the newly discovered land of Brazil. Pope Julius II confirmed the changes in 1506.^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
The treaty created more problems than it solved. Cosmologists could not determine longitude — nor would they for another two hundred years — so the line’s location was impossible to fix. The treaty failed to specify whether the line extended around the entire globe or bisected just the Western Hemisphere. Maps of 1494 mixed geography with mythology, adding phantom continents while neglecting real ones. Bergreen describes the Treaty of Tordesillas as “not even a line drawn in the sand; it was written in water.”^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]

Magellan’s Proposal: A Westward Spanish End-Run
A generation after Columbus, King Charles I of Spain (later Holy Roman Emperor Charles V) resumed the quest to establish a Spanish global empire. Ferdinand Magellan, a Portuguese nobleman who had been humiliated and rejected by King Manuel I of Portugal, offered himself and his plan to the Spanish crown.
Magellan’s proposal was elegant in its simplicity: if the Portuguese controlled the eastern route around Africa to the Spice Islands, Spain could reach them by sailing westward, finding a passage through or around South America. This would place the Moluccas within the Spanish hemisphere as defined by the Treaty of Tordesillas — or so Magellan argued. He brought letters from his friend Francisco Serrao, a Portuguese explorer who had reached Ternate in the Moluccas in 1512 and whose letters placed the Spice Islands far to the east of their true position, squarely within the Spanish sphere. Magellan displayed a globe or map depicting his planned route, invoking seven years of service in Portugal’s eastern empire.^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Magellan’s conception of the world was fatally inaccurate. Inspired by Ptolemy, he underestimated the size of the Pacific Ocean; his estimated route came to only half the actual distance. Had he comprehended the true size of the Pacific, its currents, storms, and reefs, it is unlikely he would have dared to mount the expedition.^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]

The March 1518 Contract with Charles V
On March 22, 1518, King Charles I offered Magellan and his partner, the cosmographer Ruy Faleiro, a contract “regarding the discovery of the Spice Islands.” The terms were remarkable:

A ten-year exclusive on voyages to the Spice Islands (though Charles did not honour this promise, dispatching a follow-up expedition only six years later)
One-twentieth of all lands and islands discovered
The title of Lieutenant and Governor of said lands and islands, inheritable by their heirs in freehold
Five ships: two of 130 tons, two of 90 tons, and one of 60 tons, supplied for two years
Magellan’s salary of 50,000 maravedis plus 8,000 monthly (paid directly to his wife Beatriz by royal order)

King Charles enjoined Magellan to respect Portugal’s territorial rights under the Treaty of Tordesillas, but in practice the young king intended to bend the treaty to Spain’s advantage by insisting the Spice Islands lay within the Spanish hemisphere — a point impossible to either prove or disprove.^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
The total expedition cost was 8,751,125 maravedis, of which the king’s share was 6,454,209. The financier Cristobal de Haro, representing the Fugger banking dynasty of Augsburg, advanced much of the money at 14% interest, expecting a profit of 250%.^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]

The 1529 Treaty of Saragossa
After Magellan’s death at Mactan and the return of the Victoria (the only ship of five to complete the circumnavigation), King Charles launched a series of follow-up expeditions to the Moluccas — the second Armada de Molucca under Loaysa and Elcano (1525), a third under Sebastian Cabot, and a fourth under Hernando Cortes from Mexico. All met with disaster. The second armada lost four of five ships; only 8 of 450 men returned to Spain. ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Desperately short of cash from fighting the French and with the Fugger dynasty refusing further backing, King Charles could no longer fund expeditions. He turned to diplomacy, inviting Portugal to join a commission and asking the Vatican to arbitrate. Ultimately, in 1529, Charles borrowed 350,000 ducats from King Joao III of Portugal, pledging as security the Moluccas and all islands lying to the east. Both nations signed the Treaty of Saragossa, ending the epic struggle for control of the spice trade. Just seven years after Magellan’s voyage, facing bankruptcy, Charles gave up the Spice Islands and returned them to Portugal. “In matters of empire,” Bergreen observes, “everything had its price.” ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]

Gama’s Spice Trading: From the Velho Journal
The Velho journal provides the only first-hand account of the spices Gama encountered and the specific terms of trade.
The First Voyage: Samples, Not Cargo
Gama’s first voyage returned with relatively modest quantities of pepper and cinnamon — enough to prove the route existed but not enough to transform the Portuguese economy. The journal records that the real prize was the route itself: the Calicut spices — pepper, ginger, cinnamon, cloves, and nutmeg — were all available in abundance, and the prices were a fraction of Venetian market rates. The return cargo was largely samples brought to demonstrate the commercial potential: the spices Gama loaded, stored in the holds of the worm-eaten São Gabriel and Berrio, sold for sixty times the cost of the expedition when they reached Lisbon. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
Spice Prices at Alexandria
Appendix C of the Hakluyt edition reproduces a price list from Alexandria, preserved in the Velho journal, showing the Mediterranean prices that the Portuguese aimed to undercut. The list includes the values of pepper, ginger, cinnamon, cloves, and other spices at the great Levantine emporium. These prices — the result of the twelve-hand chain of markups — were the benchmark against which Portuguese direct shipping would be measured. The price of pepper at Alexandria was roughly ten times the price at Calicut; the profit margin for direct shipping was enormous. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt, Appendix C]
The Second Voyage: Volume and Violence
On the second voyage (1502-1503), Gama returned with a heavily armed fleet of twenty ships. The objective was not merely to trade but to enforce. Gama bombarded Calicut, seized merchant vessels, and established factories at Cochin and Cannanore. The spices loaded on the second voyage were measured in tons rather than samples — pepper, cinnamon, and ginger filled the holds of the returning fleet. Subrahmanyam notes that the second voyage was the first time the Portuguese demonstrated they could move spices in volumes sufficient to break the Venetian monopoly, rather than simply proving the route existed. ^[source: career-legend-vasco-da-gama-subrahmanyam]

Portuguese Monopoly Enforcement: The Cartaz System
After Gama’s voyages, Portugal moved quickly to control not just the spice trade at its sources but the entire shipping network of the Indian Ocean. The instrument of this control was the cartaz system.
How the Cartaz Worked
Any ship trading in the Indian Ocean — Asian, Arab, or African — required a Portuguese safe-conduct pass (cartaz) proving that the vessel had paid the required duties and was carrying only permitted goods. Ships without a cartaz were subject to seizure, their cargoes confiscated, and their crews often killed or enslaved. The Portuguese navy patrolled the key chokepoints: the strait of Hormuz (controlling the Persian Gulf route), the coast of Malabar (the pepper ports), and the Strait of Malacca (the gateway to the Spice Islands). ^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart]
The cartaz system was enforced by a network of fortified trading posts (feitorias) — at Cochin, Cannanore, Goa, Malacca, and Hormuz — each armed with artillery and garrisoned with Portuguese soldiers. The Estado da Índia, as this network was known, was the first European colonial empire in Asia: a maritime empire of controlled ports and enforced trade routes, not territories.
The Carreira da Índia
The Carreira da Índia (India Run) was the annual convoy system that carried spices from India to Portugal. From 1503, Portuguese carracks sailed in convoy, protected by armed escorts, following the route Gama had pioneered: from Lisbon around the Cape of Good Hope, up the East African coast, and across the Indian Ocean to Cochin or Goa. The return voyage carried the year’s spice crop — pepper, cinnamon, ginger, and cloves — to Lisbon, where the Casa da Índia auctioned the cargo at fixed prices.
The convoy system was necessary because the spice route was vulnerable not only to storms and shipwreck — which claimed an estimated 30% of ships on the India run — but also to attack by rival European powers. The Carreira was the logistical backbone of the Portuguese spice monopoly, and it operated for over a century with remarkable consistency. ^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart]
The Economic Impact
The direct shipping of spices eliminated twelve intermediaries and their cumulative markups. Lisbon replaced Venice as the spice capital of Europe. The price of pepper in European markets fell by more than half within a decade of Gama’s first voyage. The Portuguese crown’s share of the spice trade — collected through duties at the Casa da Índia — became the largest single source of royal revenue, funding Portuguese operations in Asia, Africa, and Brazil. ^[source: career-legend-vasco-da-gama-subrahmanyam]

The English Entry: Drake at Ternate (1579)
Nearly a century after the Portuguese breakthrough, an English ship finally reached the Spice Islands. Francis Drake, on his circumnavigation of 1577–1580, arrived at the Moluccas in November 1579 — the first Englishman to reach the source of the spice trade.
The Ternate Alliance
Drake anchored at Ternate, one of the two great clove-producing islands of the Moluccas (the other being Tidore). The Sultan of Ternate, Sultan Babu, was a bitter enemy of the Portuguese, who had established themselves on neighbouring Tidore and were attempting to monopolise the clove trade. Babu welcomed the English as potential allies. Drake negotiated a trade agreement: the English would receive cloves and other spices in exchange for protection against the Portuguese. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
The First English Spice Cargo
The Golden Hind loaded six tons of cloves at Ternate — the first English spice cargo from the East Indies. Drake also took on samples of nutmeg, mace, and other spices. The cloves alone were worth a fortune; they were carried across the Indian Ocean, around the Cape of Good Hope, and back to Plymouth as part of the most valuable cargo ever brought to England. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Significance
Drake’s trade agreement at Ternate was the first breach in the Portuguese monopoly on the Spice Islands trade. It demonstrated that the Portuguese could not defend their monopoly against a determined European rival. The cloves of Ternate, brought to London and sold at enormous profit, proved that England could enter the spice trade directly — a lesson that would drive the formation of the East India Company two decades later. The agreement also gave England an ally in the Moluccas, a foothold in the most lucrative trade of the age.
But Drake’s success was not sustained. His hope of establishing regular English trade with Ternate was cut short by the Spanish Armada and the Anglo-Spanish war. It would be the Dutch — not the English — who would ultimately break the Portuguese monopoly in the East Indies, establishing the Dutch East India Company (VOC) in 1602. Drake’s voyage proved the route existed; the Dutch proved it could be commercially exploited.

Pigafetta’s First-Hand Descriptions of the Spices and Spice Trade
Pigafetta’s journal, the only surviving eyewitness account of the expedition, provides the first detailed European descriptions of the spice plants themselves — their appearance, cultivation, harvest, and trade value. His observations at Tidor in November–December 1521 are the earliest recorded European descriptions of these commodities at their source.
Cloves at Tidor
Pigafetta went ashore specifically to observe the clove harvest: “That same day, I went ashore to see how the clove grows. The clove tree is tall and as thick as a man’s body or thereabout. Its branches spread out somewhat widely in the middle, but at the top they have the shape of a summit. Its leaves resemble those of the laurel, and the bark is olive coloured. The cloves grow at the end of the twigs, ten or twenty in a cluster. Those trees have generally more cloves on one side than on the other, according to the weather conditions. When the cloves sprout they are white, when ripe, red, and when dried, black.” He recorded that cloves are gathered twice per year, at Christmas and midsummer, and that each individual possesses his own trees “although he does not cultivate them.” ^[source: pigafetta_magellan.txt]
Nutmeg and Mace
Pigafetta described nutmeg trees growing alongside the cloves: “The tree resembles our walnut tree, and has leaves like it. When the nut is gathered it is as large as a small quince, with the same sort of down, and it is of the same color. Its first rind is as thick as the green rind of our walnut. Under that there is a thin layer, under which is found the mace, which is a brilliant red and is wrapped about the rind of the nut, and within that is the nutmeg.” ^[source: pigafetta_magellan.txt]
Ginger
“Ginger is found throughout those islands: we ate it green like bread. Ginger is not a tree, but a small plant that puts forth from the ground certain shoots a span in length that resemble reeds, and whose leaves resemble those of the reed, except that they are narrower. Those shoots are worthless, but the roots form the ginger, and it is not so strong green as dry. Those people dry it in lime, for otherwise it would not keep.” ^[source: pigafetta_magellan.txt]
The Sultan’s Palace and the Trade at Tidor
Pigafetta described the court of the Sultan of Tidore, who maintained a large house with two hundred women and a like number of female servants. The king ate alone or with his chief wife “in a high place like a gallery.” Trade was brisk: “for ten cubits of red cloth of very good quality, they gave us one bahar of cloves, which is equivalent to four quintals and six pounds (one quintal is one hundred pounds).” Other exchange rates included fifteen hatchets for a bahar, thirty-five glass drinking cups for a bahar, forty caps for a bahar, and one quintal of bronze for a bahar. ^[source: pigafetta_magellan.txt]
Loading of the Victoria
The Victoria loaded its precious cargo of cloves at Tidore. The ship was so heavily laden that the king of Batjan’s gift of ten bahars of cloves could not be taken — “the ships could not carry them as they were so heavily laden.” Before departure, the crew had to unload sixty quintals of cloves, fearing the ship would “break open.” On December 21, 1521, the Victoria departed with “forty-seven men and thirteen Indians,” its holds full of the spices that would prove the expedition’s commercial success and establish the value of the Spice Islands trade. ^[source: pigafetta_magellan.txt]

Chronology

Relationship to Other Entities

Ferdinand Magellan — The navigator who conceived and led the westward expedition to the Spice Islands
Magellan Ships — The five ships of the Armada de Molucca
Magellan Crew — The men who sailed under Magellan’s command

concepts/voyage-of-the-golden-hind.title: Voyage of The Golden Hind
concepts/voyage-of-the-golden-hind.content:
Voyage of the Golden Hind (1577-1580)

Drake’s circumnavigation route (orange). Plymouth → Strait of Magellan → Pacific raids (Valparaiso, Callao, Cacafuego) → Nova Albion (California) → Ternate (Moluccas) → Celebes → Cape of Good Hope → Plymouth. The outward route is shown solid, with key ports and raid sites marked.
Overview
Francis Drake’s circumnavigation of the globe (1577-1580) was the first English voyage to sail around the world and only the second complete circumnavigation in history, following the Magellan-Elcano expedition (1519-1522). It was a voyage of exploration, diplomacy, and — above all — privateering, combining the discovery of new lands with the systematic plunder of Spanish shipping along the Pacific coast of the Americas. Drake returned to England with immense treasure, was knighted by Queen Elizabeth I, and became a national hero. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Planning and Preparation
The Strategic Context
The voyage was conceived in the context of rising tensions between England and Spain. Philip II’s Spain controlled vast territories in the Americas and claimed exclusive access to the Pacific Ocean. Elizabeth I, while formally at peace with Spain, was increasingly willing to challenge Spanish monopolies by supporting English adventurers. Drake’s voyage was a deliberate provocation — a strike at the heart of Spain’s undefended Pacific empire. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Backers and Secrecy
The expedition was financed by a syndicate of investors including prominent figures at Elizabeth’s court:

Sir Francis Walsingham (the queen’s principal secretary)
Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester
Sir Christopher Hatton (the lord chancellor)
The queen herself, who contributed 1,000 crowns

No formal commission was issued; the queen’s sanction was given verbally. The voyage was shrouded in secrecy. A fictitious cover story was circulated that the ships were bound for Alexandria and Constantinople on a trading voyage. Even the mariners were recruited on that basis. “These devices seem to have worked, because it was not until after Drake had sailed that Spanish suspicions were aroused; even then none guessed his true destination.” ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
The Fleet
The Pelican (later Golden Hind)
Drake’s flagship was the Pelican, built in 1576 at Plymouth. She was later renamed the Golden Hind in August 1578 as the fleet entered the Strait of Magellan. The new name honoured Sir Christopher Hatton, whose family crest featured a golden hind (a female deer). ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
The Golden Hind was a small ship by modern standards — about 150 tons burden and approximately 80 feet from stem to sternpost. She carried an armament of eighteen brass and iron guns and was described as a good sailer with a sturdy hull, sheathed with extra planking to protect against rot. She was designed to carry up to eighty men. Despite her modest size, she would go on to become one of the most famous ships in maritime history, her portrait eventually gracing the British halfpenny. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Other Vessels
The expedition originally consisted of five ships:

Pelican (flagship, later Golden Hind) — ~150 tons, commanded by Drake
Elizabeth — ~80 tons, commanded by Captain John Winter
Swan — a flyboat, commanded by John Chester
Marigold — a pinnace, commanded by Captain John Thomas
Christopher — a small ship, commanded by Tom Moone

The fleet was later supplemented by a captured Portuguese ship. The company included mariners, artisans (coopers, carpenters, a blacksmith), and a complement of soldiers. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
The Voyage
Departure from Plymouth
The expedition made its first start in November 1577 but was forced back by bad weather. On 13 December 1577, Drake departed Plymouth for the second time. The fleet ran south-westerly along the coast of north-west Africa, quickly making it clear that the Mediterranean was not their destination. Some discontent arose among the crew, who had been told they were bound for Alexandria. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Atlantic Crossing
After calling at the Cape Verde Islands for provisions (obtained by force from the Portuguese), the fleet crossed the Atlantic and made landfall on the coast of Brazil. From there, they worked their way south along the South American coast toward the Strait of Magellan. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
The Strait of Magellan (August-September 1578)
The Cape of Virgins, marking the entrance to the Magellan Strait, was sighted on 20 August 1578. Drake held a ceremony, saluting the queen, conducting a religious service, and rechristening his flagship the Golden Hind. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
The passage through the strait took only 14 days — remarkably fast for such a treacherous waterway. The Strait of Magellan was so dangerous that it had fallen into disuse by the Spanish. No European had ever been south of Cape Horn; the geography before Drake’s voyage simply did not know of it. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
The Storms and Dispersion
Immediately after clearing the strait and entering the Pacific, the fleet was struck by ferocious storms that scattered the ships. The Marigold went down with all hands. The Elizabeth, under Captain John Winter, turned back and eventually returned to England through the Strait of Magellan. Only the Golden Hind continued alone up the Pacific coast of South America. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Raiding the Pacific Coast
For the first time, an English ship was operating in the Pacific, which the Spanish considered their private lake. The undefended Spanish settlements were taken completely by surprise:

Valparaiso: Drake raided the port, capturing a ship laden with wine and gold.
Callao: The port of Lima, the capital of Spanish Peru. Drake entered the harbour and cut the cables of the ships anchored there, though he found little treasure.
Capture of the Cacafuego: Off the coast of Ecuador, Drake captured the treasure ship Nuestra Senora de la Concepcion, nicknamed the Cacafuego (“Spitfire”). She had left Callao for Panama richly laden with silver. The prize yielded an immense haul — the richest single capture of Drake’s career. The Spaniards irreverently rechristened her the Cacafuego; Sugden notes that from a prize Drake “learned that he was three days behind her,” but he soon caught up and “sent the Nuestra Senora de la Concepcion on her way” — emptied of her treasure. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]

Nova Albion (California)
After completing his raiding along the South American coast, Drake sailed north to avoid further Spanish pursuit and to search for a passage back to the Atlantic (the fabled Northwest Passage). He explored the coast of present-day California, which he claimed for England under the name Nova Albion (“New England”), “in respect of the white banks and cliffs, which lie” — a reference to the white cliffs of Dover. He erected a post with a plaque claiming the territory for Queen Elizabeth. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
The English spent several weeks in the area, careening the Golden Hind and trading with the local Native American population. The specific location of Nova Albion was kept secret to prevent the Spanish from finding it, and the exact site (generally believed to be Drake’s Bay, north of San Francisco) remains debated. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Crossing the Pacific
From California, Drake struck westward across the vast Pacific Ocean. His navigational knowledge was limited for this region — “for many regions he had no guidance” — yet he successfully navigated to the Moluccas (the Spice Islands) in the East Indies. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
The Moluccas and Ternate
In the Moluccas, Drake made contact with Sultan Babu of Ternate, one of the most powerful rulers in the region. The sultan had no love for the Portuguese, who had driven him from his islands of Ternate, Motir, and Maquiam and were entrenched on neighbouring Tidore. Babu therefore welcomed the English as potential allies against the Portuguese. A trade agreement was reached, opening the possibility of English access to the valuable spice trade. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Drake was invited to the fortress of Ternate at the port of Talangam, where he was “well received and provided with certain supplies.” ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Grounding in the Celebes Sea
After leaving Ternate, Drake sailed westward, planning to pass around Celebes (modern Sulawesi) into the Celebes Sea and Makassar Strait, where “the greatest peril of the whole voyage” awaited. The Golden Hind grounded on a reef in the Celebes Sea. The ship was stuck fast, and the situation appeared desperate. “Ahead the greatest peril of the whole voyage” threatened, “the warm green seas that washed the east coast of Celebes, its ragged and unknown reefs.” ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Through a combination of skill, luck, and determination, the crew managed to free the ship by lightening her (throwing cargo overboard) and waiting for the tide. The Golden Hind survived, though it was a near-disaster. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Return Journey
The Golden Hind crossed the Indian Ocean, rounded the Cape of Good Hope, and called at Sierra Leone on the west coast of Africa for provisions. From there, she sailed north across the Atlantic toward England. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Arrival at Plymouth
On 26 September 1580, fishermen working their nets in the English Channel sighted a small, heavily laden ship making for Plymouth Sound. As she passed, a man aboard hailed the fishermen with a strange question: “Is the queen alive?”
She was alive and in good health. The Golden Hind sailed home.
Drake had been away for almost three years. He had plundered the King of Spain, and his hold was full of treasure. His first concern was whether Elizabeth still reigned, for if the Catholic Mary Queen of Scots had succeeded to the throne, “his head sat loosely on his shoulders.” ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Aftermath
The Treasure
The treasure brought back by the Golden Hind was immense. The cargo of the Nuestra Senora de la Concepcion alone was valued at a fortune. The total haul made Drake and his investors rich and significantly boosted the English treasury. The treasure was eventually stored at the Tower of London, but only after a political struggle between Drake’s supporters (Walsingham, Leicester, Hatton) and those who favoured restitution to Spain. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Knighthood
Queen Elizabeth interviewed Drake privately for over six hours aboard the Golden Hind. She heard “stirring stories that the queen did not fail to appreciate, great tales of adventure, of the Elizabeth Islands and Nova Albion, of the capture of the treasure ship and the trade agreement with Ternate, tales the like of which none had brought her before.” On 4 April 1581, Elizabeth knighted Sir Francis Drake aboard the Golden Hind, making him the second Englishman to circumnavigate the globe. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Historical Significance

First English circumnavigation and second overall after Magellan-Elcano
Extended English knowledge of geography, particularly the Pacific and the Spice Islands
Established the viability of English long-distance voyages
Demonstrated the vulnerability of Spain’s Pacific possessions
Laid groundwork for future English claims in North America (Nova Albion)
Initiated English contact with the Spice Islands and the Moluccas
Made Drake a national hero and a symbol of English maritime ambition ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]

entities/alvaro-velho.title: Alvaro Velho
entities/alvaro-velho.content:
Alvaro Velho
Álvaro Velho is the traditionally attributed author of the Roteiro (Journal) of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama, the only first-hand account of the 1497–1499 expedition to India. His identity is uncertain, and the attribution rests on tradition and circumstantial evidence. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt] ^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart]
Identity and Role
Velho is believed to have been a soldier on Vasco da Gama’s first voyage, possibly serving in a capacity that allowed him to observe and record the journey’s events. The journal describes him as being present on the expedition and witnessing the events firsthand. Ravenstein, in his introduction to the Hakluyt Society edition, discusses the evidence for Velho’s identity — noting that the name ‘Álvaro Velho’ appears in other Portuguese records from the period but without definitive connection to the journal. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt] ^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart]
The Roteiro (Journal)
Velho’s manuscript, called the Roteiro (itinerary or sea journal), is the only surviving first-hand narrative of the first voyage. It provides a detailed day-by-day account of the fleet’s progress, including navigational observations, descriptions of the peoples encountered along the African coast, the reception at Calicut, and the harrowing return voyage. The manuscript survived in a single copy, discovered and published long after the voyage. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt] ^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart]
Significance
As the only direct eyewitness account of Gama’s pioneering voyage, Velho’s journal is the foundational primary source for all historical scholarship on the first voyage. Subsequent historians, including Hart and Subrahmanyam, rely on it heavily. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt] ^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart]

entities/barcelona-seville-valladolid.title: Barcelona, Seville, and Valladolid — Columbus's Spanish Cities
entities/barcelona-seville-valladolid.content:
Barcelona, Seville, and Valladolid — Columbus’s Spanish Cities
Three Spanish cities mark the triumphal peak, the declining years, and the final end of Christopher Columbus’s career in Spain: Barcelona, where he received his greatest honor; Seville, where he fell ill and petitioned in vain; and Valladolid, where he died.

Barcelona — Triumphal Reception (April 1493)
Barcelona, at the time the seat of the royal court of Ferdinand and Isabella, was the scene of Columbus’s most magnificent public honor. After his return from the first voyage, he was commanded by the sovereigns to present himself at court. Having made dispositions at Seville, he set out for Barcelona, taking with him six Taíno Indians, the various curiosities and natural productions of the New World, and samples of gold. ^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book V Ch. VI]
Journey to Barcelona
The fame of his discovery had resounded throughout the nation. Columbus’s journey resembled the progress of a sovereign: wherever he passed, inhabitants poured forth to line the roads and throng the villages. In the large towns, streets, windows, and balconies were filled with spectators acclaiming him. His progress was continually impeded by multitudes pressing to see him and the Indians, who were regarded with as much astonishment as if they had been natives of another planet.^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book V Ch. VI]
Ceremonial Reception
It was about the middle of April 1493 that Columbus arrived at Barcelona. Every preparation had been made for a solemn and magnificent reception. The beauty and serenity of the spring weather in that favored climate added splendor to the ceremony.
The procession entered the city in Roman-triumph style:

First came the Indians, painted in their savage fashion and decorated with national ornaments of gold
Then various kinds of live parrots, stuffed birds and animals of unknown species, and rare plants
A conspicuous display of Indian coronets, bracelets, and other decorations of gold
Finally Columbus on horseback, surrounded by a brilliant cavalcade of Spanish chivalry

The streets were almost impassable from the multitude; windows and balconies were crowded; even the roofs were covered with spectators. The event was looked upon as a vast and signal dispensation of Providence in reward for the piety of the monarchs.^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book V Ch. VI]
Audience with the Sovereigns
Ferdinand and Isabella had ordered their throne to be placed in public under a rich canopy of brocade of gold in a vast and splendid saloon. There the King and Queen awaited his arrival, seated in state with Prince Juan beside them, attended by the dignitaries of their court and the principal nobility of Castile, Valencia, Catalonia, and Aragon.
When Columbus entered the hall, the sovereigns rose as if receiving a person of the highest rank. He bent his knees to kiss their hands, but they raised him in the most gracious manner and ordered him to seat himself in their presence — a rare honor in that proud and punctilious court.
At their request, Columbus gave an account of the most striking events of his voyage and a description of the islands he had discovered. He displayed the specimens of unknown birds and animals, rare plants of medicinal and aromatic virtues, native gold in dust and crude masses or labored into barbaric ornaments, and above all the natives themselves. All these he pronounced mere harbingers of greater discoveries yet to make.
When he finished, the sovereigns sank to their knees and, with clasped hands raised to heaven and eyes filled with tears of joy and gratitude, poured forth thanks to God. The anthem of Te Deum laudamus was chanted by the choir of the royal chapel. As the venerable Las Casas wrote, “it seemed as if in that hour they communicated with celestial delights.”^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book V Ch. VI]
Sojourn at Barcelona
For many days Columbus was the object of universal curiosity; wherever he appeared he was surrounded by an admiring multitude. During his sojourn at Barcelona, the sovereigns took every occasion to bestow personal marks of their high consideration:

He was admitted at all times to the royal presence
The Queen delighted to converse with him on his enterprises
The King appeared on horseback with Prince Juan on one side and Columbus on the other
A coat of arms was assigned to him, quartering the royal castles and lions with a group of islands surrounded by waves
He was permitted to establish a mayorazgo (hereditary succession to his titles and estates)

Flush with success, Columbus also revived his pious scheme for the deliverance of the Holy Sepulchre, vowing to furnish an army of four thousand horse and fifty thousand foot within seven years for a crusade to rescue Jerusalem.^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book V Ch. VII]

Seville — Illness and Petition (1504–1505)
Seville (Sevilla), the great inland port on the Guadalquivir River in Andalusia, was Columbus’s primary residence in Spain during his final years. It was the city from which he organized his second voyage in 1493, and to which he returned after his fourth and final voyage in 1504.
Return and Residence
After the disastrous fourth voyage, Columbus arrived back in Spain in November 1504, physically worn and burdened by the loss of his official positions and the collapse of his governorship. He took up residence in Seville, where he had long maintained connections. The city served as the administrative center for the affairs of the Indies, and Columbus’s brother Bartholomew Columbus had also spent time there.^[source: irving-columbus-vol4.md, Book XVIII Ch. II]
Illness at Seville
Following his return, Columbus’s health deteriorated sharply. He suffered from gout and arthritis, the cumulative effects of decades of exposure and hardship at sea. His illness confined him much of the time and prevented him from personally pressing his claims at court with the energy he would have wished. Irving describes him during this period as “worn down by malady and vexation, and emaciated by care.”^[source: irving-columbus-vol4.md, Book XVIII Ch. II]
Petition to the Crown
From his sickbed in Seville, Columbus launched a sustained and ultimately fruitless campaign to restore his titles and revenues. He wrote lengthy letters and memorials to King Ferdinand, invoking the Capitulations of Santa Fe of 1492, which had granted him the titles of Admiral, Viceroy, and Governor of all lands he might discover, with a tenth of all revenues.
His petitions were met with evasion and delay. The Crown, under the influence of Bishop Juan Rodriguez de Fonseca and other adversaries, was reluctant to restore the extraordinary powers granted to Columbus a decade earlier. The legal and political obstacles raised against his claims proved insurmountable.^[source: irving-columbus-vol4.md, Book XVIII Ch. II]
Death of Queen Isabella (November 26, 1504)
The death of Queen Isabella in November 1504 was a devastating blow to Columbus’s cause. Isabella had been his most steadfast patron at court, the one who had originally championed his enterprise against the doubts of Ferdinand and the Talavera commission. With her death, Columbus lost his most powerful advocate. King Ferdinand, never as enthusiastic about Columbus’s privileges, became the sole arbiter of his claims and proved far less sympathetic.^[source: irving-columbus-vol4.md, Book XVIII Ch. II]
Journey to Court
In May 1505, Columbus — still suffering from illness and able to travel only with difficulty — journeyed from Seville to the court of King Ferdinand at Segovia for a personal audience. There he pleaded his case again, offering to accompany the king on any expedition and even proposing to finance a crusade to the Holy Land from his prospective revenues. Ferdinand, however, offered only vague promises; the titles and governance of the Indies would never be restored to Columbus.^[source: irving-columbus-vol4.md, Book XVIII Ch. III]

Valladolid — Death of Columbus (May 20, 1506)
Valladolid, a city in the region of Old Castile on the Pisuerga River, was the place where Christopher Columbus died on May 20, 1506. The city was then a frequent residence of the royal court and lay approximately 120 miles north of Madrid.
Final Illness
After the failure of his petitions at court, Columbus’s health continued to decline. He followed the peripatetic royal court in its movements, and in early 1506 he was at Valladolid, where the court was then residing. There, in a modest house, he took to his bed for the last time. His final illness was a combination of gout, arthritis, and the general physical exhaustion of a man who had spent decades at sea and was now about 55 years old.^[source: irving-columbus-vol4.md, Book XVIII Ch. IV]
Death and Testamentary Arrangements
On Ascension Day, May 20, 1506, Christopher Columbus died. His last days were spent in the presence of his two sons:

Diego Columbus — his legitimate son and heir, the future second Admiral of the Indies and Viceroy
Fernando (Ferdinand) Columbus — his natural son, the scholar and bibliophile who would later write his biography and amass the great Biblioteca Colombina in Seville

Also present were a few faithful servants and, according to some accounts, his brother Bartholomew.
In his final testamentary arrangements, Columbus reaffirmed the provisions of the mayorazgo (entailed estate) he had established at Seville in 1498. He directed that his remains be buried in the Cathedral of Santo Domingo in Hispaniola, the land he had discovered — a wish that would take several decades to fulfill and would involve multiple transfers of his bones across the Atlantic.^[source: irving-columbus-vol4.md, Book XVIII Ch. IV]
Circumstances of His Passing
The death of Columbus in Valladolid was a modest affair, far removed from the triumphal reception at Barcelona thirteen years earlier. He died in relative obscurity, his titles still unreinstated and his fortunes diminished. The court of King Ferdinand, preoccupied with other affairs, took little public notice. It was not until years later that the full measure of his achievement would be widely recognized.
Subsequent Translations of His Remains
Columbus’s body was originally buried in Valladolid, but his remains were later moved — first to the Monastery of La Cartuja in Seville, then (in 1542) to the Cathedral of Santo Domingo in Hispaniola, and finally (in 1795) to Havana, Cuba. Following the Cuban Revolution, they are now believed to rest in the Cathedral of Seville.^[source: irving-columbus-vol4.md, Appendix No. I]

entities/bartholomeu-dias.title: Bartolomeu Dias
entities/bartholomeu-dias.content:
Bartolomeu Dias
Bartholomeu Dias de Novaes (c. 1450–1500) was a Portuguese navigator and explorer who became the first European to sail around the southern tip of Africa, the Cape of Good Hope, in 1488. His voyage proved that a sea route to the Indian Ocean existed, laying the groundwork for Vasco da Gama’s later expedition to India. ^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart] ^[source: career-legend-vasco-da-gama-subrahmanyam]
The Voyage to the Cape (1487–1488)
Dias commanded an expedition of three ships that departed Lisbon in August 1487. He sailed down the African coast, passed the southernmost point of the continent, and rounded what he initially named the ‘Cape of Storms’ (Cabo Tormentoso). After rounding the cape, he sailed up the east coast of Africa as far as the Great Fish River (Rio do Infante) before his crew compelled him to turn back. King John II later renamed the cape the ‘Cape of Good Hope’ (Cabo da Boa Esperança) because of the optimism it raised for reaching India. ^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart]
Contribution to Gama’s Fleet
After returning to Portugal, Dias supervised the construction and preparation of Vasco da Gama’s fleet for the first voyage. His expertise in ship design and navigation was instrumental in fitting out the vessels. He also accompanied the fleet part of the way, sailing to the Cape Verde Islands with da Gama before separating. ^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart] ^[source: career-legend-vasco-da-gama-subrahmanyam]
Later Voyage and Death
In 1500, Dias served as a captain in Pedro Álvares Cabral’s fleet bound for India. After the fleet reached Brazil and then turned east toward Africa, four ships were lost in a storm off the Cape of Good Hope — the very cape Dias had first rounded twelve years earlier. Dias perished in this storm. ^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart]
Family
Dias came from a family of navigators. He was possibly related to João Dias, who first doubled Cape Bojador in 1434. ^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart]

entities/bartholomew-columbus.title: Bartholomew Columbus
entities/bartholomew-columbus.content:
Bartholomew Columbus
Bartholomew Columbus (c. 1461–1514) was a Genoese navigator, cartographer, and colonial administrator who served as adelantado (lieutenant-governor) of Hispaniola under his older brother Christopher Columbus. A loyal and capable deputy, he governed the colony during the Admiral’s absences, led military campaigns against the native caciques Caonabo and Guarionex, and accompanied his brother on the fourth voyage. His strict and severe administration provoked the rebellion of Francisco Roldan, and he was arrested alongside Christopher and Diego Columbus by Francisco de Bobadilla in 1500 and returned to Spain in chains.

Early Career in Portugal
Bartholomew Columbus was the second of the four children of Domenico Colombo, a wool-comber of Genoa. He was the constant companion of his elder brother Christopher in youth, and like him, took early to the sea.^[source: irving_columbus_full.txt]
When Christopher Columbus left Portugal for Spain around 1485, he entrusted Bartholomew with a crucial mission: to travel to England and propose the westward project to King Henry VII of England. However, according to accounts by both Fernando Columbus and Bartolome de las Casas, Bartholomew did not proceed directly to England. Las Casas found a memorandum in Bartholomew’s handwriting suggesting that he first accompanied Bartholomew Diaz in 1486 on a Portuguese voyage along the coast of Africa, serving the king of Portugal. This expedition rounded the southern tip of Africa and discovered the Cape of Good Hope, returning to Lisbon in December 1487. The memorandum, written in a barbarous mixture of Latin and Spanish in the margin of a treatise on the form of the globe belonging to Christopher Columbus, recorded the voyage league by league and bore the note: “in all which, adds the writer, I was present.”^[source: irving_columbus_carvill_v2.txt, Book VIII Ch. I]

Mission to England
After the African voyage, Bartholomew Columbus proceeded to England to present his brother’s plan to King Henry VII. On his way, he was captured and plundered by a corsair and reduced to such poverty that he had to struggle for a mere subsistence for a long time by making sea charts, so that several years elapsed before he could make his application to the English monarch.^[source: irving_columbus_carvill_v2.txt, Book VIII Ch. I]
When the proposition was eventually made to Henry VII, it met with a more ready attention than from any other sovereign. An agreement was actually concluded with Bartholomew for the prosecution of the enterprise, and he departed for Spain to find his brother. Reaching Paris, he first received the joyful intelligence that the discovery had already been made — Christopher Columbus had returned to Spain in triumph. King Charles VIII of France, understanding Bartholomew was low in purse, furnished him with one hundred crowns to defray the expenses of his journey to Spain. He reached Seville just as his brother had departed on the second voyage. Bartholomew immediately repaired to court at Valladolid, taking with him his two nephews, Diego and Fernando. He was received with distinguished favour by Ferdinand and Isabella, who found him an able and accomplished navigator and gave him the command of three ships freighted with supplies for the colony, sending him to aid his brother.^[source: irving_columbus_carvill_v2.txt, Book VIII Ch. I]

Arrival in Hispaniola (1494)
Bartholomew Columbus reached the settlement of Isabella on the island of Hispaniola just after his brother’s departure for the coast of Cuba. The colony was suffering from famine and disease, and the admiral’s return in September 1494 brought a joyful reunion. Irving records that Columbus found at his bedside “his brother Bartholomew, the companion of his youth, his confidential coadjutor, and in a manner his second self, from whom he had been separated for several years.”^[source: irving_columbus_carvill_v2.txt, Book VIII Ch. I]

Character and Appointment as Adelantado
The character of Bartholomew Columbus is preserved by Las Casas from personal observation. He was:

Prompt, active, decided, and fearless — whatever he determined, he carried into instant execution, without regard to difficulty or danger.
Physically commanding — tall, muscular, vigorous, with an air of great authority but somewhat stern, lacking the sweetness and benignity that tempered the Admiral’s authoritative demeanour.
Stern in manner — there was a certain asperity in his temper and a dryness and abruptness in his manners that made him many enemies, yet he was of generous disposition, free from arrogance or malevolence, and as placable as he was brave.
A thorough seaman — understanding both the theory and practice of navigation, having been formed largely under the eye of the Admiral, and being little inferior to him in science. He was superior to the Admiral in the exercise of the pen, according to Las Casas, who had letters and manuscripts of both in his possession. He was acquainted with Latin though not highly educated, his knowledge being chiefly derived from varied experience and attentive observation.
Pragmatic and worldly — equally vigorous and penetrating in intellect with the Admiral but less enthusiastic in spirit and soaring in imagination, with less simplicity of heart. He surpassed Christopher in the subtle and adroit management of business, was more attentive to his interests, and had more of that worldly wisdom important in the ordinary concerns of life.^[source: irving_columbus_carvill_v2.txt, Book VIII Ch. I]

Anxious to relieve himself from the pressure of public business during his present malady, Columbus immediately invested his brother Bartholomew with the title and authority of Adelantado, an office equivalent to lieutenant-governor. Columbus considered himself entitled to do so from the articles of his arrangement with the sovereigns, but King Ferdinand later looked upon this as an undue assumption of power, a matter that gave great offence to that jealous monarch.^[source: irving_columbus_carvill_v2.txt, Book VIII Ch. I]

Campaigns against Caonabo
During Columbus’s absence exploring Cuba and Jamaica in 1494, the colony had fallen into disorder. The Carib cacique Caonabo, the most fierce and puissant of the native chieftains and the inveterate enemy of the white men, attacked the fortress of Santo Tomas. Alonso de Ojeda defended the post with a small force and subsequently lured Caonabo into captivity using a famous ruse involving polished manacles. Caonabo was brought to Isabella in chains.^[source: irving_columbus_carvill_v2.txt, Book VIII Ch. III–IV]
After Caonabo’s capture, Columbus marched into the Vega Real with 200 infantry, 20 cavalry, and dogs, routing the native forces. He imposed a system of tribute on the native population — every Indian over fourteen had to pay a hawk’s bell full of gold every three months — a system that proved unworkable and generated deep resentment.^[source: irving_columbus_carvill_v2.txt, Book VIII Ch. VI–VII]

Administration and Campaigns against Guarionex
When Columbus returned to Spain in April 1496, he left Bartholomew as adelantado with full governing authority over the colony. Under Bartholomew’s administration, Isabella was abandoned, and the settlement was moved to the southern coast at the mouth of the Ozema River, where the town of Santo Domingo was founded — the first permanent European settlement in the Americas.^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book IX Ch. I]
Bartholomew established a chain of fortified military posts across the island. The cacique Guarionex of the Royal Vega, who had initially been more tractable than Caonabo, grew restive under the Spanish tribute demands and the heavy hand of Spanish rule. He rose in rebellion in 1497, leading a major insurrection.
The Adelantado acted swiftly. He marched against Guarionex and defeated him in the Vega, but the cacique escaped and fled to the mountains of Ciguay. Bartholomew pursued him through forests and mountains in a gruelling campaign, eventually capturing Guarionex and ending organized native resistance in the northern part of the island.^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book XI Ch. II, VI–VII]

Expedition to Xaragua
After the revolt of Guarionex was suppressed, Bartholomew turned his attention to the western province of Xaragua, the most populous and extensive domain on the island, ruled by the female cacique Anacaona. Her brother, the sovereign Behechio, had recently died. The province was wealthy and described by Irving as having inhabitants “finely formed, with a nobler air, a more agreeable elocution, and more soft and graceful manners than the natives of the other parts of the island.”^[source: irving_columbus_carvill_v2.txt, Book XI Ch. III]
The Adelantado led an expedition into Xaragua in 1498, demonstrating Spanish military power while negotiating for the submission of the province. He established contact with Anacaona and her nobles, demanding tribute in recognition of Spanish sovereignty. The negotiations were outwardly peaceful but tense, and Bartholomew later returned to collect tribute from the province.^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book XI Ch. I, III]

The Roldan Rebellion
Upon Christopher Columbus’s return from the third voyage in August 1498, he found the colony in chaos. The Adelantado’s strict governance had created widespread discontent among the Spanish colonists. Francisco Roldan, the alcalde mayor (chief magistrate), organized a conspiracy in 1497 against the Columbus brothers, accusing them of tyranny, misgovernment, and favouring foreigners over native Castilians.
Roldan withdrew to Xaragua and established a rival government, allying himself with Anacaona and gathering malcontents. The Adelantado attempted to negotiate with Roldan but the rebel leader refused to submit. Columbus, weakened by illness and with no military option available, was forced into humiliating concessions — amnesty for Roldan and his followers, reinstatement of Roldan as alcalde mayor, and grants of land and native labour (encomiendas).^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book XI Ch. IV–V; irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XII Ch. I–V]
Fresh conspiracies followed. Hernando de Guevara and Adrian de Moxica hatched a new plot against the Adelantado. The conspiracy was discovered and suppressed: Moxica was captured and executed, and Guevara was imprisoned. But the persistence of rebellion demonstrated that the Columbus brothers’ authority had been fatally undermined.^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XII Ch. VIII]

Arrest and Return to Spain in Chains
The rebels who returned to Spain carried accounts that painted Columbus and his brothers as arrogant and oppressive foreigners unfit to govern. Their complaints found a receptive audience at court, where Bishop Juan Rodriguez de Fonseca and other enemies of Columbus had long been working against the Admiral. In 1500, King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella dispatched Francisco de Bobadilla as royal commissioner with full powers to investigate Columbus’s conduct.
Bobadilla arrived at San Domingo and, without any prior investigation, publicly read his commission, seized the fortress, took command of the colony, and ordered the seizure of the Columbus brothers’ property. He invited depositions from the very men who had rebelled under Roldan. Columbus was summoned from the fortress of Conception and, upon his return to San Domingo, was arrested and placed in chains.
Bartholomew and his younger brother Diego Columbus were arrested alongside the Admiral. Bobadilla clapped them all in irons. They were shipped to Spain as prisoners. The governor of the caravel refused to remove the chains despite Christopher’s age and infirmity, and Columbus famously refused to have his irons removed during the voyage, maintaining a dignified composure throughout the passage.^[source: irving-columbus-v3.md, Book XIII Ch. I–IV]
The arrival of the Columbus brothers in chains at Cadiz created a public outcry. Queen Isabella was outraged at their treatment. They were ordered released and summoned to court at Granada, where they were received with kindness. However, Columbus was never restored to his governorship, and Bartholomew’s authority in Hispaniola was permanently ended.^[source: irving-columbus-v3.md, Book XIV Ch. I]

Fourth Voyage
Bartholomew accompanied his brother on the fourth and final voyage (1502–1504). He was present during the exploration of the coasts of Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama (Veragua). When the two remaining ships were worm-riddled and beached on Jamaica, he played a critical role:

He led an inland expedition in Veragua, making contact with the native chief Quibian and learning of nearby gold mines.^[source: irving-columbus-v3.md, Book XV Ch. VI]
He led a preemptive expedition to surprise and capture Quibian when the natives conspired to attack the Spanish settlement on the River Belen.^[source: irving-columbus-v3.md, Book XV Ch. VII]
When the mutiny of Francisco de Porras broke out on Jamaica, Bartholomew led the loyal Spaniards against the mutineers in a pitched battle on the beach. Porras was defeated and captured, and the mutineers were pardoned by Columbus, restoring order among the castaways.^[source: irving-columbus-v3.md, Book XVI Ch. VI]

After the fourth voyage, Bartholomew Columbus returned to Spain with his brother. He died around 1514, predeceasing Christopher by several years (Christopher died in 1506). His later years were spent in relative obscurity, overshadowed by the eclipse of his brother’s fortunes.

entities/cadiz.title: Cadiz
entities/cadiz.content:
Cadiz


Top: Cadiz and other Iberian ports. Bottom: Drake’s 1587 raid — over 30 ships destroyed in the Bay of Cadiz, delaying the Armada by a year.
Overview
Cadiz is a major Spanish port city in Andalusia on the Atlantic coast. One of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in Europe, it was established by the Phoenicians as Gadir. In the Elizabethan era, Cadiz served as a primary assembly point for the Spanish treasure fleets from the Americas and, critically, for the Spanish Armada of 1588.
Drake’s Raid (1587)
Drake’s famous raid of 1587 saw him enter Cadiz harbor and destroy over 30 ships being assembled for the Armada, along with vast stores of supplies. Drake called the operation “singeing the King of Spain’s beard.” The raid delayed the Armada by a full year, giving England more time to prepare its defenses.
Strategic Significance

Primary assembly port for the Spanish Armada (1587-1588)
Wealthy hub for the Spanish American trade (silver, gold, spices)
Deep-water harbor capable of hosting large fleets
Sitting at the crossroads of Atlantic and Mediterranean maritime routes

Historical Background
Founded by Phoenician traders as Gadir around 1100 BCE, Cadiz is considered one of the oldest continuously inhabited settlements in Western Europe. It later came under Carthaginian and then Roman rule. Under the Romans it became a wealthy city known as Gades. After the fall of the Roman Empire, it passed through Visigothic and Moorish hands before being reconquered by Castile in the 13th century.

Provenance: Information drawn from Sugden’s biography of Sir Francis Drake and supplementary historical sources on the Spanish Armada.

entities/calicut-kozhikode.title: Calicut (Kozhikode)
entities/calicut-kozhikode.content:
Overview
Calicut (modern Kozhikode) was the most important port city on the Malabar coast of Kerala, India. It served as the economic heart of the spice trade, the primary destination of Vasco da Gama’s first voyage, and the stage for his diplomatic mission to the Zamorin. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
Spice Trade Center
Calicut was the dominant emporium for the pepper trade, alongside ginger, cardamom, cinnamon, and other spices. The city’s markets drew merchant vessels from across the Indian Ocean and beyond. The wealth of Calicut was described in detail both by the anonymous author of the Roteiro (the Velho journal) and by later Portuguese chroniclers. ^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart]
Ruled by the Zamorin
The city was ruled by a Hindu monarch titled the Zamorin (Samudri Raja — “king of the sea”). The Zamorin’s palace was a sprawling complex that impressed the Portuguese upon their arrival. The Zamorin received Gama and his envoys at the palace, where the initial diplomatic exchanges, gifts, and tense negotiations over trade privileges took place. ^[source: career-legend-vasco-da-gama-subrahmanyam]
Gama’s Arrival
Vasco da Gama’s fleet arrived off the coast of Calicut on May 20, 1498, anchoring at the port of Pandarani (possibly modern Kappad, north of the city). This marked the first direct European maritime contact with India since antiquity. The landing party was greeted by officials and escorted into the city. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
Diverse Merchant Population
Calicut was a cosmopolitan hub. Its population included:

Arab merchants — dominant in the long-distance spice trade and well-established in the city’s commercial life
Gujarati traders — prominent across the Indian Ocean networks
Chinese merchants — remnants of the earlier Ming trading missions
Jewish communities — engaged in commerce along the coast

The Arab merchant community, in particular, viewed the arrival of the Portuguese as a direct threat to their established monopoly and worked to turn the Zamorin against them. ^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart]
Gama’s Diplomatic Mission
The diplomatic mission unfolded over several months. Gama’s initial audience with the Zamorin led to an exchange of letters and gifts, though the Portuguese presents were deemed insufficient by the court. Tensions escalated due to misunderstandings, religious differences, and the machinations of Arab merchants. Gama was detained for a time, and the Portuguese detained hostages in return. Ultimately, Gama departed without a formal trade treaty but with samples of spices and a letter to the King of Portugal. ^[source: career-legend-vasco-da-gama-subrahmanyam]
Legacy
Calicut remained the central prize of the spice trade and a primary target of Portuguese state policy in the decades following Gama’s voyage. The city’s significance as the gateway to the Malabar pepper trade shaped the early history of the Portuguese Estado da Índia. ^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart]
