entities/cuba-columbus.title: Cuba (Columbus Era)
entities/cuba-columbus.content:
Cuba (Columbus Era)
Cuba — the largest island of the Greater Antilles — was first sighted by Christopher Columbus on October 28, 1492, during his first voyage across the Atlantic. Columbus named it Juana in honour of Prince Juan, heir to the Spanish throne. The island figured centrally in the Admiral’s geographical misconceptions: he first believed it was Cipango (Japan), then concluded it was part of the Asiatic mainland. Two embassies were sent inland seeking the Grand Khan of Cathay, and on a later expedition (Book VII, 1494) he explored its southern coast through the labyrinthine islands he named the Queen’s Garden (Jardines de la Reina). So convinced was Columbus that Cuba was a continent that he compelled his entire crew to swear a notarised oath to that effect under penalty of fine, flogging, and mutilation. ^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book IV Ch. III-IV] ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VII Ch. III-V]

Discovery (Book IV, Chapter III)
On the morning of October 28, 1492, after three days’ sailing from the island of Isabella (present-day Rum Cay, Bahamas), Columbus arrived in sight of Cuba. He had set sail at midnight on October 24, the wind, as he noted, blowing “most amorously.” Touching at a group of seven or eight small islands he called Islas de Arena (the modern Mucaras Islands), he crossed the Bahama bank and channel. The part first sighted is supposed to be the coast west of Nuevitas del Principe. ^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book IV Ch. III]
Columbus was struck by the grandeur of the landscape — “its high and airy mountains, which reminded him of those of Sicily; its fertile valleys, and long sweeping plains watered by noble rivers; its stately forests; its bold promontories, and stretching headlands, which melted away into the remotest distance.” He anchored in a beautiful river, free from rocks or shoals, of transparent water, its banks overhung with trees. Landing and taking possession, he gave the island the name Juana and the river the name San Salvador. ^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book IV Ch. III]
Two canoes had put off from the shore on the arrival of the ships, but their occupants fled in affright when the Spanish boat approached to sound the river. Columbus visited two abandoned cabins, finding only fishing implements — nets of palm fibre, hooks and harpoons of bone — and one of the same kind of mute dogs encountered on the smaller islands. He ordered that nothing be disturbed. ^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book IV Ch. III]

Columbus’s Impression: Cipango and the Gilded Reports
During his cruise through the Bahamas, Columbus had gathered from the natives — through the imperfect medium of signs — reports of a great island to the south called Cuba. These reports, “coloured, and gilded, and exaggerated by his imagination,” led him to understand the land was of great extent, abounding in gold, pearls, and spices, frequented by large merchant ships. Comparing these misinterpreted accounts with the coast of Asia as laid down on Toscanelli’s map and the descriptions of Marco Polo, Columbus concluded that this island must be Cipango (Japan), and that the merchant ships belonged to the Grand Khan, who maintained extensive commerce in these seas. ^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book IV Ch. II-III]
He formed a plan: to sail for Cipango, establish relations of trade, seek the magnificent capital Quinsai (Hangzhou, described by Marco Polo), deliver the letters of the Castilian Sovereigns to the Grand Khan, receive his reply, and return triumphantly to Spain. ^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book IV Ch. II]
Coasting westward along Cuba, every new observation seemed to confirm the delusion. Columbus found shells of the kind of oyster that produces pearls, fragrant woods he believed were oriental spices, and the grass growing to the very edge of the water seemed proof of perpetual calm. “Cuba broke upon him like an elysium,” Irving writes. “It is the most beautiful island that eyes ever beheld, full of excellent ports and profound rivers.” ^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book IV Ch. III]

Embassy Inland Searching for the Grand Khan (Book IV, Chapters III-IV)
At the Cape of Palms (eastern entrance to the Laguna de Moron), three Indians from Guanahani informed Martin Alonso Pinzon that behind the cape lay a river from which it was but four days’ journey to Cubanacan, a province abounding in gold — the name meaning “the midst” in their language. Pinzon, steeped in Toscanelli’s map and Columbus’s Asian theories, mistook the word for Cublay Khan, the Tartar sovereign described by Marco Polo. He reported to Columbus that Cuba was not an island but terra firma, and that a local king was at war with the Great Khan. ^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book IV Ch. III]
This communication “put an end to the delusion in which the Admiral had hitherto indulged, that this was the island of Cipango; but it substituted another no less agreeable.” Columbus now concluded he had reached the mainland of Asia (India), at no great distance from Mangi and Cathay, the ultimate destination of his voyage. He resolved to despatch a present to the supposed oriental monarch with the letters of recommendation from the Spanish sovereigns. ^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book IV Ch. III]
After several days of contrary winds, he returned to a river he had named Rio de los Mares. On November 1, he sent boats ashore, but the inhabitants fled, fearing the armament was a slaving expedition of the Grand Khan. An interpreter swam to shore and calmed their fears; within hours, more than sixteen canoes surrounded the ships, bringing cotton yarn. Columbus forbade all trading for anything but gold. One native wore a piece of wrought silver in his nose and indicated — as Columbus understood it — that a king lived four days’ journey inland and that messengers had been sent to give him tidings of the strangers. ^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book IV Ch. III]
Poring over Toscanelli’s map and musing on the misinterpreted words of the Indians, Columbus imagined himself on the borders of Cathay, about one hundred leagues from the capital of the Grand Khan. He determined not to wait for messengers, but to despatch two envoys to seek the monarch. ^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book IV Ch. III]
The envoys were Rodrigo de Jerez and Luis de Torres — the latter a converted Jew who knew Hebrew and Chaldaic, languages Columbus supposed might be known to an oriental prince. Two Indians guided them, one from Guanahani and one from the river hamlet. They carried strings of beads for travelling expenses, specimens of spices and drugs, and instructions to inform the king that Columbus had been sent by the Castilian Sovereigns to establish amicable intercourse. They were also to ascertain the situation and distances of provinces, ports, and rivers that the Admiral specified by name from his descriptions of Asia. ^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book IV Ch. III]
After penetrating twelve leagues, the envoys reached a village of fifty houses containing at least a thousand inhabitants. They were received with solemnity, seated on chairs of state carved from single pieces of wood in the form of quadrupeds, and offered fruits and vegetables. Luis de Torres found his Hebrew, Chaldaic, and Arabic of no avail — the Lucayan interpreter had to be the orator. He extolled the power and munificence of the white men, and the Indians crowded around the envoys, touching them, kissing their hands and feet. Some women wore a slight covering of netted cotton; most of the inhabitants were entirely naked. There appeared to be ranks of society and a chieftain with some authority, unlike the complete equality prevailing among the islanders previously encountered. ^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book IV Ch. IV]
There was, however, “no appearance of gold, or other precious articles.” When shown specimens of cinnamon, pepper, and other spices, the inhabitants replied that such things were not to be found nearby, but far off to the southwest. The envoys returned, bringing with them one of the principal men, his son, and a domestic. On the return journey they witnessed, for the first time by Europeans, the smoking of tobacco — dried herbs rolled in a leaf, lit at one end and puffed from the mouth. ^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book IV Ch. IV]
The report of the envoys dispelled many of Columbus’s splendid fancies about the barbaric prince and his capital. “Such were all the traces they found of the oriental city and court which they had anticipated.” ^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book IV Ch. IV]

Exploration of the Southern Coast and the Queen’s Garden (Book VII, 1494)
During his second voyage, Columbus set sail from the harbour of Isabella (Hispaniola) on April 24, 1494, with the plan of revisiting the coast of Cuba at the point where he had abandoned it during the first voyage. He still believed it to be a continent — the extreme end of Asia — and reasoned that by following its shores he must eventually arrive at Cathay. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VII Ch. I]
Crossing the channel from Hispaniola, he sailed along the southern coast of Cuba, anchoring at Puerto Grande (Guantanamo), which he named for its size. The landscape was heavily cultivated, the shores “enlivened by numerous villages … cultivated to such a degree as to resemble gardens and orchards.” ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VII Ch. I]
After discovering Jamaica and exploring its northern coast, Columbus returned to the southern coast of Cuba. Near the province of Macaca, a friendly cacique explained that Cuba was an island “of infinite extent,” but that no one had ever seen its end. This left the question of continent versus island unresolved. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VII Ch. II-III]
Pressing westward, Columbus entered a labyrinth of keys, sandbanks, and small islands. “Finding them to increase in number, so as to render it impossible to give names to each, the admiral gave this whole labyrinth of islands, which in a manner enamelled the face of the ocean with variegated verdure, the name of the Queen’s Garden” (Jardines de la Reina), in honour of Queen Isabella. He recalled that Sir John Mandeville and Marco Polo had mentioned the coast of Asia was fringed with islands to the amount of several thousands, and persuaded himself that he was among that cluster. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VII Ch. III]
The navigation was perilous: “The ships were obliged, in a manner, to grope their way, with men stationed at the mast-head, and the lead continually going.” They frequently touched upon sand banks. The variable weather followed a pattern — the wind rose in the east with the sun and died away in the west at sunset; heavy clouds gathered at evening, menacing tempests that melted away as the moon rose. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VII Ch. III]
Among these islands, Columbus observed a remarkable fishing technique: the natives used a small fish with a flat head furnished with numerous suckers, tying a line to its tail and allowing it to swim until it attached itself to a turtle or larger fish, which was then drawn up. The Spaniards witnessed the taking of an immense turtle in this manner. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VII Ch. III]
After emerging from the archipelago, Columbus landed at a large village on June 3, where he was received with the kindness and amity that distinguished the inhabitants of Cuba, whom “he extolled above all the other islanders for their mild and pacific character.” Here he erected a large cross with great ceremony, celebrated solemn mass on a Sunday morning, and received a remarkable address from a venerable Indian of fourscore years who warned Columbus against harming the innocent, speaking of rewards and punishments in the afterlife. Columbus was deeply moved by the “simple eloquence of this untutored savage.” ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VII Ch. IV-V]

The Oath: Requiring the Crew to Swear Cuba Was a Continent (Book VII, Chapter V)
As Columbus continued coasting the southern side of Cuba, the ships became strained and leaky from repeated groundings, provisions grew scanty, and the crews — worn out by incessant labour — remonstrated against persisting further. They had already followed the coast far enough to satisfy their minds that it was a continent. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VII Ch. V]
Columbus, “as his imagination cooled, was himself aware of the inadequacy of his vessels to the voyage he had contemplated; but he felt it of importance to his fame, and to the popularity of his enterprizes, to furnish satisfactory proofs that the land he had discovered was a continent.” He persisted four more days exploring the coast as it bent to the southwest, until every one declared there could no longer be a doubt. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VII Ch. V]
The Admiral was determined, however, that “the fact should not rest merely on his own assertion, having had recent proofs of a disposition to gainsay his statements, and depreciate his discoveries.” He sent round a public notary, Fernan Perez de Luna, accompanied by four witnesses, to each of the vessels. Formal demand was made of every person on board — from the captain to the ship-boy — whether he had any doubt that the land before him was a continent: “the beginning and end of the Indias, by which any one might return overland to Spain.” If any entertained a doubt, he was called upon to express it, that it might be removed. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VII Ch. V]
The experienced navigators examined their maps, charts, reckonings, and journals, and after mature deliberation “declared under oath that they had no doubt upon the subject.” They grounded their belief on having coasted for three hundred and thirty-five leagues — an extent “unheard of as appertaining to an island” — while the land stretched forward interminably. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VII Ch. V]
Lest they should subsequently contradict the opinion thus solemnly avowed, a penalty was proclaimed by the notary: if any should offend in such manner, an officer would pay ten thousand maravedis; a ship-boy or person of like rank would receive a hundred lashes and have his tongue cut out. A formal statement was drawn up, including the depositions and names of every individual — a document that still existed in Irving’s time. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VII Ch. V]
This singular process took place near what is now called the Bay of Philippina or Bay of Cortes. As Irving notes, “at this very time, a ship-boy, from the mast-head, might have overlooked the group of islands to the south, and have beheld the open sea beyond. Two or three days further sail would have carried Columbus round the extremity of Cuba, would have dispelled his illusion, and might have given an entirely different course to his subsequent discoveries. In his present conviction he lived and died; believing to his last hour, that Cuba was the extremity of the Asiatic continent.” ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VII Ch. V]
Relinquishing further investigation, Columbus stood to the southeast on June 13, sighted the island he named Evangelista (present-day Isle of Pines), and subsequently continued to the island of Jamaica and then back to Hispaniola, closing the five-month exploration of the second voyage. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VII Ch. V-VII]

entities/deptford.title: Deptford
entities/deptford.content:
Deptford

Overview
Deptford is a shipyard town on the River Thames downstream from London. During the Elizabethan era it housed the Royal Navy’s primary dockyard and became the center of English naval innovation.
Drake’s Knighthood
Deptford is most famously the site where Sir Francis Drake was knighted aboard the Golden Hind by Queen Elizabeth I on April 4, 1581. The ceremony involved the French ambassador, from whom the Queen reportedly borrowed the sword used for the knighting. A special bridge was constructed from the shore to the ship to accommodate the Queen and her retinue. The knighthood, bestowed on the deck of Drake’s own ship, was a deliberate provocation to Spain.
The Golden Hind at Deptford
After the knighting ceremony, Queen Elizabeth ordered that the Golden Hind be preserved as a monument. The ship remained at Deptford for nearly a century, becoming a popular tourist attraction and one of the first preserved historic ships in England.
Naval Significance

Primary dockyard of the Royal Navy in the Elizabethan period
Center of English naval shipbuilding and innovation
John Hawkins oversaw naval construction here, developing new ship designs (the race-built galleon)
Site where many ships of the Spanish Armada campaign were outfitted


Provenance: Information drawn from Sugden’s biography of Sir Francis Drake and supplementary historical sources on Elizabethan naval history.

entities/diogo-dias.title: Diogo Dias
entities/diogo-dias.content:
Diogo Dias
Diogo Dias (also known as Diogo Dias) was the clerk and factor (commercial agent) on Vasco da Gama’s first voyage to India (1497–1499). He served as interpreter and emissary to the Zamorin of Calicut and was briefly held prisoner. Not to be confused with Bartolomeu Dias, the navigator who first rounded the Cape of Good Hope. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt] ^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart]
Role on the First Voyage
Dias served as the expedition’s factor — the commercial agent responsible for negotiating trade agreements and handling merchandise. He also doubled as a scribe and interpreter during diplomatic exchanges with the Zamorin’s court. When da Gama first landed near Calicut, Dias was among those sent ashore to establish contact. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt] ^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart]
Imprisonment
During the tense negotiations with the Zamorin, Dias was held briefly as a prisoner. The Zamorin’s court detained him in an effort to pressure da Gama or in response to Portuguese demands. He was eventually released, and the fleet departed Calicut in August 1498. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt] ^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart]

entities/enrique-of-malacca.title: Enrique of Malacca — Magellan's Slave and Interpreter
entities/enrique-of-malacca.content:
Enrique of Malacca — Magellan’s Slave and Interpreter
Enrique of Malacca (also known as Enrique de Malacca; c. 1495–post-1521) was the slave and personal interpreter of Ferdinand Magellan who played a decisive role in the first circumnavigation of the globe — and who may, in fact, have been the first person in history to circle the earth and return to his starting point. His ability to communicate with the peoples of the Philippines in a Malay dialect allowed the Armada de Molucca to establish the diplomatic alliances that marked the expedition’s final phase, and his betrayal after Magellan’s death at Mactan triggered the Sebu massacre that killed 27 officers. Immediately after the massacre, Enrique disappears from history.^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Background and Acquisition
Magellan acquired Enrique approximately ten years before the circumnavigation, in the Portuguese trading entrepôt of Malacca (on the Malay Peninsula, in present-day Malaysia), where Enrique was baptized with the Christian name Enrique.^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Bergreen speculates: “If Enrique had originally come from these islands, been captured as a boy by slave raiders from Sumatra, and sold to Magellan at a slave mart in Malacca, the chain of circumstances would account for his understanding the local language.” This chain of events would also mean that Enrique, not Elcano, was the first person to complete a full circumnavigation of the globe — having been taken from his homeland in the Malay/Philippine archipelago to Malacca, then to Africa and Europe with Magellan, and finally returning to the same islands with the Armada de Molucca.^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Role in the Expedition
Magellan displayed Enrique before the Spanish court in Valladolid in 1518 to dramatize his claim that the Spice Islands lay within the Spanish hemisphere. Enrique was believed to be a native of the Spice Islands and could serve as interpreter — though this was not entirely accurate geographically, he could indeed act as a translator in the Malay lingua franca of the region.^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Magellan’s will, drawn up before departure, specifically provided for Enrique’s freedom: “I declare and ordain as free and quit of every obligation of captivity, subjection, and slavery, my captured slave Enrique, mulatto, native of the city of Malacca, of the age of twenty-six years more or less, that from the day of my death thenceforward forever the said Enrique may be free and manumitted… and that he may act as he desires and thinks fit.” The will also bequeathed Enrique 10,000 maravedís.^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
The Limasawa Contact — March 1521
When the fleet reached the Philippines after the horrific 99-day Pacific crossing, Enrique’s linguistic skills proved decisive. At the island of Homonhon, after the fleet had anchored and made contact with local islanders in small boats, “Magellan’s slave, Enrique, addressed them in a Malay dialect, and to Magellan’s astonishment, the men appeared to understand him and replied in the same tongue.” No one aboard could explain how Enrique managed to converse with the islanders — not even Magellan knew. It was the first clear sign that the armada had reached the fringe of the Malay-speaking world.^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
On Good Friday, 1521, Magellan sent Enrique ashore at Limasawa as his ambassador. Enrique asked the Limasawan ruler, Rajah Kolambu, to send food to the fleet, explaining “that they would be well satisfied with us, for he [Magellan] had come to the island as friends and not as enemies.” The king responded favorably, came aboard the flagship, and the two leaders established a blood-brotherhood (casicasi) relationship.^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Diplomatic Work at Cebu
When the fleet reached Cebu in April 1521, Enrique again served as interpreter and diplomat. After the initial show of force — the cannon fire that terrified the inhabitants — Enrique went ashore with Magellan’s illegitimate son Cristóvão Rebêlo as the expedition’s emissaries. Enrique assured the frightened Cebuans “that it was the fleet’s custom to discharge their weapons when entering such places, as a sign of peace and friendship.”^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Enrique then announced that his captain owed allegiance to the “greatest king and prince in the world” and was en route to the Moluccas. When King Humabon demanded tribute — as a Siamese junk had recently paid — Enrique relayed Magellan’s blunt refusal: the captain would “not pay tribute to any sovereign in the world.” When Humabon grew angry and half-rose, clutching his short sword, Enrique backed up the threat with a warning that the Spanish king could “sweep you and your subjects off the face of the earth.” The combination of diplomacy and intimidation worked; Humabon relented, and trade was established.^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
After the mass conversion of Cebu, Pigafetta and Enrique together served as the primary intermediaries between Magellan and the Cebuan court. Enrique accompanied Pigafetta to the palace of Humabon, where the king was found “seated on a palm mat on the ground” eating turtle eggs and drinking palm wine.^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt, pigafetta_magellan.txt]
Betrayal — The Sebu Massacre
After Magellan’s death at the Battle of Mactan on April 27, 1521, the fleet elected new commanders: Duarte Barbosa and Juan Serrano. The new leadership attempted to maintain Enrique as an interpreter, but he refused to obey, claiming — correctly — that Magellan’s will had freed him. When Barbosa told Enrique “in a loud voice that, although his master was dead, he would not be set free or released, but that, when we reached Spain, he would still be the slave of Madame Beatriz,” the confrontation escalated.^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Elcano’s account gives an even harsher version, in which Serrano “reprimanded him with bitter words, telling him that in spite of his Master, Magellan, being dead, he was still a slave and that he would be whipped if he did not obey everything that he [Serrano] commanded. The slave became enraged by Serrano’s threats. Ire overtook his heart.”^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Enrique furiously left the ship. Pigafetta believed he sought out King Humabon and conspired against the armada, revealing “that we were about to depart immediately” and urging Humabon to attack so that “he would gain all our ships and merchandise.” Elcano’s account agrees: Enrique “secretly spoke with the master of Cebu — Humabon — telling him that the Castilians were endlessly greedy and that they would come back and arrest him.”^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
On Wednesday, May 1, 1521, Humabon invited the fleet’s officers to a feast — an invitation delivered, presumably, by Enrique. Around thirty men, most of the armada’s remaining leadership, attended. As the banquet ended, armed Cebuans emerged from a palm grove and attacked the guests, killing 27. The victims included Duarte Barbosa, Juan Serrano, Andrés de San Martín, and Father Valderrama. The ships, hearing the cries, raised anchor and fled, abandoning Serrano on the shore where he was eventually killed.^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Disappearance and Legacy
After the massacre, Enrique disappears entirely from history. The historian Bergreen writes: “Enrique, whose treachery had set the stage for the ambush, disappears from history at this point, as does the wily Humabon.” His ultimate fate is unknown — whether he remained in Cebu as a free man, returned to his place of origin in the archipelago, or met some other end is not recorded in any surviving source.^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
The claim that Enrique was the first person to circumnavigate the globe rests on his likely origin. If he came originally from the Malay-Philippine archipelago (as his linguistic ability strongly suggests), then his journey from those islands to Malacca as a slave, then to Africa and Europe with Magellan, and finally back to the same region with the Armada de Molucca, completed a full circle of the earth before Elcano’s Victoria reached Spain. Magellan himself did not complete the circumnavigation; he died at Mactan less than halfway through the return journey. Elcano completed the voyage but was born in Europe and had never been to the East before. Enrique, by contrast, if born in the archipelago, would have returned to his point of origin after a westward journey that took him through Africa, Europe, South America, the Pacific, and back to the Philippines — a true circumnavigation.^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Key Facts

entities/ferdinand-and-isabella.title: Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile
entities/ferdinand-and-isabella.content:
Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile
The Catholic Monarchs (Los Reyes Catolicos) — Joint sovereigns of a unified Spain whose patronage of Christopher Columbus launched the European discovery of the Americas. Their marriage in 1469 united the crowns of Aragon and Castile; their completion of the Reconquista in 1492 freed the resources and attention needed to sponsor Columbus’s first voyage.
Key Dates

1469 — Marriage of Ferdinand and Isabella at Valladolid, uniting the Kingdoms of Aragon and Castile under a single joint monarchy.
1474-1479 — Isabella secures the throne of Castile in the War of Castilian Succession against Joanna la Beltraneja and King Alfonso V of Portugal.
1486 — Columbus first appears before the Spanish court at Cordova; a commission under Hernando de Talavera is appointed to examine his proposals.
January 2, 1492 — Surrender of Granada, completing the Reconquista and ending 780 years of Muslim rule in the Iberian Peninsula.
April 17, 1492 — The Capitulations of Santa Fe: Ferdinand and Isabella agree to sponsor Columbus’s voyage, granting him the titles of Admiral, Viceroy, and Governor, plus one-tenth of all discoveries.
October 12, 1492 — Columbus discovers land in the Bahamas, claiming it for Spain.
April 1493 — Columbus is received with full honors by Ferdinand and Isabella at Barcelona.
1500 — Columbus returns to Spain in chains after his arrest in Hispaniola; Isabella, outraged, orders his release and summons him to court at Granada for a favourable reception.
November 26, 1504 — Death of Queen Isabella at Medina del Campo.
May 20, 1506 — Death of Christopher Columbus at Valladolid, having lost his most influential patron with Isabella’s passing.
January 23, 1516 — Death of Ferdinand II at Madrigalejo.

Roles in Sponsoring Columbus
Columbus spent nearly seven years (1486-1492) petitioning the Spanish court, following it from camp to camp during the Granada War. The sovereigns, while intrigued, were preoccupied with completing the Reconquista and were influenced by the Talavera commission’s sceptical reports of Columbus’s proposals. Irving describes the prolonged negotiations as a test of Columbus’s perseverance; the monarchs’ hesitation was driven both by the expense of the war and by the cautious theological and scientific objections of their advisors.
The critical turning point came immediately after the surrender of Granada. Columbus, having received the Talavera commission’s final rejection, was leaving the court when Luis de Santangel, keeper of the royal privy purse, intervened. Santangel persuaded Isabella to reconsider, pointing out the relatively modest cost compared to the potential gain, and even offered to lend the funds himself. Irving highlights Isabella as the decisive figure: her “quick and generous spirit” was moved by Santangel’s appeal, and she overruled Ferdinand’s caution and the scholars’ objections.^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book II, Chapter VII-VIII]
The financing was arranged through a loan from the Santa Hermandad (the Castilian holy brotherhood) and Santangel’s personal credit. Columbus departed from Palos in August 1492, three months after the agreement. Upon his triumphant return in 1493, Ferdinand and Isabella received him at Barcelona in a ceremonial audience that Irving describes as the peak of Columbus’s public favour — seated beside the sovereigns and treated as a figure of equal dignity.^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book V, Chapter VI]
Isabella remained Columbus’s most consistent defender at court, particularly during the crises of his governorship. When he returned from Hispaniola in irons in 1500, Irving records that “Isabella was shocked and indignant” at Bobadilla’s excesses; the queen ordered his release and summoned him to Granada, where the sovereigns assured him of their favour. However, Ferdinand — more pragmatic and wary of Columbus’s privileges — ultimately declined to restore him to the governorship, appointing Nicolas de Ovando instead. Isabella’s death in November 1504 removed Columbus’s principal advocate, and his subsequent petitions to Ferdinand were fruitless.^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XIV, Chapter I; irving-columbus-vol4.md, Book XVIII, Chapter II]
Characters as Described by Irving
Irving devotes a full chapter (Book II, Chapter II) to the characters of Ferdinand and Isabella, portraying them as complementary forces whose union transformed Spain.
Ferdinand II of Aragon — Irving characterizes Ferdinand as “a prince of great political sagacity” whose talents lay in statecraft, diplomacy, and military organization. He was calculating, deliberate, and cautious with resources — traits that made him initially reluctant to commit to Columbus’s uncertain enterprise. Irving notes Ferdinand’s prudence sometimes bordered on parsimony, but credits him with the administrative skill that consolidated the Spanish monarchy and built the institutions (the Santa Hermandad, the reformed judiciary, the territorial unification) that made Columbus’s voyage possible. After Isabella’s death, Ferdinand’s more pragmatic, legalistic handling of Columbus’s claims stands in contrast to the queen’s personal loyalty.^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book II, Chapter II]
Isabella I of Castile — Irving’s portrait of Isabella is markedly more laudatory. He describes her as “a woman of great religious fervour and strong will,” combining deep piety with decisive action. Irving emphasizes her quick and generous spirit, her personal courage (she was known to ride among the troops during the Granada campaign), and her intellectual curiosity, which made her more receptive than Ferdinand to Columbus’s visionary proposals. Isabella is presented as the moral centre of the court: she was outraged by the enslavement of the indigenous people and by Bobadilla’s treatment of Columbus, and her personal intervention on multiple occasions determined the course of events. Irving also notes her patronage of learning and the arts, her founding of schools and hospitals, and her attention to the administration of justice. Her death, Irving writes, was “a fatal blow” to Columbus, “as she had ever been his steadfast friend at court.”^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book II, Chapter II; irving-columbus-vol4.md, Book XVIII, Chapter II]
Their partnership — Irving presents their joint rule as a model of complementary strengths: Ferdinand’s political calculation balanced by Isabella’s intuitive decisiveness; his administrative rigour paired with her personal warmth. Together, they transformed the patchwork of Iberian kingdoms into a unified European power, completed the centuries-long Reconquista, established the Spanish Inquisition, and redirected Spanish energy from internal warfare to Atlantic exploration — creating the conditions for Columbus’s epochal voyage.
Relationship to Other Entities

christopher-columbus — The navigator they sponsored; their patronage enabled his four transatlantic voyages and the European discovery of the Americas.
irving-columbus — Washington Irving’s primary-source biography containing the fullest portraits of their characters and roles.
irving-columbus-vol2 — Documents Columbus’s reception at Burgos (1496) and the sovereigns’ gradual cooling toward him.
irving-columbus-vol3 — Covers Isabella’s outrage at Columbus’s arrest and Ferdinand’s decision to appoint Ovando.
irving-columbus-vol4 — Documents Isabella’s death (1504) and its consequences for Columbus’s final petitions.

entities/ferdinand-magellan.title: Ferdinand Magellan
entities/ferdinand-magellan.content:
Ferdinand Magellan


Ferdinand Magellan (Portuguese: Fernao de Magalhaes; Spanish: Fernando de Magallanes; c. 1480–1521) was a Portuguese-born navigator and explorer who led the first expedition to circumnavigate the globe. Originally in the service of Portugal, he transferred his allegiance to Spain and commanded the Armada de Molucca (five ships, 1519–1522), discovering the Strait of Magellan at the southern tip of South America and becoming the first European to cross the Pacific Ocean. He was killed at the Battle of Mactan in the Philippines before the voyage was completed; the expedition’s sole surviving ship, the Victoria, returned to Spain under Juan Sebastian Elcano. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
Narrative Overview
Magellan was born around 1480 near the town of Villa Real in the province of Traz os Montes, in northern Portugal. He was the son of a noble but not wealthy hidalgo (minor noble) who maintained a fortified ancestral home in the mountainous region. Young Fernan (as he was then called) was raised in comfort, spending his boyhood hunting wild boar and deer in the mountains, fighting brigands who infested the region, and enjoying the rough outdoor life of the Portuguese countryside. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
His family spent part of each year in Oporto, the port city on the Atlantic. There the young Magellan became fascinated with the sea: he befriended captains and sailors, explored the caravels in the harbor, and listened to tales of perilous voyages, shipwrecks, and the discoveries of Columbus and Vasco da Gama. He yearned for a life of adventure beyond the quiet valleys of his home. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
At about age twenty, Magellan asked his father for permission to go to the royal court in Lisbon to seek a career. His father consented, equipped him with fine clothes, armor, and a white horse, and Magellan traveled to Lisbon to seek service with King Manuel of Portugal. The king received him graciously and gave him a place in the royal household. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
Bergreen notes that at age twelve Magellan and his brother Diogo moved to Lisbon to become pages at the royal court, where Ferdinand received education in “religion, writing, mathematics, music and dance, horsemanship, martial arts, and, thanks to the legacy of Prince Henry the Navigator, algebra, geometry, astronomy, and navigation.” He came of age hearing about Portuguese and Spanish discoveries in the Indies and was privy to the secrets of Portuguese exploration of the ocean, even assisting with preparing fleets leaving for India. ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Service in India Under Albuquerque and the Battle of Diu
Magellan’s court service did not satisfy his ambition. The return of Vasco da Gama from India and the preparations for a major expedition under Francisco D’Almeyda, the first viceroy of India, stirred him to action. He secured a place in D’Almeyda’s fleet and sailed for India at about age twenty-five. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
In India and East Africa, Magellan fought in numerous battles: the assault on Quiloa, the capture of Mombaza, and the campaigns at Cochin, Cananore, Coulam, and Onor. He served under both D’Almeyda and the great Portuguese general Alfonso de Albuquerque, taking part in the attack on Ormuz (1507). He distinguished himself for bravery and leadership, notably when he voluntarily remained on a stranded ship while officers evacuated, inspiring the sailors to remain calm. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
Bergreen provides additional depth on this period: following the death of his patron King Joao II in 1495, Manuel I mistrusted Magellan, who had been allied with the opposition. Finally in 1505, after a decade of anonymous court service, Magellan and his brother Diogo received assignments aboard a fleet of twenty-two ships bound for India under Francisco de Almeida. Magellan spent the next eight years trying to establish a permanent Portuguese presence in India, “dashing from one trading post to another, and from one battle to the next; he survived multiple wounds and, if nothing else, learned to stay alive in a hostile environment.” ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
He fell out with Albuquerque by opposing the planned attack on Goa in a council of war, arguing that contrary winds would prevent the ships from returning to Portugal that year. This opposition cost him Albuquerque’s favor and effectively ended his service in India. During this period he invested most of his fortune with a merchant who soon died; in the ensuing confusion, Magellan lost most of his assets. He petitioned King Manuel for restitution, but the king refused. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt] ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
The Moroccan Campaign and Permanent Lameness
Magellan then transferred to Morocco, where he commanded Portuguese troops at the settlement of Azamor, engaging in almost continual conflicts with Moors and Arabs. In one rash sally, he was struck by a poisoned javelin that entered his leg. Though he recovered, he was permanently lame from that wound for the rest of his life. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
Bergreen recounts the Moroccan campaign in greater detail. In 1513, when the city of Azamor refused to pay its annual tribute to Portugal, King Manuel responded with the largest seaborne force ever to sail for his kingdom: five hundred ships and fifteen thousand soldiers. Among them was Magellan, riding an aging steed — the only mount he could afford on his reduced budget. He lost his horse to the Arabs and barely escaped the siege with his life. Insulted that the Portuguese army offered only a fraction of the horse’s value as compensation, Magellan wrote directly to the king, circumventing ministers — an act of hotheadedness and tactlessness that typified his career. The king dismissed the request. ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Magellan stubbornly remained at his post, acquired a new horse, and participated in daily skirmishes with Arabs who swooped out of the desert to harass Portuguese soldiers guarding Azamor. “In one confrontation, he received a serious wound from an Arab lance, which left him with a shattered knee and a lifelong limp; it also ended his career as a soldier.” His battle service earned him promotion to quartermaster, entitling him to a share of spoils. In a subsequent battle, Arabs surrendered a herd of over 200,000 goats, camels, and horses. Magellan was among the officers responsible for distributing spoils and decided to pay off tribal allies with some captured animals. He and another officer were indicted for selling four hundred goats to the enemy and keeping the proceeds. The charges were preposterous — Magellan was entitled to his spoils — but he failed to respond, left Morocco without authorization, and appeared before King Manuel demanding an increase in his allowance, lecturing the king on his lifelong service and wounds. “Jealous rivals whispered behind Magellan’s back that his limp was merely an act designed to elicit sympathy.” ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
King Manuel ordered Magellan to return to Morocco to face charges of treason, corruption, and leaving the army without authorization. A tribunal dismissed all charges, and he returned with a letter of recommendation. But when he again demanded an increased allowance, the king refused. “Short and dark, and teetering on the brink of poverty, he looked nothing like the aristocrat he thought himself to be.” ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Rejection by King Manuel I and Renunciation of Portuguese Citizenship
Disillusioned with the petty wars in Morocco and convinced that greater glory lay in exploration, Magellan returned to Lisbon to petition King Manuel for an expedition to find a westward route to the Molucca (Spice) Islands. His proposal was based on his study of maps and his friendship with Francisco Serrano, who had written of the riches of the Moluccas. King Manuel, who had taken a dislike to Magellan (partly due to the Goa incident), curtly refused. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
Bergreen reveals that Magellan brought Ruy Faleiro, a mathematician, astronomer, and nautical scholar, to help persuade the king. But King Manuel was already prejudiced against both men. At age fifty-one, the king had entered a personal crisis: his wife died in childbirth, he briefly abdicated, then changed his mind and arranged to marry his son’s fiancee, Leonor, King Charles’s sister — a situation causing scandal. “Three times, Magellan asked for royal authorization for a voyage to the Indies to discover a water route to the fabled but little known Spice Islands. Three times, the king, who had disliked and mistrusted Magellan for more than twenty years, refused.” ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Finally, in September 1517, Magellan asked if he could offer his services elsewhere. To his astonishment, the king replied that Magellan was free to do as he pleased. “When Magellan knelt to kiss the king’s hands, as custom dictated, King Manuel concealed them behind his cloak and turned his back on his petitioner.” Within days of arriving in Seville, Magellan signed documents formally making him a subject of Castile and its young king, Charles I. No longer Fernao de Magalhaes, he became known as Hernando de Magallanes. He had formally renounced his allegiance to King Manuel and given his loyalty to King Charles. ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Marriage to Beatriz Barbosa
In the palace corridor after his rejection, Magellan was approached by his friend Ruy Faleiro, an astrologer, who encouraged him to offer his services to King Charles of Spain instead. Taking Faleiro’s advice, Magellan resigned his Portuguese commission and traveled to Seville, where his cousin Diego Barbosa was mayor. There he reunited with Barbosa’s daughter Beatrix (whom he had known in Lisbon), courted her, and won her hand in marriage. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
Bergreen adds that Magellan became acquainted with Diogo Barbosa, another Portuguese expatriate who had settled in Seville fourteen years earlier and was now Knight Commander of the Order of Santiago. “At the same time, Magellan began to woo Diogo’s daughter Beatriz; the relationship developed very quickly, and they married before the year was out. Suddenly, Magellan had an important sponsor in Seville, as well as a financial stake, because Beatriz brought with her a dowry of 600,000 maravedis. She might have been pregnant at the time of their marriage; the child, named Rodrigo, was born the following year.” ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Magellan and Faleiro traveled to Valladolid to present their proposal to King Charles (later Emperor Charles V). Despite opposition from Portuguese Ambassador Alvaro da Costa (who attempted to bribe, persuade, and even assassinate Magellan), and from jealous Spanish courtiers, Charles approved the expedition. The agreement granted Magellan command of five ships, the title of admiral, a twentieth of revenues from discovered lands, and the governorship of any islands discovered. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
Bergreen notes that the Portuguese ambassador, Alvaro da Costa, sought out Magellan, promising King Manuel would reconsider. “Magellan refused to be swayed by the ambassador’s entreaties. He suspected that if he returned to Portugal he would be thrown into jail, tried for treason, and executed.” ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Political Context: The Line of Demarcation and the Spice Trade
Bergreen situates Magellan’s voyage within the broader geopolitics of the era. On June 7, 1494, Pope Alexander VI — a Spaniard, Rodrigo de Borja — divided the world between Spain and Portugal through the Treaty of Tordesillas. The line of demarcation extended from the North Pole to the South Pole, one hundred leagues (about four hundred miles) west of the Cape Verde Islands. Spain received the western portion, Portugal the eastern. ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
The spice trade was the driving economic force: “Like oil today, the European quest for spices drove the world’s economy and influenced global politics.” Cloves, nutmeg, cinnamon, pepper, and mace were the most precious commodities. Arab merchants maintained a monopoly by concealing the origins of spices, insisting they came from Africa when they actually grew in India, China, and Southeast Asia. The fall of Constantinople in 1453 severed the overland spice routes, opening new possibilities for any European nation able to master the seas. For those willing to assume the risks, “the rewards of an oceanic spice trade, combined with control over the world’s economy, were irresistible.” ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Magellan’s proposal to Charles V argued that the Spice Islands lay within the Spanish hemisphere, based partly on the map of his friend Francisco Serrano, who had written from Ternate describing “a new world richer and greater than that of Vasco da Gama.” Magellan also displayed his slave Enrique, a native of the Spice Islands, as an interpreter. The contract signed on March 22, 1518, granted Magellan a ten-year exclusive on voyages to the Spice Islands (which Charles ultimately violated by dispatching follow-up expeditions), 5 percent of revenues from discovered lands, and governorship of any islands discovered. ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Command of the Armada de Molucca
Magellan’s fleet consisted of five ships: the Trinidad (flagship, 100 tons), the San Antonio (80 tons), the Conception (80 tons), the Victoria (60 tons), and the Santiago (60 tons). The captains were Spanish: Juan de Cartagena (San Antonio), Gaspar de Quesada (Conception), and Luis de Mendoza (Victoria); with Juan Serrano (Santiago) as Magellan’s trusted friend. The fleet carried 250 men, 80 cannon, and enough provisions for two years. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
Bergreen adds crucial context about the political intrigues. Archbishop Juan Rodriguez de Fonseca, who controlled the Casa de Contratacion and despised Magellan, appointed his own illegitimate son Juan de Cartagena as inspector general with a salary higher than Magellan’s. Fonseca also appointed his close allies Luis de Mendoza and Gaspar de Quesada as captains. “Not surprisingly, all three captains appointed by Fonseca — Cartagena, Quesada, and Mendoza — despised and looked down on Magellan from the moment they came on board.” The ship names and tonnages also differ slightly in Bergreen: San Antonio 120 tons, Concepcion 90 tons, Victoria 85 tons, Santiago 75 tons. ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Magellan married Beatrix Barbosa in the Seville Cathedral before departing. He left her pregnant, never to see her again. The fleet sailed from Seville in August 1519 and from San Lucar on September 20, 1519. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
The Circumnavigation
The fleet crossed the Atlantic, stopping at the Canary and Cape Verde Islands, and reached the coast of Brazil in December 1519. They encountered friendly natives who worshipped them as rain-bringers, endured storms, and observed marine wonders (sharks, flying fish). They explored the Rio de la Plata and continued southward as winter approached. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
The Port St. Julian Mutiny: Mendoza’s Death, Quesada’s Beheading, Cartagena Marooned
At Port St. Julian (Argentina), Magellan wintered from March to August 1520. There he faced a serious mutiny led by Cartagena, Quesada, and Mendoza. He suppressed it ruthlessly: Mendoza was killed on his own deck by Magellan’s constable, Cartagena was executed by firing squad, and Quesada was imprisoned. The mutineers’ bodies were quartered and displayed. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
Bergreen provides far richer detail. The Easter mutiny of 1520 saw Quesada and Cartagena seize three ships — the San Antonio, Concepcion, and Victoria — leaving Magellan with only the Trinidad and the Santiago. Bergreen describes how Magellan’s constable, Gonzalo Gomez de Espinosa, along with several loyalists, approached the Victoria in a longboat. Espinosa boarded, stabbed Captain Luis de Mendoza through the throat, and killed him on his own deck. Magellan’s men then cut the anchor cables, leaving the mutinous ship to drift. ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
The San Antonio and Concepcion attempted to escape the harbor at night, but their anchor cables parted in the current and they drifted helplessly past the Trinidad, where Magellan’s gunners opened fire. The mutineers’ ships were captured. Magellan convened a trial; Gaspar de Quesada was condemned to death, beheaded, and his body drawn and quartered, with his severed head displayed on a pike at the harbor’s entrance. Juan de Cartagena and a priest, Pero Sanchez de la Reina, were not executed but were sentenced to marooning. On August 11, 1520, both were left on a small island in sight of the ships “with no longboat, no firewood, and scant clothing. Their supplies consisted mainly of bread and wine, enough to last them the summer.” Their fate was never known; they were never rescued. ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
At St. Julian, Magellan encountered the Patagonian giants, whom he and his men observed with great curiosity. He captured two as interpreters. The Santiago was wrecked on a scouting mission. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
Bergreen narrates the Patagonian encounters at length: Magellan’s initial friendly contact with the Tehuelche people, the conversion of one giant named “John” to Christianity, the subsequent deterioration of relations when Magellan’s men discovered a cache of Indian weapons, the trick of luring four giants aboard the Trinidad and fettering them, and the final violent clash that left crew member Diego Barrasa dead from a poisoned arrow. Two Patagonian captives remained aboard, one of whom (named “Paul”) later died and was buried at sea after conversion by Pigafetta. ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Discovery of the Strait
On October 21, 1520 (the Day of the Eleven Thousand Virgins), after sailing south from St. Julian, Magellan discovered the strait that now bears his name. The passage was treacherous and winding, with branching channels. The San Antonio deserted and returned to Spain. After five weeks, Magellan emerged into the open ocean at the western end, weeping for joy at the discovery. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
Bergreen describes the 350-mile strait as a “nautical nightmare” with tides exceeding twenty-four feet and powerful currents. He recounts how Magellan dispatched the San Antonio and Concepcion to scout ahead, the terrifying “williwaw” storms (violent squalls peculiar to the strait), and the dramatic reunion when the two scout ships returned “with sails full and banners flying to the wind” discharging mortars in celebration. Bergreen also details the desertion of the San Antonio under Esteban Gomes, who had long resented Magellan’s leadership and whose opposition had “set the stage for another mutiny.” Gomes stabbed Magellan’s cousin Alvaro de Mesquita, seized the ship, and returned to Spain. ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
The 99-Day Pacific Crossing: Starvation, Scurvy, Rats, Leather, and Sawdust
The subsequent crossing of the Pacific took 99 days. Magellan named the ocean “Pacific” because of its placid surface. The crossing was a nightmare of starvation: the sailors ate rats, leather from the rigging, and sawdust; scurvy ravaged the crew; many died. They sighted only two barren uninhabited islands before reaching Guam in the Marianas in March 1521. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
Bergreen’s account is harrowing and comprehensive. He explains the sheer scale of the Pacific — encompassing one-third of the earth’s surface, sixty-three million square miles — and Magellan’s fatal underestimation of its size. For ninety-eight days after leaving the strait, the fleet saw nothing but ocean. ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Pigafetta’s account, quoted by Bergreen, describes the appalling deterioration: “We were three months and twenty days without getting any kind of fresh food. We ate biscuit which was no longer biscuit, but powder of biscuits swarming with worms, for they had eaten the good. It stank strongly of the urine of rats. We drank yellow water that had been putrid for many days. We also ate some ox hides that covered the top of the mainyard to prevent the yard from chafing the shrouds, and which had become exceedingly hard because of the sun, rain, and wind. We left them in the sea for four or five days, and then placed them for a few moments on top of the embers, and so ate them; and often we ate sawdust from boards. Rats were sold for one-half ducado apiece, and even then we could not get them.” ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Scurvy claimed at least twenty-nine men. Gums swelled, teeth fell out, old scars reopened, and men’s bodies literally fell apart. Bergreen explains that Magellan and his officers were spared because they regularly ate preserved quince, which unknowingly contained an antiscorbutic. “Throughout the ordeal, the officers regularly dipped into their supply of preserved quince, an applelike fruit, without realizing it was actually a potent antiscorbutic.” The only landfall before Guam were two barren atolls — San Pablo (January 24) and Shark Island (February 4) — where no anchorage could be found. Desperate, Magellan “flung his useless maps overboard, crying, ‘With the pardon of the cartographers, the Moluccas are not to be found in their appointed place!‘” ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
The Philippines and Death at Mactan
From Guam the fleet reached the Philippines, first landing at the island of Mazzava, where Magellan established friendly relations with the local king through a blood-brotherhood ceremony and the exchange of gifts. The Malay interpreter he had brought with him from earlier voyages proved invaluable. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
Pigafetta’s Easter Sunday Cross (March 31, 1521)
Pigafetta, who was present throughout, provides the sole eyewitness account of the Easter Sunday ceremonies at Mazzava (Limasawa). “Early on the morning of Sunday, the last of March, and Easter Day, the captain-general sent the priest with many men to prepare for saying mass, and the interpreter went to tell the king that we were not going to land in order to dine with him, but to say mass.” The king sent two slaughtered swine. “When the hour for mass arrived, we landed with about fifty men, without our body armour, but carrying our other arms, and dressed in our best clothes.” Magellan sprinkled the two kings with musk water before the mass began. “We set up the cross there, for those people were heathens.” Had they been Moors, Pigafetta notes, “we would have erected there a column as a sign of greater harshness, for the Moors are much harder to convert than the heathens.” ^[source: pigafetta_magellan.txt]
Pigafetta’s Account of Magellan’s Death at Mactan (April 27, 1521)
Pigafetta’s journal is the sole surviving eyewitness report of the Mactan battle. He records that Magellan took sixty men in three boats, crossing at midnight under a calm, starlit sky. The boats could not approach the shore due to coral rocks and shallow water, so the Spaniards waded through the surf. The native force numbered approximately 1,500. “So many of them charged down upon us that they shot the captain through the right leg with a poisoned arrow.” Magellan ordered a slow retreat, but the men fled. “The natives shot only at our legs because they were naked.” Only six or eight men remained with the captain. “Recognizing the captain, so many turned upon him that they knocked his helmet off his head twice, but he always stood firm like a good knight.” After more than an hour of fighting: “An Indian hurled a bamboo spear into the captain’s face. The latter immediately killed him with his lance.” Magellan then “trying to lay hand on sword, he could draw it out only halfway, because he had been wounded in the arm with a bamboo spear.” At that moment “one of them wounded him on the left leg with a large terciado, which resembles a scimitar, only being larger; that caused the captain to fall face downward. Immediately they rushed upon him with iron and bamboo spears and with their cutlasses, until they killed our mirror, our light, our comfort, and our true guide.” Pigafetta’s eulogy follows: “Among the other virtues, he was more constant than anyone else in the greatest of storms; he endured hunger better than all others; and more accurately than any man in the world did he chart and navigate.” After the battle, the Christian king of Cebu sent a message offering merchandise for Magellan’s body. The people of Mactan “answered that they would not give up such a man, as we had hoped they would, and that they would not give him up for all the riches in the world, but that they intended to keep him as a memorial.” ^[source: pigafetta_magellan.txt]
Proceeding to the larger island of Sebu (Cebu), Magellan negotiated an alliance with its king, who agreed to become a Christian and a vassal of Spain. On April 14, 1521, the king and his court were baptized in an elaborate ceremony; hundreds of his subjects followed. The king then asked Magellan’s help in subduing a neighboring chief, Cilapulapu of the nearby island of Matan (Mactan), who refused to submit. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
On April 27, 1521, Magellan attacked Mactan with sixty men in three boats. The water was too shallow for the boats to approach the shore, so the Spaniards waded through the surf. They were met by a large force of natives armed with arrows, spears, stones, and scimitars. The battle was fierce; Magellan fought at the front of his men. He received a lance wound in the face, a javelin wound in the right arm, and a scimitar blow to the left leg that brought him down. A swarm of natives fell upon him with spears and stones, and Magellan was killed on the beach. Cilapulapu refused to surrender his body, saying he would keep it as a monument of his triumph. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
Bergreen adds that Magellan’s landing force consisted of only forty-nine men against approximately 1,500 warriors. The dead included Cristovao Rebelo, Magellan’s illegitimate son who had served as his constant companion on the voyage. Bergreen also discusses the historiographical controversy: “In his misguided quest for glory, Magellan had squandered lives and the resources of the armada.” Pigafetta’s eulogy is quoted: “Among the other virtues that he possessed, he was more constant than anyone else in the greatest adversity. He endured hunger better than all the others.” ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
The Sebu Massacre: 27 Killed
After Magellan’s death, the expedition elected Edward Barbosa (his brother-in-law) as commander. Barbosa was invited to a feast by the king of Sebu, who had reverted to his old allegiances; Barbosa, Serrano, and most of the officers were massacred. The remaining men abandoned the Conception, burning her, and sailed on with the Trinidad and the Victoria. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
Bergreen’s account is far more detailed. After Magellan’s death, Enrique (Magellan’s slave and interpreter) was told by Duarte Barbosa that he would remain a slave of Beatriz Barbosa. Enraged, Enrique “sought out Humabon, ‘the Christian King,’ to scheme against the armada,” revealing that the Europeans were about to depart and urging Humabon to attack. On Wednesday, May 1, Humabon invited the armada’s leaders to a feast. Around thirty men, most of them officers, accepted. ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
“As the banquet was about to end, some armed people emerged from the palm grove and attacked the invitees, killing twenty-seven of them.” The victims included Duarte Barbosa (commander for just three days), Juan Serrano, Andres de San Martin (the astrologer), Father Valderrama, and numerous other officers and sailors. Juan Serrano was brought to the shore, weeping, pleading for rescue, but the ships weighed anchor and abandoned him. “Only 115 men remained of the 260 who had left Spain.” ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Aftermath: The Trinidad’s Fate and the Trial of Survivors
After further adventures at Borneo, the fleet finally reached the Molucca (Spice) Islands. There the Trinidad was found too leaky to continue and was left behind (later captured by the Portuguese). The Victoria, under Juan Sebastian Elcano, sailed west across the Indian Ocean, rounded the Cape of Good Hope, and after great hardship (only 18 of the original 250 men survived) reached San Lucar, Spain, on September 6, 1522 — the first ship to circumnavigate the globe. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
Bergreen traces the Trinidad’s tragic fate in detail. Under Gonzalo Gomez de Espinosa, the Trinidad attempted to sail back to Panama but was caught by contrary winds, storms, and scurvy. After seven months at sea and thirty deaths, Espinosa retreated to Tidore, where a Portuguese fleet under Antonio de Brito had arrived. The Portuguese seized the ship, stripped her, and a storm smashed her remains into driftwood. “The flagship of the Armada de Molucca ended up as driftwood.” Most of her crew were imprisoned; some were forced to work on a Portuguese fort built from the Trinidad’s own timbers. ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
The return of the Victoria triggered a fierce legal and political battle. The San Antonio’s mutineers had already returned to Seville in May 1521 and given depositions accusing Magellan of brutality, torture, and disloyalty to Spain. Fifty-three of the fifty-five crew members gave testimony. In their account, Magellan was “a Portuguese tyrant… a cunning agent of his native land.” Archbishop Fonseca, Cartagena’s father, responded to the depositions with shock and dismay at Magellan’s treatment of Spanish officers. The mutineers went free; Gomes even received a royal appointment to another expedition. ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Magellan’s wife, Beatriz, was placed under house arrest with her young son while the inquiry continued, “not knowing that her husband had died only weeks before.” His father-in-law, Diogo Barbosa, wrote a long defense of Magellan to King Charles, arguing that Magellan “had to take great care so that it would be to your advantage… when the men he brought with him mutinied with three of the principal ships, he did not punish them severely when he could have.” Alvaro de Mesquita, who had been tortured by the mutineers, languished in jail for a year despite his innocence. Ruy Faleiro, the brilliant cosmologist who had co-created the expedition, was imprisoned in Portugal, suffered a breakdown, and later returned to Seville destitute. ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
When the Victoria returned, Elcano faced an inquiry in Valladolid in October 1522. He condemned Magellan to exculpate himself, claiming Magellan had defied the king’s orders and “abandoned the fleet to its fate.” King Charles waived duties on the spices, awarded Elcano a knighthood, a coat of arms depicting a globe with the legend “Primus circumdedesti me” (Thou first circled me), and an annual pension. “Meanwhile, the coat of arms for the Magellan family remained defaced and dishonored.” Mesquita was finally freed in the general amnesty and fled to Portugal. ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Legacy for Cartography and Empire
Bergreen synthesizes the expedition’s enduring significance. The circumnavigation “forever altered the Western world’s ideas about cosmology… as well as geography. It demonstrated, among other things, that the earth was round, that the Americas were not part of India but were actually a separate continent, and that oceans covered most of the earth’s surface. The voyage conclusively demonstrated that the earth is, after all, one world.” ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
In cartography, Pigafetta’s observations of two dwarf galaxies — now known as the Magellanic Clouds — marked a significant astronomical discovery. Oronce Fine’s 1531 map placed the Strait of Magellan accurately in South America, naming the Pacific “Magellanicum.” Gerardus Mercator canonized the strait on his famous globe in 1536. The name “Magellan” ultimately designated only the strait, not the territories he dreamed of bequeathing to his heirs. ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
The voyage established that the Pacific was not a small gulf but an ocean covering one-third of the earth’s surface. It added seven thousand miles to the globe’s circumference. The international date line, necessitated by the circumnavigation, was another enduring legacy — when the Victoria reached the Cape Verde Islands, the crew discovered they had lost a day, an error that “took the first circumnavigation to demonstrate the need for a twenty-four hour gain.” ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Politically, the voyage triggered a race to claim the Spice Islands. King Charles dispatched multiple follow-up expeditions, all ending in disaster (the second Armada de Molucca under Loaysa and Elcano lost all but one ship, with only 8 of 450 men surviving). Finally, in 1529, facing bankruptcy, Charles signed the Treaty of Saragossa, pledging the Moluccas to Portugal. Not until 1580 did Francis Drake complete the second circumnavigation, relying on knowledge “so painfully and heroically acquired by the Captain General and his crew.” ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
“Worthier, indeed, are our sailors of eternal fame than the Argonauts who sailed with Jason,” wrote Peter Martyr, Magellan’s contemporary. “And much more worthy was their ship of being placed along the stars than that old Argo; for they only sailed from Greece through Pontus, but ours through the whole west and southern hemisphere, penetrating into the east, and again returned to the west.” ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]

Key Figures in Magellan’s Story

King Manuel I of Portugal — Rejected Magellan’s services, driving him to Spain; turned his back when Magellan knelt to kiss his hands
King Charles I of Spain (later Emperor Charles V) — Sponsored Magellan’s expedition; never mourned Magellan’s death
Ruy Faleiro — Portuguese astrologer, mathematician, and cosmologist; co-created the expedition but was removed due to mental instability; later imprisoned in Portugal
Juan Rodriguez de Fonseca — Bishop of Burgos, head of Casa de Contratacion; Cartagena’s father; worked to undermine Magellan’s authority
Diego Barbosa — Magellan’s father-in-law, Knight Commander of Order of Santiago; defended Magellan after his death
Beatriz Barbosa — Magellan’s wife, married 1517–1518; placed under house arrest after the San Antonio returned
Juan de Cartagena — Fonseca’s illegitimate son; Spanish captain of the San Antonio; led the mutiny at St. Julian; marooned on Patagonian coast
Luis de Mendoza — Spanish captain of the Victoria; mutineer killed by Espinosa on his own deck
Gaspar de Quesada — Spanish captain of the Conception; mutineer; beheaded, drawn and quartered
Juan Serrano — Faithful captain of the Santiago; later killed in the Sebu massacre
Duarte Barbosa — Magellan’s brother-in-law; succeeded him as commander for three days; killed in the Sebu massacre
Juan Sebastian Elcano — Basque master of the Conception; completed circumnavigation in command of Victoria; condemned Magellan to exculpate himself at the Valladolid inquiry; died on a follow-up expedition in 1526
Lapu-Lapu (Cilapulapu) — Chieftain of Mactan who led the forces that killed Magellan; now a Filipino national hero
Antonio Pigafetta — Italian nobleman and chronicler whose journal preserved the detailed account of the voyage; his diary is the most important surviving document of the expedition
Esteban Gomes — Portuguese pilot of the San Antonio; led the desertion at the strait; returned to Spain and gave damning testimony against Magellan
Humabon — King of Cebu; initially allied with Magellan; after Magellan’s death, massacred 27 Spaniards at a feast
Enrique of Malacca — Magellan’s slave and interpreter; after Magellan’s death was told he would remain a slave; betrayed the Europeans to Humabon, triggering the Sebu massacre

Source Text
This page draws on two primary sources:


magellan-towle — George M. Towle’s Magellan, or the First Voyage Round the World (1880), a 19th-century popular biography of Magellan.


bergreen-magellan — Laurence Bergreen, Over the Edge of the World: Magellan’s Terrifying Circumnavigation of the Globe (HarperCollins, 2003). Bergreen’s work is a modern narrative history based on primary sources including Antonio Pigafetta’s journal, Francisco Albo’s pilot log, the memoirs of Gines de Mafra, Portuguese and Spanish archives, and contemporary scholarship. The book treats the voyage as a story of survival, leadership, and cultural encounter. Bergreen draws on the earliest English translation of Pigafetta (by James A. Robertson, 1906) and R. A. Skelton’s 1969 translation. He also uses newly translated materials including de Mafra’s memoir and legal documents from the Archive of the Indies in Seville. Bergreen acknowledges his debt to naval historian Samuel Eliot Morison’s The European Discovery of America: The Southern Voyages (1974) and to F.H.H. Guillemard’s Life of Ferdinand Magellan (1890), the standard biography for over a century. Bergreen’s source file is bergreen_magellan.txt (~147,000 words).

entities/francis-walsingham.title: Francis Walsingham
entities/francis-walsingham.content:
Sir Francis Walsingham (c. 1532–1590)
Overview
Sir Francis Walsingham (c. 1532 – April 1590). Queen Elizabeth’s Principal Secretary and spymaster. A key patron of Drake’s ventures and a leading advocate of Protestant activism against Catholic Spain. His intelligence network provided crucial information about Spanish Armada preparations. His death in 1590 removed a key patron from Drake’s support network. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Appearance and Character
At forty-four years of age, Walsingham’s long narrow face displayed the gravity of a Puritan frustrated by Elizabeth’s moderation and afflicted by a sickly constitution. Like Drake a Protestant from childhood, he had left England during the Marian persecutions. He was one of Philip II’s most ardent foes in Elizabeth’s court. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt, lines 5447-5450]
Patron of Drake
Walsingham was among Drake’s most powerful supporters. When Drake carried a letter of introduction from the Earl of Essex to Walsingham, the Joint Principal Secretary of State read that Drake was a useful man in any enterprise against Spain and sent for him, spreading a map and asking how Philip might be best assailed. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt, lines 5396-5406]
Drake gathered around his circumnavigation project a small band of influential courtiers and Privy Councillors: the Earl of Lincoln, Christopher Hatton, the Earl of Leicester, and Walsingham himself. The syndicate backed Drake with the understanding the expedition was anti-Spanish from the start. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt, lines 5416-5420, 5443-5446]
Spymaster and Intelligence
Walsingham’s intricate spy system extended across Europe. His intelligence network detected the Spanish Armada preparations and kept the English government informed of Philip’s movements. His agents also tracked threats against Drake personally — including a plot to recruit John Doughty to kill or kidnap Drake for 20,000 ducats offered by Philip II. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt, lines 8708-8714]
Foreign Policy
Walsingham headed the bellicose cabal of councillors who urged greater English intervention on behalf of embattled Protestants in France and the Netherlands. He was frustrated by Elizabeth’s moderation and sought a more aggressive anti-Spanish policy. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt, lines 4585-4588]
Correspondence with Drake
Drake frequently corresponded with Walsingham. His dispatches were described as “frequently prayers” and in one typical example he addressed Walsingham in 1588. The survival of these letters provides key insights into Drake’s character and the conduct of the Armada campaign. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt, lines 654-658]
Death and Legacy
Walsingham died in London in April 1590 after a lifetime of poor health. He had not only been Drake’s friend, but the buttress of his influence in the Privy Council. Drake, who had already lost Leicester in September 1588, could ill afford to lose Walsingham as well. His death marked the beginning of the erosion of Drake’s standing at court. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt, lines 16386-16392]
Notably, even Walsingham — that devoted servant of state — earned no higher accolade than knighthood, highlighting the significance of the knighthood awarded to Drake, a man of humbler background. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt, lines 8641-8643]
