entities/francisco-roldan.content:
Francisco Roldan
Francisco Roldan (fl. 1490s–1500s) was a Spanish colonial administrator who served as alcalde mayor (chief magistrate) of Hispaniola under Christopher Columbus and his brother Bartholomew Columbus. He led the most serious rebellion against Columbus’s authority, establishing a rival government in the province of Xaragua, forcing Columbus into humiliating concessions — including grants of land and native labour to the rebels — and ultimately contributing to Columbus’s downfall and arrest.

Role in the Colony
Roldan was appointed alcalde mayor of Hispaniola, holding the highest judicial office in the colony under the Columbus brothers. During Columbus’s absence on the third voyage (1498) and the period of Bartholomew Columbus’s administration as adelantado, Roldan was entrusted with significant authority. However, the colony suffered from famine, disease, and the severe administration of Bartholomew, whose harsh discipline and imposition of tribute on the native population created widespread discontent among the Spanish colonists.^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book XI Ch. IV]

Conspiracy of Roldan
Taking advantage of the growing dissatisfaction, Roldan organized a conspiracy in 1497 against the Columbus brothers. As chief magistrate, he leveraged his position to gather malcontents around him — colonists who resented Bartholomew’s strict governance, those who had been punished for misconduct, and adventurers who chafed under the Admiral’s authority. Roldan accused the Columbus brothers of tyranny, misgovernment, and favouring foreigners over native Castilians.^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book XI Ch. IV]
When the Adelantado attempted to negotiate with Roldan, the rebel leader refused to submit. The interview ended in deadlock, and Roldan withdrew from the settlements to establish an independent base of operations.^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book XI Ch. V]

Establishment of a Rival Government at Xaragua
Roldan and his followers moved into the province of Xaragua (in the southwest of Hispaniola, near present-day Leogane, Haiti), a wealthy region ruled by the female cacique Anacaona. There, Roldan established a de facto rival government. The rebels lived licentiously among the native Taíno population, taking native women, appropriating food and resources, and effectively setting themselves up as independent lords beyond Columbus’s reach.^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XII Ch. I]
Xaragua became a refuge for all who were discontented with Columbus’s rule. The rebels enjoyed the hospitality and alliance of Anacaona, who appears to have calculated that supporting the Spanish rebels was preferable to submitting to Columbus’s tribute demands. Roldan’s position was strengthened by a stroke of fortune: three caravels that had separated from Columbus’s squadron at the Canary Islands drifted to Xaragua by currents, and Roldan deceived their captains into supplying him with arms, ammunition, and military stores, while his followers secretly recruited defectors among the ships’ crews.^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XII Ch. I]

Columbus’s Return and Negotiations
Columbus returned to St. Domingo on August 30, 1498, exhausted and ill with gout and ophthalmia, to find the colony in ruins. Famine had set in, cultivation had been neglected, and native villages were depopulated. The treasury was empty, and the rebel faction under Roldan controlled Xaragua with impunity.^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XII Ch. I]
Unable to suppress the rebellion by force — his health was broken, his forces depleted, and the colony’s resources exhausted — Columbus opened negotiations with Roldan through emissaries. Roldan responded with a formal list of grievances against the Columbus brothers, portraying them as oppressive foreigners. Columbus attempted to reconcile the rebels, offering terms for their return to obedience.^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XII Ch. II]
First Agreement
A provisional arrangement was reached: Roldan and his followers would return to submission in exchange for amnesty. The foundations of a settlement were laid, and several ships departed for Spain carrying Columbus’s dispatches alongside the accounts of the state of the colony.^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XII Ch. III]
Second Mutiny and Further Concessions
The first agreement quickly broke down. Roldan’s followers renewed their insubordination, demanding more substantial guarantees. Columbus, in a humiliating position and with no military option available, was forced into a second negotiation. This time the terms were far more damaging: Columbus formally reinstated Roldan as alcalde mayor and granted the rebel leader and his principal followers extensive land grants and assignments of native Indians (encomiendas).^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XII Ch. IV]

Grants of Land and Indian Labour
The grants to Roldan and his followers represented a landmark in colonial administration. Columbus, desperate to pacify the colony, authorized the distribution of land and the allocation of native labour to specific Spanish settlers — a precursor to the formal encomienda system. Roldan himself received substantial territories in Xaragua, along with the right to the labour of the Indians living there. These grants effectively rewarded rebellion and set a dangerous precedent by showing that armed insurrection against the crown’s representative could yield tangible rewards.^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XII Ch. V]
Several of the rebel leaders, having secured their fortunes, departed for Spain. Once there, their accounts — hostile to Columbus — fuelled the growing campaign at court against the Admiral.^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XII Ch. V]

Confrontation with Alonso de Ojeda
Shortly after the rebellion was settled, Alonso de Ojeda arrived on the western coast of Hispaniola with his own squadron, having obtained a license for discovery from Bishop Fonseca. Ojeda began independent operations and encroached on Columbus’s jurisdiction. Demonstrating Roldan’s newfound loyalty — or Columbus’s need to keep potential troublemakers busy — Columbus dispatched Roldan to confront Ojeda and assert the Admiral’s authority.^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XII Ch. VI]
Roldan and Ojeda engaged in a series of manoeuvres and negotiations. Ojeda attempted to win over Roldan’s followers and establish his own authority, but Roldan skillfully outmaneuvered him. Ojeda was eventually forced to depart from the island and returned to Spain with reports further damaging to Columbus.^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XII Ch. VII]

Conspiracy of Guevara and Moxica
While Roldan was now nominally reconciled, fresh conspiracies continued to erupt. Hernando de Guevara and Adrian de Moxica hatched a new plot against Bartholomew Columbus. The conspiracy was discovered and suppressed: Moxica was captured and executed, and Guevara was imprisoned. The persistence of rebellion in the colony — encouraged by the precedent Roldan had set — demonstrated that Columbus’s authority had been fatally undermined.^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XII Ch. VIII]

Aftermath: Bobadilla and Columbus’s Arrest
The rebels who returned to Spain were welcomed by Columbus’s enemies at court, including Bishop Juan Rodriguez de Fonseca. Every returning vessel brought fresh complaints against Columbus and his brothers, painting them as arrogant and oppressive foreigners unfit to govern. King Ferdinand’s patience was exhausted. In 1500, the sovereigns dispatched Francisco de Bobadilla as royal commissioner with full powers to investigate Columbus’s conduct and, if necessary, assume the government.^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XIII Ch. I]
Bobadilla arrived at San Domingo and, without any prior investigation, publicly read his commission, seized the fortress, took command of the colony, and ordered the seizure of Columbus’s property. He invited depositions against Columbus and his brothers — drawing testimony from the very men who had rebelled under Roldan.^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XIII Ch. II]
Columbus was arrested and sent to Spain in chains. The Roldan rebellion thus achieved, indirectly, what the rebels had sought: the removal of Columbus from government. Bobadilla himself was later superseded by Nicolas de Ovando, who arrived in 1502 with a massive fleet of 30 ships and 2,500 men.^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XIV Ch. III]

Significance
The rebellion of Francisco Roldan was the most consequential challenge to Columbus’s authority in the New World. It demonstrated the fragility of colonial governance, the vulnerability of an absentee governor, and the willingness of Spanish colonists to revolt against crown authority when their interests were denied. The concessions Columbus was forced to make — amnesty for rebels, reinstatement of Roldan, and the distribution of land and Indian labour — set important precedents for the encomienda system that would define Spanish colonial administration in the Caribbean for decades.
The rebellion also fatally damaged Columbus’s reputation. The rebels’ accusations, carried to Spain by every departing ship, convinced Ferdinand and Isabella that Columbus was incapable of governing. The appointment of Bobadilla and Columbus’s arrest in chains were direct consequences of the disorder Roldan had created.

Key Facts

entities/genoa-lisbon.title: Genoa and Lisbon — Columbus's Birthplace and Adopted Home
entities/genoa-lisbon.content:
Genoa and Lisbon — Columbus’s Birthplace and Adopted Home

Genoa
Genoa (Italian: Genova; Latin: Genua) is a port city on the Ligurian coast of northwestern Italy. In the fifteenth century it was a powerful maritime republic with a far-flung commercial empire reaching across the Mediterranean and into the Black Sea. It was the birthplace of Christopher Columbus, who was born there around 1435–1436, though the exact date and year remain uncertain.^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book I Ch. I]
Columbus’s Family Background
Columbus’s father, Domenico Colombo, was a wool-comber (lanaiuolo or cardatore di lana) who had long resided in Genoa. His trade was honest but humble, and the family was poor though respectable. Columbus was the eldest of four children. His brothers were Bartholomew (Bartolomeo) and Giacomo (also called Diego, the Spanish translation of his name). He had one sister, who married a man of obscure station named Giacomo Bavarello; nothing further is known of her.^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book I Ch. I]
The family surname in Italian is Colombo (meaning “dove”). Columbus himself latinized it to Columbus in his earlier letters, following the scholarly custom of the age. When he later moved to Spain he altered the name to Cristóbal Colón, a form derived from the supposed Latin root Colonus, adapted to Castilian.^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book I Ch. I]
Early Education
Columbus received a limited education, as befitted his family’s modest means. While still a child he was taught reading and writing — and wrote so good a hand, according to Las Casas, that he could have earned his bread by it. He also studied arithmetic, drawing, and painting, acquiring enough skill in each to have gained a livelihood. For a short time he was sent to the University of Pavia, the great school of learning in Lombardy, where he studied grammar and the Latin tongue. His education, however, was principally directed toward the sciences of maritime life: geometry, geography, astronomy (then called astrology), and navigation.^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book I Ch. I]
From his earliest childhood he evinced a strong passion for geographical science and an irresistible inclination for the sea. He later looked back on this early determination as a secret impulse from the Deity guiding him toward his destiny.^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book I Ch. I]
Apprenticeship at Sea
Columbus began his nautical career at the age of fourteen. Genoa, a city walled in by rugged mountains on the land side, offered little scope for enterprise on shore; but its opulent commerce and roving marine drew its youth naturally to the sea. The Mediterranean of this era was a rugged school: commercial voyages often resembled warlike cruises, piracy was semi-legitimized, and the seas were scenes of constant encounters between Italian states, Catalan privateers, and Mahometan powers.^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book I Ch. II]
The first recorded voyage of Columbus was a naval expedition outfitted at Genoa in 1459 by John of Anjou, Duke of Calabria, to recover the kingdom of Naples for his father King René (Reinier) of Provence. The republic of Genoa furnished ships and money; many private adventurers also fitted out vessels under the Anjou banner. Among these was a hardy sea-captain named Colombo — actually two naval characters, an uncle and nephew, whom Fernando Columbus claimed as family connections. With these commanders Columbus sailed on several occasions and for a considerable length of time.^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book I Ch. II]
Columbus at one time held a separate command in the service of King René and was employed in a daring enterprise to cut out a galley from the port of Tunis. The incident is preserved in Columbus’s own letter to Ferdinand and Isabella, written many years later. When his crew became fearful upon learning that two ships and a carrack were guarding the galley, and resolved to return to Marseilles, Columbus feigned compliance. He altered the ship’s compass at evening, and by the next morning the vessel was off Cape Carthagena while the crew still believed they were sailing toward Marseilles — a stratagem foreshadowing the false reckoning he would later employ on his first voyage of discovery.^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book I Ch. II]
There follows an interval of many years during which only shadowy traces of Columbus survive. He is supposed to have been principally engaged in the Mediterranean and the Levant, sometimes in commerce, sometimes in warlike contests between Italian states, sometimes in expeditions against the infidels. He visited the island of Scio (Chios) and saw the harvesting of mastic. According to some authorities, he commanded several Genoese ships in the service of Louis XI of France in 1474, and attacked Spanish galleys as reprisal for an incursion into Roussillon. Another report places him in command of a Genoese squadron off Cyprus in 1475–1476.^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book I Ch. II]
The Shipwreck off Portugal
The most dramatic episode of Columbus’s early maritime career — and the event that brought him to Portugal — is the desperate sea-fight narrated by his son Fernando. A Genoese corsair named Colombo the Younger, a kinsman of Columbus and a notorious rover, intercepted four richly laden Venetian galleys returning from Flanders on the Portuguese coast, between Lisbon and Cape St. Vincent. A furious engagement ensued, lasting from morning until evening. Columbus commanded a vessel that grappled with a huge Venetian galley; hand-grenades and fiery missiles were exchanged, and the galley burst into flames. The two ships, locked together by chains and iron grapplings, could not be separated, and both were consumed in a single conflagration. The crews threw themselves into the sea. Columbus seized a floating oar and, being an expert swimmer, reached the shore after a swim of two full leagues (approximately six miles).^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book I Ch. II]
After recovering from his exhaustion, Columbus repaired to Lisbon, where he found many of his Genoese countrymen and was induced to take up residence there. Modern historians note that the dating of this battle is problematic — it may have occurred in 1485, well after Columbus had left Portugal — and Fernando may have confused it with another action. Nonetheless, the story captures the hardihood and resourcefulness that marked Columbus’s early character.^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book I Ch. II]

Lisbon
Lisbon (Portuguese: Lisboa) is the capital and principal port of Portugal, situated on the north bank of the Tagus River where it opens into the Atlantic Ocean. In the late fifteenth century, under the reign of King Afonso V and then King John II, Lisbon became the vibrant hub of Portuguese maritime discovery — the great resort of men skilled in geographical and nautical science from all parts of the world. It was here that Columbus would spend the most formative years of his intellectual life, developing the theory that would lead to the discovery of the New World.^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book I Ch. IV]
Arrival and Marriage
Columbus arrived in Lisbon around 1470, in the full vigor of manhood. Contemporary descriptions — from his son Fernando and from Las Casas — portray him as tall, well-formed, muscular, and of an elevated and dignified demeanor. His visage was long, his complexion fair and freckled, inclined to ruddy; his nose aquiline, his cheek-bones rather high, his eyes light grey and apt to enkindle. His hair in youth was light in color, but care and trouble soon turned it grey; at thirty years of age it was quite white. He was moderate and simple in diet and apparel, eloquent in discourse, engaging and affable with strangers, and of an amiableness in domestic life that strongly attached his household to his person. His temper was naturally irritable, but he subdued it by magnanimity of spirit, comporting himself with courteous and gentle gravity. Throughout his life he was noted for strict attention to the offices of religion.^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book I Ch. IV]
While attending religious service at the Convent of All Saints in Lisbon, Columbus became acquainted with Doña Felipa Moñis de Perestrello (or Palestrello), a lady of rank who resided at the convent. She was the daughter of Bartolomeo Moñis de Perestrello, an Italian cavalier who had been one of the most distinguished navigators under Prince Henry the Navigator, and who had colonized and governed the island of Porto Santo in the Madeira archipelago. The acquaintance ripened into attachment and ended in marriage — apparently a match of mere affection, as the lady was destitute of fortune.^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book I Ch. IV]
This union fixed Columbus in Lisbon. The newly married couple went to reside with the mother of Felipa, who, perceiving Columbus’s interest in matters of the sea, related everything she knew of her late husband’s voyages and expeditions, and brought him all his papers, charts, journals, and memorandums. These were treasures to Columbus. He acquainted himself with all the routes of the Portuguese, their plans and conceptions, and by his marriage and residence became naturalized in Portugal.^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book I Ch. IV]
Years of Study and Chart-Making
Columbus sailed occasionally in Portuguese expeditions to the coast of Guinea. When on shore, he occupied himself in making maps and charts for the support of his family. His circumstances were limited, and he had to observe strict economy; nonetheless, he appropriated a part of his scanty means to the succor of his aged father in Genoa and to the education of his younger brothers.^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book I Ch. IV]
The construction of a correct map or chart in those days required considerable knowledge and skill, and the superior correctness of Columbus’s maps and charts gave him notoriety among men of science. Geography was just emerging from the darkness of the Middle Ages; Ptolemy remained the standard authority, and the maps of the fifteenth century displayed a mixture of truth and error. At this period, when the passion for maritime discovery was seeking every aid, the knowledge of an able cosmographer like Columbus was properly appreciated.^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book I Ch. IV]
As early as 1474, Columbus entered into correspondence with Paulo Toscanelli of Florence, one of the most scientific men of the day. Toscanelli’s communications had great influence in inspiriting Columbus toward his subsequent undertakings. In a letter applauding Columbus’s design of a westward voyage, Toscanelli sent him a map projected partly according to Ptolemy and partly according to the descriptions of Marco Polo. On this map, the eastern coast of Asia was depicted in front of the western coasts of Africa and Europe, with a moderate space of ocean between them, in which were placed the islands of Cipango (Japan) and Antilla at convenient distances. Columbus procured the work of Marco Polo, whose marvelous accounts of the riches of Cathay (northern China) and Mangi (southern China), and the gold-covered palace of the monarch of Cipango, inflamed his imagination and became a key to his subsequent representations to sovereigns.^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book I Ch. VI]
In 1477, Columbus made a voyage to the north of Europe, sailing one hundred leagues beyond Thule — generally supposed to be Iceland — in the month of February. He noted that the sea was not frozen, and that the tides rose and fell twenty-six fathoms. This voyage beyond the Ultima Thule of the ancients reveals his ardent and impatient desire to break away from the limits of the known world.^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book I Ch. VI]
Residence at Porto Santo
Columbus resided for some time at the recently discovered island of Porto Santo, where his wife had inherited some property. During this residence, Felipa bore him a son, whom he named Diego. Living on the very frontier of discovery, Columbus was frequently in company with his brother-in-law Pedro Correo, a navigator of note who had been governor of Porto Santo. Their domestic conversation naturally turned upon the discoveries prosecuting along the African coasts, the long-sought route to India, and the possibility of unknown lands existing in the west. The island residence was frequently visited by voyagers going to and from Guinea. Living thus surrounded by the stir and bustle of discovery, Columbus’s ardent mind kindled to enthusiasm.^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book I Ch. IV]
The Development of His Theory
Columbus’s theory of undiscovered lands in the west rested on three categories of evidence, as recorded by his son Fernando from his father’s papers:^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book I Ch. V]
1. The nature of things: The earth was a sphere that could be traveled around from east to west. Columbus, following Ptolemy and the earlier map of Marinus of Tyre, calculated that fifteen of the twenty-four hours of the earth’s circumference were known to the ancients (from the Canaries to the city of Thine in Asia). The Portuguese had advanced the western frontier (the Azores and Cape Verde) by one hour more, leaving eight hours — one-third of the globe — unknown. This space, he reasoned, must be largely filled by the eastern regions of Asia, which might extend so far as to approach the western shores of Europe and Africa. The intervening ocean would therefore be narrower than commonly supposed, especially if Alfraganus’s smaller estimate of the earth’s circumference were adopted.
2. Authority of learned writers: Aristotle, Seneca, and Pliny held that one might pass from Cadiz to the Indies in a few days. Strabo observed that the ocean surrounds the earth, bathing the shores of India on the east and those of Spain on the west. Marco Polo and Sir John Mandeville described the eastward extent of Asia far beyond Ptolemy’s limits, and their accounts of Cathay and Cipango convinced Columbus that a voyage of no great duration westward would bring him to those wealthy shores.
3. Reports of navigators: Martin Vicenti, a Portuguese pilot, reported finding a piece of carved wood — evidently not worked with an iron instrument — after sailing 450 leagues west of Cape St. Vincent. Pedro Correo had seen similar wood on Porto Santo. The King of Portugal reported giant reeds drifting from the west, which Columbus recognized as resembling the immense reeds said by Ptolemy to grow in India. Inhabitants of the Azores reported huge pine-trunks (of species unknown on those islands) and two dead men of unfamiliar features cast onto the island of Flores. A mariner from the port of St. Mary claimed to have seen land to the west while voyaging to Ireland.
From this chain of reasoning, Columbus concluded that undiscovered, fertile, and inhabited land existed in the western ocean and was attainable by a westward voyage.^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book I Ch. V]
Proposition to the Court of Portugal
After the application of the astrolabe to navigation — a timely invention that divested his enterprise of much of its hazardous character — Columbus obtained an audience with King John II of Portugal. He proposed, if the king would furnish ships and men, to undertake a shorter and more direct route to India than the African coastal route the Portuguese were pursuing. His plan was to strike directly west across the Atlantic. He unfolded his hypothesis concerning the extent of Asia and described the immense riches of the island of Cipango, the first land at which he expected to arrive.^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book I Ch. VII]
According to his son Fernando, the king listened with great attention and was initially discouraged by the cost and trouble already sustained in the African route. But Columbus supported his proposition with such excellent reasons that the king was induced to give consent; the only remaining difficulty was Columbus’s demands for high and honorable titles and rewards — demands he made, says Fernando, so that he might leave behind a name and family worthy of his deeds.
The Portuguese historian Barros, writing in a cooler spirit, attributes the king’s seeming acquiescence merely to importunity. The proposition was referred to a learned junto charged with matters of maritime discovery. This body consisted of Master Roderigo and Master Joseph (the king’s two physician-cosmographers) and Diego Ortiz de Cazadilla, Bishop of Ceuta, a man greatly reputed for learning. This scientific body treated the project as extravagant and visionary.^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book I Ch. VII]
The king convoked a larger council of prelates and learned men. The Bishop of Ceuta delivered a speech opposing not only Columbus’s project but all further African discoveries, arguing they drained the nation’s resources. The Count of Villa Real, Don Pedro de Meneses, replied with a lofty patriotic oration defending the Portuguese discoveries. The council ultimately condemned Columbus’s proposal.^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book I Ch. VII]
The Secret Caravel and Departure from Portugal
Certain councillors, seeing that the king remained dissatisfied and still harbored an inclination for the enterprise, suggested a stratagem. It was proposed that a caravel be secretly dispatched in the direction Columbus had pointed out to test his theory, while Columbus himself was kept in suspense. This perfidious advice — attributed to the Bishop of Ceuta — the king unfortunately accepted.^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book I Ch. VIII]
Columbus was required to furnish a detailed plan of his proposed voyage, with charts and documents. He complied readily. A caravel was then despatched under the pretext of carrying provisions to the Cape Verde Islands, but with private instructions to pursue the route Columbus had designated. Departing from those islands, the caravel stood westward for several days until stormy weather, the pilots’ lack of zeal, and the sight of nothing but an immeasurable waste of waves caused them to lose courage. They put back to the Cape Verdes and then to Lisbon, excusing their failure by ridiculing Columbus’s project as extravagant and irrational.^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book I Ch. VIII]
This unworthy attempt to defraud him of his enterprise aroused Columbus’s indignation. King John is said to have offered to renew the negotiation, but Columbus resolutely declined. His wife Felipa had died by this time; the domestic tie that bound him to Portugal was broken. Toward the end of 1484, he departed secretly from Lisbon, taking with him his young son Diego. He feared being prevented by the king, and his affairs had run to ruin — he was even in danger of arrest for debt.^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book I Ch. VIII]
From Portugal, Columbus carried his proposal first to Genoa, where he appealed to his native republic but received a contemptuous refusal. The Genoese republic, languishing under a long decline and embarrassed by war, was in no condition to undertake such a venture. He then proceeded to Venice, where an old tradition holds that his offer was declined due to the critical state of national affairs. After visiting his aged father in Genoa, Columbus departed to try his fortunes in the Spanish court — the beginning of a new and decisive chapter in his career.^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book I Ch. VIII]

Key Facts

entities/golden-hind.title: Golden Hind
entities/golden-hind.content:
Golden Hind
Overview
The Golden Hind (originally named the Pelican) was Drake’s flagship on his circumnavigation of the globe (1577-1580). She was destined to make but one major voyage and yet became one of the most famous ships in history. Until recently her portrait adorned the British halfpenny. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Specifications
The Pelican-Golden Hind was a galleon of little more than 150 tons and only some 80 feet from stem to stern-post. Contemporary estimates of her tonnage range between 100 and 150 tons, the discrepancy arising from different methods of calculation in Drake’s day. A dock built to enclose her at Deptford in 1581 required a wall some 180 feet in perimeter with a breadth of 24 feet to allow for a walkway. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Armament
She carried an armament of eighteen brass and iron guns. Her hull was sturdy and sheathed with extra planking to defend against rot. She proved to be a good sailer, responsive to her helm, though she shipped some water both from abeam and astern in heavy seas. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Renaming
The ship was rechristened the Golden Hind at Port St. Julian, at the entrance to the Magellan Strait, on 20 August 1578. The new name honoured Sir Christopher Hatton, the queen’s favourite courtier and Captain of the Queen’s Guard, whose family crest featured a golden hind (a female red deer). Drake probably wanted to flatter his patron after the execution of Thomas Doughty, who had been Hatton’s servant. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
The Circumnavigation
The Pelican was the flagship of a squadron of five ships: the Elizabeth (80 tons, sixteen guns), the Marigold (30 tons, sixteen guns), the Swan flyboat (50 tons, five guns), the Benedict pinnace (15 tons, one gun), plus four pinnaces carried in pieces for assembly later. The crew numbered about 160 men and boys, with up to eighty people packed into the little Pelican. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Knighthood
Drake brought the Golden Hind from Plymouth to Deptford so that Queen Elizabeth I might see her. On 1 April 1581, a vast crowd turned out to honour Drake. After a banquet aboard the ship, Elizabeth had the French ambassador, Monsieur de Marchaumont, perform the ceremony of knighthood. Elizabeth I was thus famously knighted aboard the Golden Hind. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Preservation
After the voyage the Golden Hind was preserved at Deptford for decades, enclosed in a purpose-built dock. She became a tourist attraction. Eventually she rotted away, but the name remained a symbol of English maritime achievement. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]

entities/guanahani-san-salvador.title: Guanahani / San Salvador
entities/guanahani-san-salvador.content:
Guanahani / San Salvador
Guanahani (the Taíno/Lucayan name) — renamed San Salvador by Christopher Columbus on October 12, 1492 — was the first island of the New World where Columbus set foot during his first voyage across the Atlantic. The landfall ended 33 days of sailing westward from the Canary Islands and initiated sustained European contact with the Americas. The island is part of the Bahama archipelago (the Lucayan Islands, called “Gucayos” or “Lucayos” by Irving), which stretches southeast to northwest from the coast of Florida to Hispaniola, covering the northern coast of Cuba.^[source: irving_columbus_full.txt, Book IV, Ch. I, p. 247]
The Landfall (October 12, 1492)
According to Irving’s account, drawn from Columbus’s journal as preserved by Las Casas:
On the night of October 11, Columbus thought he saw a light in the distance — “a glimmering light” like a wax candle rising and falling — which he pointed out to Pedro Gutierrez, a gentleman of the King’s bedchamber. Gutierrez also saw it, as did Rodrigo Sanchez of Segovia, though the light was so faint and uncertain that others dismissed it as an illusion. At two o’clock on the morning of October 12, the Pinta, sailing ahead, fired a signal gun: land was in sight. The lookout was Rodrigo de Triana, a seaman of that vessel.^[source: irving_columbus_full.txt, Book III, Ch. IV]
At dawn, Columbus beheld a level and beautiful island several leagues in extent, of great freshness and verdure, covered with trees “like a continual orchard.” Though everything appeared in the wild luxuriance of untamed nature, the island was clearly populous: inhabitants emerged from the woods and ran to the shore from all parts, standing and gazing at the ships in astonishment. They were perfectly naked, and from their attitudes and gestures appeared lost in wonder at the strange vessels hovering on their coast.^[source: irving_columbus_full.txt, Book IV, Ch. I, pp. 236-237]
Relevant primary-source guide: irving-columbus, Book IV, Chapter I.
Columbus’s Naming
Columbus gave the island the name San Salvador (“Holy Saviour”), reflecting his deep religious piety and his understanding of the providential nature of the discovery. He performed this naming as part of the formal ceremony of taking possession (see below). At the time, Columbus believed he had arrived at an island off the coast of Asia, somewhere in the “Chinese Sea” near the opulent regions described by Marco Polo — Cipango (Japan) and Cathay (China). This misidentification colored all his subsequent interpretations of what he encountered.^[source: irving_columbus_full.txt, Book IV, Ch. I, pp. 237, 241-242]
The native name, as recorded by Columbus and preserved in his journal, was Guanahani (spelled Guanahanè by Irving).^[source: irving_columbus_full.txt, Book IV, Ch. I, p. 247]
The Ceremonial Taking of Possession
Columbus’s landing was conducted as a formal act of state, meticulously staged to establish a legal claim under the authority of the Spanish Crown:


The approach: Columbus made signal for the ships to cast anchor and the boats to be manned and armed. He entered his own boat, richly attired in scarlet, bearing the royal standard. Martin Alonso Pinzon and Vicente Yañez Pinzon followed in their boats, each bearing the banner of the enterprise — a green cross with the letters F and I (Fernando and Isabel) surmounted by crowns.^[source: irving_columbus_full.txt, Book IV, Ch. I, p. 236]


Thanksgiving on landing: No sooner did Columbus land than he threw himself on his knees, kissed the earth, and returned thanks to God with tears of joy. His example was followed by the rest, whose hearts overflowed with gratitude.^[source: irving_columbus_full.txt, Book IV, Ch. I, p. 237]


Solemn possession: Columbus rose, drew his sword, displayed the royal standard, and assembled around him the two Pinzon captains, Rodrigo de Escobedo (notary of the armament), Rodrigo Sanchez, and all who had landed. He then took solemn possession in the name of the Catholic Sovereigns Ferdinand and Isabella, giving the island the name San Salvador. Having complied with the requisite forms and ceremonies, he called upon all present to take the oath of obedience to him as Admiral and Viceroy representing the persons of the Sovereigns.^[source: irving_columbus_full.txt, Book IV, Ch. I, p. 237]


Emotions of the crew: The crew, who had recently considered themselves “devoted men hurrying forward to destruction,” now gave themselves up to unbounded joy. They thronged around the Admiral — some embraced him, others kissed his hands. Even those who had been most mutinous and turbulent during the voyage became the most devoted and enthusiastic.^[source: irving_columbus_full.txt, Book IV, Ch. I, pp. 237-238]


Irving includes a note that a form of prayer — “Domine Deus aeterne et omnipotens, sacro tuo verbo caelum, et terram, et mare creasti…” — was later composed by Padre Claudio Clemente and, by order of the Castilian sovereigns, was used by Balboa, Cortes, and Pizarro in their discoveries.^[source: irving_columbus_full.txt, Book IV, Ch. I, p. 237, footnote]
The Taíno (Lucayan) Inhabitants
The inhabitants of Guanahani were Taíno people of the Lucayan branch, who inhabited the Bahama archipelago. Irving describes them in detail based on Columbus’s journal:


Appearance: Of tawny or copper complexion, entirely without beards, with straight coarse hair (not crisped like African peoples under the same latitude). They cut their hair short above the ears but left some locks falling on the shoulders. Their features, though obscured and disfigured by paint, were agreeable; they had lofty foreheads and remarkably fine eyes. They were of moderate stature and well-shaped; most appeared under thirty years of age. Only one female was present with the initial landing party — quite young, naked, and beautifully formed.^[source: irving_columbus_full.txt, Book IV, Ch. I, pp. 240-241]


Body painting: They painted themselves with a variety of colours — some confined to the face, nose, or around the eyes; others covering the whole body, giving a wild and fantastic appearance.^[source: irving_columbus_full.txt, Book IV, Ch. I, p. 241]


Disposition: Friendly, gentle, simple, and artless. They approached the Spaniards with great awe, frequently prostrating themselves on the earth and making signs of adoration. They universally believed the white men had come from the sky — an idea Irving notes was “universally entertained by the inhabitants of the New World.”^[source: irving_columbus_full.txt, Book IV, Ch. I, pp. 239-240]


Arms and tools: Their only weapons were lances hardened at the end by fire, or pointed with a flint, or the tooth or bone of a fish. They had no iron and did not understand its properties — when a drawn sword was presented to them, they unguardedly took it by the edge.^[source: irving_columbus_full.txt, Book IV, Ch. I, pp. 241-242]


Canoes and navigation: They used light barks called canoes, formed from a single hollowed tree, capable of holding from one to forty or fifty people. These they managed dexterously with paddles; if overturned, they righted them with great facility.^[source: irving_columbus_full.txt, Book IV, Ch. I, p. 243]


Subsistence: They cultivated yuca (cassava), a large root from which they made cassava bread — a thin broad cake that hardened and could be kept for long periods, requiring steeping in water before eating. They had abundance of cotton, which they spun into yarn and traded in large balls. They also kept domesticated parrots.^[source: irving_columbus_full.txt, Book IV, Ch. I, pp. 242-244]


Trade goods: Columbus distributed coloured caps, glass beads, hawks’-bells, and other trifles (typical of Portuguese trade on the African gold coast). The natives received these as inestimable gifts, hanging beads around their necks. They eagerly exchanged fragments of gold worn as nose ornaments for glass beads and hawks’-bells.^[source: irving_columbus_full.txt, Book IV, Ch. I, pp. 242-245]


Columbus, believing he had reached Asia, called the natives Indians (Indios) — a name that was universally adopted and extended to all aboriginals of the New World.^[source: irving_columbus_full.txt, Book IV, Ch. I, pp. 241-242]
Subsequent Exploration of the Island
On October 14, the Admiral set off at daybreak with the ship’s boats to reconnoitre the island, directing his course to the northeast. The coast was surrounded by a reef of rocks within which there was depth of water and a sufficient harbour, though the entrance was very narrow. The island appeared well-wooded with streams of water and a large lake in the centre. Passing two or three villages, the inhabitants — men and women — ran to the shores, prostrating themselves and lifting up their hands and eyes, either giving thanks to heaven or worshipping the Spaniards as supernatural beings. Many swam after the boats or followed in canoes. The expedition came to a small peninsula where they could have fortified a position, though Columbus judged no fortification necessary given the gentleness of the people.^[source: irving_columbus_full.txt, Book IV, Ch. I, pp. 247-249]
Columbus took seven natives from Guanahani to serve as interpreters and guides for the further voyage. These Lucayan interpreters later accompanied him to Cuba and Hispaniola. Irving notes that during subsequent voyages, Columbus refrained from touching at islands near Guanahani because his Indian interpreters, “who were from the island of Guanahani, only eight leagues from that of Isabella, might desert, the poor savages keeping a wistful eye in the direction of their home.”^[source: irving_columbus_full.txt, Book VIII, Ch. III]
Modern Identification Debates
The precise island at which Columbus first made landfall has been a matter of scholarly debate since at least the early nineteenth century. Irving himself notes the dispute:

“The island where Columbus had thus, for the first time, set his foot upon the New World, was called by the natives, Guanahane. It still retains the name of San Salvador, which he gave to it, though called by the English Cat Island. The light which he had seen the evening previous to his making land, may have been on Watling’s Island, which lies a few leagues to the east.”^[source: irving_columbus_full.txt, Book IV, Ch. I, p. 247]

Irving adds that “some dispute having recently arisen as to the island on which Columbus first landed,” referring readers to the “Illustrations” section of his work, Article “First Landing of Columbus,” for a full discussion.^[source: irving_columbus_full.txt, Book IV, Ch. I, p. 247, footnote]
Key candidates in the modern debate include:

























CandidateDescriptionWatlings Island (officially renamed San Salvador Island in 1926 by the Bahamian government)The most widely accepted candidate among 20th-century scholars. Fits Columbus’s log distances and descriptions. The light Columbus saw on October 11 may have been on this island.Cat Island (the original English name for what was then called San Salvador)Irving identifies this as the English name for San Salvador itself. However, the light sighting suggests a separate island to the east.Samana CayProposed by National Geographic (1986) based on computer analysis of Columbus’s log by Joseph Judge. Less accepted by subsequent scholarship.Plana Cays / Mayaguana / other Bahamian islandsVarious other candidates have been proposed, but none have achieved consensus.
The official position of the Bahamian government is that Watlings Island was renamed San Salvador Island in 1926 to recognize its historical significance as Columbus’s first landfall, though the scholarly debate continues.^[source: irving_columbus_full.txt, Book IV, Ch. I, p. 247]
Key Facts

Native name: Guanahani (recorded as Guanahane by Irving)
Columbus’s name: San Salvador (given October 12, 1492)
Modern name: San Salvador Island, Bahamas (formerly Watlings Island, 1926 renaming); also historically called Cat Island by English mariners
Coordinates: Approximately 24°N, 74°W (San Salvador Island, Bahamas)
Archipelago: Lucayan Islands (Bahamas), called “Gucayos” by the Spanish
Date of discovery: October 12, 1492 (Julian calendar)
Original inhabitants: Taíno people of the Lucayan branch
First European to sight land: Rodrigo de Triana (lookout on the Pinta)
Notary of the landing: Rodrigo de Escobedo
Interpreters taken: Seven Lucayan natives who accompanied Columbus on the remainder of the first voyage
Distance from Hispaniola: approximately 8 leagues from Isabella (Hispaniola’s northeastern coast) ^[source: irving_columbus_full.txt, Book VIII, Ch. III]

Relationship to Other Entities

Christopher Columbus — The explorer who made landfall at Guanahani and renamed it San Salvador, commencing the first voyage
Martin Alonso Pinzon — Captain of the Pinta, who commanded the lead ship that first sighted land (via lookout Rodrigo de Triana)
Ferdinand and Isabella — The Catholic Monarchs in whose name Columbus took possession of the island
Caonabo — The cacique of Maguana on Hispaniola (a different branch of the Taíno people), who led native resistance against the Spanish
irving-columbus — Primary source containing the Irving account of the landfall in Book IV, Chapter I, with additional discussion in the Appendix

entities/hispaniola.title: Hispaniola
entities/hispaniola.content:
Hispaniola: the island where Columbus founded the first European settlements, fought the Battle in the Vega Real, was arrested by Bobadilla, and where Ovando’s massacre at Xaragua ended organized Taíno resistance.
Hispaniola
Hispaniola (known to its indigenous Taino inhabitants as Hayti or Ayiti, meaning “mountainous land”) is the second-largest island of the Greater Antilles, discovered by Christopher Columbus on December 5, 1492, during his first voyage. It was the site of the first sustained European settlement in the Americas and the theatre of the earliest conflicts between Europeans and Native Americans. The island served as the administrative and economic heart of the Spanish Indies for the first three decades after discovery, and its native population was devastated within a generation by war, forced labour, and introduced disease. ^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book IV Ch. VI]

Discovery (Book IV, Chapter VI)
On December 5, 1492, after leaving the coast of Cuba and sailing east-northeast in search of the reported golden island of Babeque, Columbus’s remaining two ships — the Niña and the wrecked Santa Maria — sighted a large landmass on the horizon. From a distance the island appeared vast, mountainous, and densely wooded. Columbus named it La Isla Espanola (the Spanish Island), later Latinized as Hispaniola. The natives whom Columbus encountered called their land Hayti. ^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book IV Ch. VI]
Columbus anchored in a harbour he named Puerto de la Concepcion, near the territory of the cacique Guacanagari, who came aboard the Niña bearing gifts of gold ornaments, cotton, and cassava bread. The admiral was struck by the beauty of the island — its towering mountains, broad valleys, and rivers abundant with gold dust in their sands. Guacanagari gave Columbus reports of rich gold deposits in the interior, particularly in a mountainous region the natives called Cibao. ^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book IV Ch. VI–VII]
The fleet spent the next two weeks coasting the northern shore of Hispaniola, trading with the natives and confirming the presence of gold. On Christmas Eve 1492, the Santa Maria ran aground on a reef and was wrecked beyond salvage off the coast near present-day Limonade, Haiti. ^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book IV Ch. VIII]

Taino Name and Caciquates
At the time of Columbus’s arrival, the island was called Hayti (variously rendered as Ayiti, Bohio, or Quizqueia) by its Taino inhabitants. It was divided into five principal caciquates (chiefdoms), each ruled by a cacique who exercised authority over a defined territory and its villages. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VIII]
The five caciquates were:

Marien — The northwestern region, ruled by the friendly cacique Guacanagari, who assisted Columbus after the wreck of the Santa Maria. Marien was the first native domain contacted by the Europeans.
Maguana — The central mountainous region, encompassing the gold mines of Cibao. Ruled by the formidable Carib cacique Caonabo, the most powerful and warlike of the Taino chieftains, who led the destruction of La Navidad and organized the first organized resistance against Spanish encroachment. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VIII Ch. III]
Higuey — The easternmost province, a fertile and populous region that later offered stiff resistance to the Spanish under the cacique Cotabanama during Ovando’s governorship. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XVII Ch. III]
Maguá — The northeastern region, ruled by the cacique Guarionex, who initially submitted to Spanish tribute demands but later led two insurrections in the Vega Real before being captured by Bartholomew Columbus. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book XI Ch. II]
Xaragua — The southwestern region, centred on the fertile plain of present-day Leogane, Haiti. Ruled by the female cacique Anacaona (sister of the former cacique Behechio), Xaragua was the wealthiest and most populous of the Taino domains, renowned for its agricultural abundance and the grace and hospitality of its people. Xaragua became the refuge of Francisco Roldan’s rebels and later the site of Ovando’s infamous massacre. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XII Ch. I] ^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XVII Ch. II]


Settlement of La Navidad
After the wreck of the Santa Maria on Christmas Eve 1492, Columbus decided to establish the first European settlement in the New World using the timbers of the ruined ship. With the assistance of Guacanagari, the Spaniards built a fortified compound on the northern coast, near present-day Bord de Mer de Limonade, Haiti. Columbus named it La Navidad (The Nativity) in commemoration of the Christmas event. ^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book IV Ch. X]
Columbus selected 39 volunteers to remain as the garrison — men who, Irving notes, were eager to be released from the discipline of the ships and who anticipated easy wealth from the gold of the interior. Columbus left them with supplies, arms, and instructions to treat the natives with respect and to build a stockade. He also left one of his ships’ boats for coastal communication. On January 4, 1493, Columbus departed for Spain aboard the Niña, expecting to return within the year to a thriving settlement. ^[source: irving-columbus.md, Book IV Ch. XI]
When Columbus returned on his second voyage in November 1493, he found La Navidad utterly destroyed. The fortress had been burned to the ground, and the corpses of the 39 colonists lay among the ruins. The settlement had fallen into disorder soon after Columbus’s departure: the colonists quarrelled among themselves, abused the hospitality of the natives, and provoked the wrath of Caonabo, who led a surprise assault that annihilated the entire garrison. Only Guacanagari remained loyal to the Spaniards, claiming to have been wounded in their defence. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VIII Ch. III] ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VIII Ch. IV]

Founding of Isabella (Isabella)
With La Navidad destroyed, Columbus selected a new site for the capital of the Spanish colony on the northern coast of Hispaniola, near the mouth of the Yagui River in present-day Puerto Plata province, Dominican Republic. The settlement was named Isabella (La Isabela) in honour of Queen Isabella of Castile. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VII]
Construction began in January 1494. Isabella was the first planned European city in the Americas, laid out with a central plaza, a church, a storehouse, a municipal hall, and stone buildings. The fleet of 17 ships and 1,500 men that Columbus had brought on the second voyage provided the labour to construct the town. However, the colony was immediately stricken by disease — the Europeans, unaccustomed to the tropical climate, fell victim to fevers and dysentery. Famine set in as provisions spoiled or were exhausted. Within months, Isabella became a place of suffering, and Columbus’s authority was challenged by the insubordination of Pedro Margarite and the complaints of disaffected colonists. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VII Ch. I]
Despite its hardships, Isabella served as the base for Columbus’s expeditions into the interior — including the exploration of the Cibao gold mines and the campaign against Caonabo — and remained the capital of Hispaniola until the founding of Santo Domingo on the southern coast in 1496.

The Mines of Cibao
The mountainous interior of Hispaniola, known to the Taino as Cibao, was the principal source of gold on the island. Native reports of rich alluvial gold in the Cibao rivers had been a primary motive for Columbus’s interest in the island during his first voyage. After establishing Isabella, Columbus personally led an expedition into the Cibao mountains in early 1494, confirming the presence of gold in quantity. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VIII Ch. VI]
To secure the gold region, Columbus ordered the construction of the fortress of Santo Tomas in the heart of Cibao, garrisoned by fifty men under the command of Alonso de Ojeda. This fortress, built within the domain of Caonabo, provoked the cacique’s siege and the subsequent campaign of native resistance. Later, the even richer mines of Hayna were discovered in the southern part of the island, further fuelling Spanish expectations of limitless wealth. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VIII Ch. X]
Columbus imposed a tribute system on the native population: every Indian over the age of 14 was required to deliver a hawk’s bell full of gold dust every three months, or in lieu of gold, an arroba (25 pounds) of cotton. This levy proved impossible to collect, inflicting severe hardship on the native population and sparking the rebellion of Guarionex in the Vega Real. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VIII Ch. VII]

The Vega Real
The Vega Real (Royal Valley) was the great fertile plain in the north-central part of Hispaniola, running east-west between the Cordillera Septentrional and the Cordillera Central mountains. It was the agricultural heartland of the Taino population, especially the caciquate of Maguá under Guarionex, and was famed for its remarkable fertility and dense settlement. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VIII Ch. VI]
In March 1495, provoked by the cruelty of the Spaniards and the imposition of the gold tribute, the cacique Guarionex assembled a large army of native warriors and attacked the Spanish settlements in the Vega Real. Columbus, with his brother Bartholomew Columbus and Alonso de Ojeda, marched into the valley at the head of 200 infantry, 20 cavalry, and a number of war-dogs. The Battle of the Vega Real was the first large-scale European-Indian engagement in the New World. The Spanish cavalry, firearms, and attack dogs routed the native forces, who had never before faced horses or heard gunfire. Thousands of Taino were killed for the loss of a few Spaniards. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VIII Ch. VI]
The victory was followed by the formal imposition of tribute on the caciques of the Vega, a system that deepened native misery and led to further insurrections under Guarionex (second rebellion, 1497) and continued resistance throughout the interior. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book XI Ch. II]

The Rebellion of Roldan
The most serious internal challenge to Spanish authority in early Hispaniola was the revolt of Francisco Roldan, the alcalde mayor (chief magistrate) of the colony. During Columbus’s absence on the third voyage (1498), Roldan assembled a following of discontented colonists who resented the strict governance of Bartholomew Columbus, the adelantado. Roldan withdrew to the province of Xaragua, where he established a rival government with the backing of the female cacique Anacaona, living licentiously among the Taino and recruiting defectors from passing ships. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XII Ch. I]
When Columbus returned to San Domingo on August 30, 1498 — exhausted and ill with gout and ophthalmia — he found the colony in ruins: famine had set in, cultivation was abandoned, native villages were depopulated, and Roldan’s rebels controlled the richest province with impunity. Unable to suppress the rebellion by force, Columbus was forced to negotiate. Roldan was reinstated as alcalde mayor and received extensive grants of land and native labour (encomiendas) for himself and his principal followers — a humiliating concession that set a dangerous precedent by rewarding armed insurrection. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XII Ch. III–V]
The rebellion fatally undermined Columbus’s authority. The rebels’ accusations — carried to Spain by every departing ship — painted Columbus and his brothers as oppressive foreigners, fuelling the campaign at court that led to the dispatch of Francisco de Bobadilla. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XII Ch. V]

Bobadilla’s Administration
In 1500, the Spanish sovereigns dispatched Francisco de Bobadilla as royal commissioner with full powers to investigate Columbus’s conduct and, if necessary, assume the government of Hispaniola. Bobadilla arrived at San Domingo (the new capital on the southern coast, founded in 1496 and later renamed Santo Domingo) and, without any preliminary investigation, publicly read his commission, seized the fortress, and broadcast accusations against Columbus. He invited depositions — drawing testimony from Roldan’s former rebels — and ordered the arrest of Christopher Columbus, his brother Bartholomew, and his younger brother Diego. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XIII Ch. I–II]
Columbus was placed in chains and shipped to Spain. During the voyage, he famously refused to have the irons removed, declaring that he would wear them until the sovereigns ordered their removal. Bobadilla’s administration was marked by corruption, self-enrichment, and the further exploitation of the native population. He was himself superseded within two years by Nicolas de Ovando, who arrived in 1502 with a massive fleet of 30 ships and 2,500 settlers. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XIII Ch. IV] ^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XIV Ch. III]

Ovando’s Massacre at Xaragua
Nicolas de Ovando, the third governor of Hispaniola, embarked on a systematic policy of subjugation and exploitation of the native population. He introduced the repartimiento system, which divided Taino villages among Spanish settlers as sources of forced labour in the mines and fields. The native population suffered catastrophic decline under this system. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XVII Ch. I]
The most notorious event of Ovando’s governorship was the massacre at Xaragua in 1503. Suspecting the female cacique Anacaona of plotting rebellion — she had previously allied with Francisco Roldan — Ovando led a military expedition to Xaragua under the pretext of a friendly visit. The Spanish staged a grand festival, inviting the native nobles to participate in games and entertainments. At a prearranged signal, the Spanish fell upon the unarmed Taino nobility and massacred them. Anacaona was captured, subjected to a mock trial, and publicly executed. The province of Xaragua was devastated, and its surviving population was dispersed into the encomienda system. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XVII Ch. II]
The massacre at Xaragua was followed by the war against the eastern province of Higuey, where the cacique Cotabanama led a desperate resistance. The Spanish, employing cavalry, dogs, and brutal tactics, systematically subdued the province. By 1504, organized indigenous resistance on Hispaniola was effectively crushed. The native population, estimated at several hundred thousand at the time of Columbus’s arrival, had been reduced to a fraction of its former number through war, forced labour, introduced diseases, and outright slaughter. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XVII Ch. III–IV]

Significance
Hispaniola was the crucible of European colonization in the New World. The patterns established there — the encomienda and repartimiento systems, the use of horses and dogs in warfare, the imposition of gold tributes, the treatment of native populations as resources to be exploited — became templates for Spanish colonial administration throughout the Americas. The destruction of the Taino civilization of Hispaniola within a generation of European contact stands as the first and most complete genocide of the colonial era, and the island’s subsequent history — as the home of the first colonial capital (Santo Domingo), as the birthplace of African slavery in the Americas (with the introduction of enslaved Africans as early as 1503), and as the site of the first sustained European-native conflicts — established precedents that would echo across the hemisphere for centuries. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XVII Ch. I]

Key Facts





















































































AttributeDetailTaino NameHayti (Ayiti), meaning “mountainous land”European NameHispaniola (La Isla Espanola), also called Santo DomingoDiscoveredDecember 5, 1492 (Book IV, Chapter VI)DiscovererChristopher ColumbusFirst SettlementLa Navidad (December 1492 — destroyed 1493)First CapitalIsabella (founded January 1494)Subsequent CapitalSanto Domingo (founded 1496, southern coast)CaciquatesMarién, Maguana, Higuey, Maguá, XaraguaPrincipal Gold RegionCibao (central mountains)Great ValleyVega Real (north-central plain)Major Native LeadersGuacanagari, Caonabo, Anacaona, Guarionex, Behechio, CotabanamaMajor Spanish FiguresChristopher Columbus, Bartholomew Columbus, Alonso de Ojeda, Francisco Roldan, Francisco de Bobadilla, Nicolas de OvandoFirst GovernorChristopher Columbus (1492–1500)Second GovernorFrancisco de Bobadilla (1500–1502)Third GovernorNicolas de Ovando (1502–1509)Native Population (1492)Estimated 300,000–1,000,000 TainoNative Population (1508)Estimated 60,000–90,000 (90%+ decline in one generation)Irving CoverageVol. I, Book IV Ch. VI–XI (discovery, La Navidad); Vol. II, Book VII–XI (Isabella, Cibao, Vega Real, Roldan); Vol. III, Book XII–XVII (Roldan rebellion, Bobadilla, Ovando, Xaragua massacre)ConfidenceMedium — details drawn from Irving’s synthesis of Las Casas, Herrera, Peter Martyr, Fernando Columbus, Oviedo, and Charlevoix

entities/jamaica-columbus.title: Jamaica (Columbus)
entities/jamaica-columbus.content:
Jamaica
Jamaica (the Taíno name, preserved from Columbus’s naming attempt Santiago) is the third-largest island of the Greater Antilles, discovered by Christopher Columbus on May 5, 1494, during his second voyage. Columbus visited Jamaica twice: first in May–August 1494 during the exploration of the second voyage, and again from June 1503 to June 1504, when the island became the stage for the shipwreck, the canoe voyage of Diego Mendez, the mutiny of Porras, and the famous eclipse stratagem. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VII Ch. II–VII]

Discovery (May 1494 — Book VII, Chapter II)
On April 24, 1494, Columbus sailed from Isabella on the north coast of Hispaniola to explore the coasts of Cuba and the neighbouring islands. After coasting the eastern end of Cuba and entering the harbour of Puerto Grande (Guantánamo), he set sail southeastward. He had not sailed many leagues before the blue summits of Jamaica began to rise above the horizon. It was two days and nights before he reached the island, filled with admiration as he gradually drew near at its vast size, the beauty of its mountains, the majesty of its forests, the fertility of its valleys, and the great number of villages animating the face of the country. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VII Ch. II]
On approaching the land, at least seventy canoes filled with savages gaily painted and decorated with feathers sallied forth more than a league from shore. They advanced in warlike array, uttering loud yells and brandishing lances of pointed wood. The mediation of the interpreter and a few presents to one of the canoes that ventured nearer than the rest soothed this angry armada, and the squadron pursued its course unmolested. Columbus anchored in a harbour about the centre of the island, which from the great beauty of the surrounding country he named Santa Gloria — it is the same at present called St. Ann’s Bay. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VII Ch. II]
First Landing and Coasting of the North Shore
The following morning, Columbus weighed anchor and coasted westward in search of a sheltered harbour where his ship could be careened. After proceeding a few leagues, two large canoes filled with Indians issued forth to oppose their landing. The entire beach was covered with Indians painted in a variety of colours, chiefly black, wearing tufts and coronets of tropical feathers. Unlike the hospitable islanders of Cuba and Hayti, these appeared to partake of the warlike character of the Caribs. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VII Ch. II]
Columbus ordered the boats, well manned and armed, to row close to shore and let fly a volley of arrows from crossbows, wounding several Indians and throwing the rest into confusion. The Spaniards sprang on shore and put the multitude to flight, letting loose upon them a dog who pursued them with sanguinary fury. This is the first instance of the use of dogs against the natives in the New World, a tactic later employed with cruel effect in the Indian wars. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VII Ch. II]
Columbus now landed and took formal possession of the island, giving it the name Santiago; but fortunately it retained its original Taíno name of Jamaica. The harbour, from its commodiousness, he called Puerto Bueno (now Dry Harbour); it was in the form of a horse-shoe with a river in its vicinity. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VII Ch. II]
After three days of amicable intercourse, the natives appeared more ingenious as well as more warlike than their neighbours of Cuba and Hayti. Their canoes were better constructed, ornamented with carving and painting. Many were of great size, formed from the trunks of single mahogany trees. Columbus measured one that was ninety-six feet long and eight feet broad. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VII Ch. II]
Proceeding about twenty-four leagues along the coast, Columbus approached the western extremity, where the coast bent south. Being disappointed in his hopes of finding gold in Jamaica, and a fair breeze springing up for Cuba, he determined to return thither. To the last place at which he touched he gave the name of the Gulf of Buen-tiempo (Fair Weather) on account of the propitious wind. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VII Ch. II]
Coasting of the South Shore (July–August 1494 — Book VII, Chapter VI)
After exploring the southern coast of Cuba and navigating the labyrinth of the Queen’s Garden (Jardines de la Reina), Columbus, the wind continuing contrary for Hispaniola, stood across for Jamaica on July 22, 1494, intending to complete the circumnavigation of that island. For nearly a month he continued beating to the eastward along its southern coast, landing at a large village where the cacique presented gifts. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VII Ch. VI]
On August 19, 1494, Columbus lost sight of the eastern extremity of Jamaica, to which he gave the name Cape Farol (at present called Point Morant). Steering eastward, he beheld the long mountainous coast of Hispaniola on the following day and returned to Isabella in September 1494 after an absence of five months. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VII Ch. VII]

Shipwreck on Jamaica (Fourth Voyage — Book XV, Chapter X, June 1503)
During his fourth voyage, Columbus departed the disastrous coast of Veragua at the end of April 1503 with two remaining caravels, both riddled by shipworms and barely seaworthy. One caravel had already been abandoned at Puerto Bello. After struggling against contrary winds and currents, and finding it impossible to reach Hispaniola, Columbus stood in despair for Jamaica. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XV Ch. X]
On the eve of St. John, June 23, 1503, they put into Puerto Bueno (Dry Harbour), but found no natives and no fresh water. Suffering from hunger and thirst, they sailed eastward the following day to another harbour, which Columbus named Port San Gloria (now known as Don Christopher’s Cove). ^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XV Ch. X]
Here, at last, Columbus gave up his long and arduous struggle. His ships, reduced to mere wrecks, could no longer keep the sea and were ready to sink even in port. He ordered them to be run aground within a bow-shot of the shore and fastened together side by side. They soon filled with water to the decks. Thatched cabins were erected at the prow and stern for the accommodation of the crews, and the wreck was placed in the best possible state of defence. Thus castled in the sea, Columbus trusted to repel any sudden attack of the natives and to keep his men from roving about the neighbourhood. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XV Ch. X]

Diego Mendez and the Arrangement for Provisions (Book XVI, Chapter I)
The island was extremely populous and fertile, and the harbour soon swarmed with Indians bringing provisions to barter. To regulate this trade, two persons were appointed to superintend all bargains. However, the provisions from the immediate neighbourhood proved insufficient and irregular. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XVI Ch. I]
Diego Mendez volunteered to forage across the island with three men. He made arrangements with caciques along the coast — including a cacique named Huarco and another named Ameyro — who agreed to supply provisions regularly in exchange for knives, combs, beads, fish-hooks, and hawks’-bells. Mendez bought an excellent canoe from Ameyro for a brass basin, a short frock, and one of his two shirts. He returned in triumph with a canoe loaded with provisions, and thereafter Indians arrived daily from the marts he had established. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XVI Ch. I]
Diego Mendez and Fiesco’s Canoe Voyage to Hispaniola (Book XVI, Chapters I & V)
With provisions secured, Columbus turned to the problem of escape. The only hope of relief was to send word to Nicolas de Ovando, the governor of Hispaniola, across a gulf of forty leagues swept by contrary currents. Columbus summoned the company and proposed the enterprise; all declined. Diego Mendez then came forward and volunteered. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XVI Ch. I]
Mendez was accompanied by Bartholomew Fiesco, a Genoese mariner, with ten Indians to navigate the canoe, and they carried provisions of cassava bread and water. Bartholomew Columbus, the adelantado, kept pace along the coast with an armed band to protect them from the natives. They remained three days at the eastern end of Jamaica waiting for calm weather. At length, with a serene sea, they committed themselves to the broad ocean, and the adelantado watched until they became mere specks on the water. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XVI Ch. I]
Their voyage was desperate: they endured thirst, storms, and exhaustion. Mendez and Fiesco succeeded in reaching the coast of Hispaniola. Fiesco was to return to Jamaica with the news, while Mendez proceeded to San Domingo to deliver Columbus’s letter to Ovando. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XVI Ch. V]
Ovando’s Delay and the Mission of Diego de Escobar (Book XVI, Chapter IV)
Eight months elapsed with no word of Mendez and Fiesco. Ovando, when he received Mendez, showed little urgency. He dispatched Diego de Escobar in a small caravel to reconnoitre Jamaica, who approached the wreck, exchanged messages with Columbus, and returned without taking any of the castaways aboard — leaving Columbus and his men in the deepest despair. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XVI Ch. IV]

Mutiny of Porras (Book XVI, Chapter II)
While waiting for relief, the Spaniards grew sickly from the hardships of the voyage, crowded quarters in the moist climate, and unaccustomed diet. Suspense corroded their spirits. Murmurs broke forth. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XVI Ch. II]
Francisco de Porras, commander of one of the caravels, conspired with his brother Diego de Porras and other malcontents. They accused Columbus of purposely delaying on Jamaica to prolong his own suffering and make his misfortunes more celebrated. The mutineers seized ten canoes and attempted to paddle across to Hispaniola, but were driven back by contrary winds and currents. After failing to reach Hispaniola, they established a separate camp on the island, plundered the natives, and turned them against Columbus and the loyal Spaniards. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XVI Ch. II]

The Eclipse Stratagem (Book XVI, Chapter III)
With the natives now alienated by the depredations of Porras’s mutineers, provisions grew scarce and the loyal Spaniards faced the prospect of starvation or massacre. In this extremity, a fortunate idea presented itself to Columbus. From his knowledge of astronomy, he ascertained that within three days there would be a total eclipse of the moon in the early part of the night. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XVI Ch. III]
He sent an Indian interpreter to summon the principal caciques to a grand conference on the day of the eclipse. When all were assembled, he told them that he and his followers were worshippers of a Deity who lived in the skies; that this Deity favoured such as did well but punished transgressors. The Deity, he said, was incensed against the Indians who had refused or neglected to supply provisions, and would chastise them with famine and pestilence. Lest they should disbelieve this warning, a signal would be given that very night — the moon would change its colour and gradually lose its light. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XVI Ch. III]
Many were alarmed at the solemnity of this prediction; others treated it with derision. All, however, awaited the coming of night with solicitude. When they beheld a dark shadow stealing over the moon, they began to tremble. Their fears increased with the progress of the eclipse, and when they saw a mysterious darkness covering the whole face of nature, there were no bounds to their terror. Seizing whatever provisions they could procure, they hurried to the ships, threw themselves at the feet of Columbus, implored him to intercede with his God, and assured him they would bring whatever he required. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XVI Ch. III]
Columbus retired to his cabin during the increase of the eclipse, the forests and shores resounding with the howlings and supplications of the savages. When the eclipse was about to diminish, he came forth and informed the natives that he had interceded for them with his God, who, on condition of their fulfilling their promises, had deigned to pardon them — in sign of which he would withdraw the darkness from the moon. When the Indians saw the planet restored to its brightness, they overwhelmed the admiral with thanks and repaired to their homes, regarding Columbus with awe and reverence as a man in the peculiar favour and confidence of the Deity. Supplies again arrived daily, and from that time forward there was no want of provisions. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XVI Ch. III]

Battle of the Adelantado with Porras (Book XVI, Chapter VI)
Columbus made overtures of peace to the mutineers, offering a free pardon if they would submit. Porras and his followers refused. At length, Bartholomew Columbus, the adelantado, led the loyal Spaniards against the mutineers in a pitched battle on the beach. Porras was defeated and captured, and his followers were taken. Columbus, demonstrating the clemency that characterized his dealings with his own men, pardoned the mutineers and restored them to good standing, re-establishing order among the castaways. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XVI Ch. VI]
Final Rescue
Eventually, Ovando was persuaded to dispatch a ship to Jamaica. Columbus and his remaining men were taken off the wreck, ending their year-long ordeal. They arrived in San Domingo in August 1504, and Columbus prepared for his final return to Spain. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol3.md, Book XVII]

entities/king-manuel-i.title: King Manuel I
entities/king-manuel-i.content:
King Manuel I
Manuel I (1469–1521), known as Manuel the Fortunate, was King of Portugal from 1495 to 1521. His reign coincided with the expansion of Portuguese influence across the Atlantic and Indian Oceans, most notably through his sponsorship of Vasco da Gama’s three voyages to India. ^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart]
Sponsorship of the Indian Voyages
Manuel I ascended the throne just as Bartolomeu Dias had rounded the Cape of Good Hope. He approved and funded Vasco da Gama’s first expedition (1497–1499) with the goal of reaching India and breaking the Venetian and Ottoman monopoly on the spice trade. After the success of the first voyage, he dispatched da Gama on a second, heavily armed expedition (1502–1503) and later sent him as Viceroy (1524). ^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart] ^[source: career-legend-vasco-da-gama-subrahmanyam]
Grand Titles and Commemorations
Following the return of da Gama’s first voyage, Manuel I added grand titles to the Portuguese crown’s official style: ‘Lord of Guinea and of the Conquests, Navigation and Commerce of Ethiopia, Arabia, Persia, and India’. He also struck a new gold coin called the ‘portuguez’ to commemorate the discovery of the sea route to India. ^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart]
Character
Hart describes Manuel I as frivolous and turbulent, though he was also politically astute and ambitious for Portugal’s global reach. His reign saw Portugal transform from a small European kingdom into a global maritime power with outposts stretching from Brazil to the Spice Islands. ^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart]
