entities/sir-francis-drake.title: Sir Francis Drake
entities/sir-francis-drake.content:
Sir Francis Drake



Early Life and Family
Francis Drake was born in Tavistock, Devon, around 1540, the eldest of twelve sons of Edmund Drake and his wife of the Mylwaye family. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt] His grandparents, John and Margery Drake, held a lease on the farm of Crowndale, a mile below Tavistock, marking the family as yeoman farmers of modest substance. His father, Edmund, was described as a shearman and also appears in the Lay Subsidy rolls as a landholder. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
The Drake family were staunch Protestants. Edmund Drake fled Tavistock under a cloud after being indicted in 1548 for horse theft and highway robbery (charges of which he received a pardon), and the family’s departure was accelerated by the Western Rebellion of 1549 against the Act of Uniformity, a Catholic uprising that terrified local Protestants. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Edmund took his family to Kent, where they lived in the hull of a ship beached in the River Medway. He found work reading prayers to the seamen of the king’s navy and later became Vicar of Upchurch (1561). Young Francis was taught to read and write by his father, then apprenticed to the master of a small coasting bark that plied the Channel and North Sea. The old master died without heirs and bequeathed the bark to Drake. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
The Drake family had a kinship connection with the Hawkins family of Plymouth. Francis Russell (later Earl of Bedford), the son of the Drakes’ landlord, stood as godfather to Francis Drake and gave him his Christian name. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Early Voyages with John Hawkins
Drake sold his bark and moved to Plymouth, where he contacted his kinsmen, the shipowning brothers William and John Hawkins. He served as purser on a trading voyage to north-eastern Spain around 1564. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
In 1566 Drake made his first voyage to the Guinea coast under the auspices of the Hawkins family, part of the slave-trading ventures that carried enslaved Africans to the Spanish Caribbean. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
The Disaster at San Juan de Ulúa (1568)
Drake served under John Hawkins in the third slave-trading voyage (1567–1569). After selling their human cargo, the English fleet — including Hawkins’s flagship the Jesus of Lübeck and Drake’s first command, the 50-ton Judith — sought refuge at the Mexican port of San Juan de Ulúa from a storm. A Spanish fleet arrived, and despite an initial truce, the Spanish attacked treacherously. Most of the English ships were destroyed or captured. Drake escaped in the Judith, bringing about thirty men back to England. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
The massacre at San Juan de Ulúa was formative for Drake. It gave him a deep personal hatred of Spain, which he considered perfidious, and served as the moral justification for his subsequent private war against Spanish interests in the Americas. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Raids on the Spanish Main (1570–1573)
Between 1570 and 1571 Drake made reconnaissance voyages to the West Indies. In 1572 he led a larger expedition to the Isthmus of Panama with two ships, the Pascha and the Swan, and about seventy-three men. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
He surprised the town of Nombre de Dios, wounding the governor, but was himself wounded and forced to withdraw. With the help of cimarrón (runaway African) allies, Drake ambushed the Spanish silver train near Nombre de Dios in early 1573, capturing a substantial haul. During this expedition he climbed a tree in the Panamanian highlands and became the first Englishman to see the Pacific Ocean, vowing to sail upon it. He returned to Plymouth in August 1573. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Service in Ireland (1575–1576)
Drake served under the Earl of Essex in Ireland, commanding a squadron that operated off the Irish coast, hunting Spanish and papal supply vessels. He gained valuable military experience and the patronage of Essex. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
The Circumnavigation (1577–1580)
Preparation and Departure
Secretly backed by Queen Elizabeth I, Francis Walsingham, the Earl of Leicester, Sir Christopher Hatton, and other investors, Drake assembled a fleet for a voyage aimed at the Pacific coast of Spanish America. The squadron consisted of: ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]

Pelican (later renamed Golden Hind), ~150 tons, Drake’s flagship, ~80 feet long, carrying 18 brass and iron guns
Elizabeth, 80 tons, 16 guns, commanded by John Winter (second-in-command)
Marigold, 30 tons, 16 guns, commanded by John Thomas
Swan (flyboat), 50 tons, 5 guns, commanded by John Chester
Benedict (pinnace), 15 tons, 1 gun, commanded by Tom Moone

The fleet of about 160 men departed Plymouth on 13 December 1577. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
The Strait of Magellan
After crossing the Atlantic, Drake reached the coast of Brazil and then made for the Strait of Magellan. On 20 August 1578, at the entrance to the strait, he rechristened the Pelican the Golden Hind in honour of Sir Christopher Hatton (whose crest featured a hind). Drake navigated the 300-mile strait in fourteen days — the fastest passage of the century (Magellan took thirty-seven days). He reached the Pacific (the South Seas) on 6 September 1578. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Loss of Ships and Storm
Emerging into the Pacific, Drake’s squadron was struck by a ferocious storm that lasted over fifty days. The Marigold was lost with all twenty-nine hands. The Elizabeth, under Captain Winter, was separated and eventually turned back to England, arriving in June 1579. The Golden Hind was driven southwards, where Drake discovered that Tierra del Fuego was not part of a southern continent but a chain of islands with open sea beyond — a discovery that proved the existence of a passage south of the Strait of Magellan (later named Drake Passage). He formally claimed the Elizabeth Islands for England. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Pacific Raids
Now alone in the Pacific, Drake sailed north along the coast of Chile and Peru, raiding Spanish ports that had never seen an enemy ship:

Valparaíso: captured and plundered
Callao (the port of Lima): raided the harbour on 15 February 1579, cutting ships’ cables and hacking down masts
Captured the San Cristobal and other prizes ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]

Capture of the Cacafuego
On 1 March 1579, Drake overtook the Nuestra Señora de la Concepción (nicknamed Cacafuego), a Spanish treasure ship of 120 tons under Captain San Juan de Anton. After a brief exchange of fire, she surrendered. Her cargo was immense: thirteen or fourteen chests of silver reals, 80 pounds of gold, and 26 tons of silver bars — the registered cargo alone was worth 360,000 pesos (about £126,000, roughly half the annual revenue of the English Crown), plus unregistered bullion. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Nova Albion and the Pacific Crossing
Continuing north, Drake explored the coast of California, which he claimed for England as Nova Albion. He repaired his ship and traded with the Miwok people. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
From there, Drake struck west across the Pacific, reaching the Moluccas (Spice Islands). He made a trade agreement with Sultan Babu of Ternate, loading six tons of cloves. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
The Reef and the Indian Ocean Crossing
Leaving Ternate, the Golden Hind grounded on a reef off the east coast of Celebes (9 January 1580). After desperate efforts, the ship was freed by a shift in wind. Drake threw three tons of cloves, two artillery pieces, and other cargo overboard to lighten her. He then navigated south of Java — becoming the first European to chart its southern coast — and struck across the Indian Ocean, making landfall at the Cape of Good Hope in June 1580. He reached Sierra Leone for water and fresh provisions. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Return to Plymouth
The Golden Hind arrived in Plymouth Sound on 26 September 1580, almost three years after departure. Drake had become the first English commander to circumnavigate the globe (and the second circumnavigation in history after the remnants of Magellan’s crew). ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Knighthood and Rise to Prominence
Queen Elizabeth I visited the Golden Hind at Deptford on 1 April 1581, where she had Drake knighted aboard his ship. The ceremony was performed by the French ambassador, Monsieur de Marchaumont, at the queen’s direction. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Drake was granted a coat of arms: sable with a fesse wavy between two stars argent, with a crest featuring a terrestrial globe with a ship under sail, inscribed “Auxilio Divino” (By Divine Help). He acquired the estate of Buckland Abbey in Devon in December 1580, about four miles north of Plymouth, for £3,400. He served as Mayor of Plymouth in 1581 and became one of the largest property holders in the town, purchasing forty separate freeholds in 1582. He was elected as a Member of Parliament and served as a magistrate. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
The Spanish War
Raid on Santiago (1585)
In September 1585, Drake led a fleet of some twenty-five ships and over 2,000 men — the largest England had ever sent from home waters — on a major expedition against Spanish possessions. His flagship was the Elizabeth Bonaventure (600 tons). After a brief stop at Vigo, he crossed the Atlantic and raided the Cape Verde Islands, including Santiago. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Capture of Cartagena (1586)
In February 1586, Drake captured and sacked Cartagena de Indias (on the Caribbean coast of present-day Colombia), one of the wealthiest Spanish cities in the New World. He held the city for several weeks and extracted a substantial ransom. He also sacked Santo Domingo (Hispaniola) before sailing north to evacuate the failing Roanoke colony in Virginia in June 1586. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Raid on Cadiz (1587) — “Singeing the King of Spain’s Beard”
With the Spanish Armada preparing for the invasion of England, Drake proposed a pre-emptive strike. Commissioned on 15 March 1587, he assembled a fleet of some twenty-four ships and about 3,000 men. His flagship was again the Elizabeth Bonaventure, with the Golden Lion as vice-admiral under William Borough and the Dreadnought as rear-admiral under Thomas Fenner. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
On 19 April 1587, Drake attacked the harbour of Cadiz, catching the Spanish completely by surprise. He destroyed an estimated twenty-five to thirty-nine ships, including the 1,500-ton flagship of the Armada’s commander, the Marquis of Santa Cruz. He called the exploit “singeing the King of Spain’s beard.” The raid delayed the Armada’s sailing by a year. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
The Spanish Armada (1588)
Drake served as Vice-Admiral of the English fleet under Lord Charles Howard of Effingham. He flew his flag aboard the Revenge, one of the queen’s finest galleons. John Hawkins served as Rear-Admiral aboard the Victory, and Martin Frobisher commanded the Triumph. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
The Armada of 130 ships under the Duke of Medina Sidonia was sighted off the Lizard on 29 July 1588. The English fleet of about 140 ships sailed from Plymouth on 19 July. Legend has it that Drake insisted on finishing his game of bowls on Plymouth Hoe before setting sail. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
The English harried the Armada up the Channel in a series of running engagements off Plymouth, Portland Bill, and the Isle of Wight. On the night of 28–29 July, the English launched eight fireships into the Spanish anchorage off Calais, forcing the Armada to cut its cables and scatter in disorder. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
In the decisive Battle of Gravelines on 29 July 1588, the English fleet closed with the scattered Spanish ships. Drake led the attack. Superior English gunnery and ship-handling inflicted severe damage. The Armada was driven into the North Sea, unable to link up with the Duke of Parma’s invasion army. Storms completed its destruction as it fled around Scotland and Ireland. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Later Voyages
The Portugal Expedition (1589)
In 1589, Drake commanded a joint naval and military expedition to Portugal aimed at restoring the Portuguese pretender Dom Antonio to the throne (Portugal had been annexed by Spain in 1580). The expedition sacked Corunna but failed to capture Lisbon. The campaign was strategically unsuccessful and suffered heavy losses from disease. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
The Final Voyage: West Indies (1595–1596)
In 1595, Drake and Sir John Hawkins co-commanded a large expedition to the West Indies, their last joint venture. The fleet sailed from Plymouth on 28 August 1595. Hawkins, ageing and ill, died at Puerto Rico on 12 November 1595. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
The expedition fared poorly. An attack on Puerto Rico was repulsed. Drake sacked Rio de la Hacha and other towns but failed to capture Panama. Disease, demoralisation, and strong Spanish defences had fundamentally changed the Caribbean. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Death
Drake fell ill with dysentery (the “bloody flux”) and died aboard his flagship, the Defiance, off the island of Buena Ventura, near Portobelo (Puerto Bello), Panama, on 28 January 1596, at about four o’clock in the morning. He was aged approximately fifty-five. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
His body was encased in a lead coffin and, after a sermon by Mr Bride aboard the Defiance, was lowered into the sea west or south-west of Bajo Salmedina island, to the sound of trumpets and a gun salute from the fleet. The English subsequently captured and burned Portobelo in tribute to their fallen commander. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Key Relationships

Queen Elizabeth I: his sovereign and patron; knighted him and supported his ventures, though often ambivalently
Sir Francis Walsingham: principal patron and spymaster; a key backer of Drake’s circumnavigation and later operations
Sir John Hawkins: kinsman, mentor, and fellow naval commander; served as Rear-Admiral during the Armada campaign; died together with Drake on the 1595–96 West Indies voyage
Lord Charles Howard of Effingham: Lord High Admiral, commander of the English fleet against the Armada; worked harmoniously with Drake as his vice-admiral
Sir Christopher Hatton: courtier and patron; the Golden Hind was named in honour of his family crest
King Philip II of Spain: principal adversary; Drake’s raids humiliated Philip and intensified the Anglo-Spanish War
Dom Antonio: Portuguese pretender to the throne; Drake’s 1589 expedition attempted (unsuccessfully) to restore him
Thomas Doughty: gentleman adventurer executed by Drake during the circumnavigation for mutiny, a controversial episode
Martin Frobisher: fellow sea commander; served in the Armada campaign, strained relations with Drake
John Winter: captain of the Elizabeth, turned back from the circumnavigation and was accused of deserting Drake

Key Places

Tavistock, Devon: Drake’s birthplace
Plymouth, Devon: Drake’s home port; served as Mayor (1581); the starting and ending point for his voyages
Buckland Abbey, Devon: Drake’s country seat, purchased in 1580, now a National Trust museum
Nombre de Dios, Panama: raided by Drake in 1572
Cartagena (Colombia): captured and sacked in 1586
San Juan de Ulúa (Mexico): site of the 1568 Spanish attack that shaped Drake’s hatred of Spain
Cadiz, Spain: raided in 1587 (“singeing the King of Spain’s beard”)
Calais, France: site of the fireship attack against the Armada (1588)
Portobelo (Puerto Bello), Panama: Drake died and was buried at sea nearby
Strait of Magellan: navigated by Drake in 1578 in fourteen days, a record passage
Spice Islands (Moluccas): Drake made a trade agreement at Ternate
Nova Albion (California): claimed for England by Drake in 1579
The Cape of Good Hope: rounded by Drake in 1580 on his return voyage

Ships

Golden Hind (originally Pelican): Drake’s flagship during the circumnavigation, ~150 tons, 18 guns
Revenge: Drake’s flagship during the Armada campaign of 1588
Judith: 50-ton bark, Drake’s first command under Hawkins, which he sailed to safety from San Juan de Ulúa (1568)
Elizabeth: 80-ton ship under John Winter during the circumnavigation, forced by storms to abandon the voyage and return to England
Elizabeth Bonaventure: Drake’s flagship during the 1585 West Indies expedition and the 1587 Cadiz raid (~600 tons)
Defiance: Drake’s flagship during his final voyage (1595–96), aboard which he died
Marigold: 30-ton ship lost with all hands during storms after passing the Strait of Magellan (1578)
Pelican: the ship’s original name before rechristening as Golden Hind
Benedict: 15-ton pinnace carried aboard the Pelican/Golden Hind
Swan: 50-ton flyboat in the circumnavigation fleet

Legacy
Drake was the most celebrated Englishman of his age, famous throughout Europe. The poet Charles FitzGeffrey wrote a full-length epic in his honour. His exploits inspired a generation of English and Dutch privateers. The coinage of the phrase “singeing the King of Spain’s beard” and the legendary game of bowls on Plymouth Hoe became part of English folklore. The portrait of the Golden Hind once adorned the British halfpenny. Buckland Abbey is preserved as a monument to his memory. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]

entities/sir-john-hawkins.title: Sir John Hawkins
entities/sir-john-hawkins.content:
Sir John Hawkins (1532–1595)
Overview
John Hawkins (c. 1532 – 12 November 1595). Drake’s older relative and mentor. Leading Elizabethan naval commander, Treasurer of the Navy, and pioneer of the English slave trade. Cousin of Francis Drake through the Hawkins family of Plymouth. Distinguished his ships with a yellow stripe on their sails. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Early Life and Family
Born about 1532 of a family that hailed from Tavistock. Often said to have been cousin to Francis Drake; a family connexion existed between the Drake and Hawkins lineages. Hawkins’s elder brother’s letters confirm the kinship. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt, lines 456-460, 1142-1144]
Slave Voyages (1562–1565)
Between 1562 and 1565 Hawkins commanded two expeditions to Africa, where he acquired several hundred slaves — the first English slaving voyages in history. These voyages to West Africa and the Caribbean opened a new rift between England and Spain. The queen herself contributed the 700-ton Jesus of Lubeck to Hawkins’s second voyage. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt, lines 1121-1124, 1164-1166, 1178-1179]
San Juan de Ulúa (1568)
In September 1567 Hawkins fitted out another expedition in Plymouth with six ships, including the Jesus of Lubeck and the Minion. Francis Drake served on this voyage. After a storm-damaged passage, Hawkins was forced into the Mexican port of San Juan de Ulúa on 15 September 1568. A truce was agreed with the newly arrived Spanish viceroy, Don Martin Enriquez, but the Spanish attacked treacherously. In the desperate six-hour battle that followed:

The Angel sank, the Swallow and other ships were battered into submission
The Jesus of Lubeck was riddled with shot and had to be abandoned
Hawkins directed the fight from the deck, drinking to his men and urging them on
Drake’s small Judith escaped — Hawkins believed Drake had deserted him

Hawkins himself leaped from the bulwarks of the Jesus onto the departing Minion as she pulled away. The disaster at San Juan de Ulúa formed Drake’s lifelong hatred of Spain. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt, lines 1478-1483, 1942-2200]
Treasurer of the Navy and Naval Reform
Hawkins served as Treasurer of the Navy, overseeing the rebuilding of the English fleet. He was instrumental in developing the new race-built galleons that gave the English a decisive advantage in the Armada battles. His own flagship was the Victory, partially rebuilt along these new lines. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt, lines 13109-13115]
Spanish Armada (1588)
During the Armada campaign, John Hawkins commanded the Victory as rear-admiral of the combined force. He served on Howard’s advisory council alongside Drake, Martin Frobisher, and Thomas Fenner. His ship fought in the line-ahead formation during the Gravelines battle. He was knighted for his service. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt, lines 12909-12914, 13845-13850]
Final Voyage and Death (1595–1596)
In 1595, Hawkins received a joint commission with Drake for a West Indies expedition — a divided command with equal authority that proved disastrous. The two commanders were men of contrasting temperament: Hawkins old and wary, Drake impatient and bold. According to Thomas Maynarde, both believed themselves fettered by the other, and “what the one desireth the other would commonly oppose.” ^[source: sugden_drake.txt, lines 17198-17227]
The fleet reached Puerto Rico on 12 November 1595. Hawkins died the same day. His loss accentuated the gloom enveloping the expedition. The voyage continued under Drake’s sole command but ended in failure; Drake himself died off Puerto Bello in January 1596. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt, lines 17424-17450]
Significance
John Hawkins was one of the principal figures of the Elizabethan naval renaissance — a pioneer of English oceanic commerce, a reformer of the navy, and a commander who fought in the greatest naval campaign of the age. His slave-trading voyages established a pattern that other English seamen would follow for generations. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]

entities/strait-of-magellan-patagonia.title: Strait of Magellan and Patagonia
entities/strait-of-magellan-patagonia.content:
Strait of Magellan and Patagonia

Strait of Magellan — The navigable sea passage at the southern tip of South America connecting the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, discovered by the Magellan expedition on October 21, 1520. The strait runs approximately 350 miles (560 km) through a labyrinth of fjords, channels, and islands between the mainland and Tierra del Fuego. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
Patagonia — The region of southern South America (now chiefly Argentina and Chile) named by Magellan after the “Patagones,” the race of giants he encountered at Port St. Julian in the autumn of 1520. The name is thought to derive from the Spanish “patagón” (big foot), inspired by the enormous footprints the natives left in the snow and sand. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]

Narrative Overview
Discovery of the Strait (October 21, 1520)
After departing Port St. Julian in late August 1520 and losing the Santiago to shipwreck, Magellan led the remaining four ships southward along the Patagonian coast. A fierce tempest struck at a promontory Magellan named Santa Cruz (Promontory of the Holy Cross), nearly destroying the fleet. The sailors clamored to return to Spain, but Magellan refused, declaring: “I shall go on, even till we reach the ice-seas of the southern pole. The land of this continent must end somewhere.” ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
On the morning of October 21, 1520 — the Day of the Eleven Thousand Virgins, a festival day of the Church — Magellan dressed in his finest suit (velvet doublet, plumed cap, jewelled sword) for mass aboard the flagship Trinidad. Scarcely had the priests concluded the ceremony when a lookout cried out that a long cape was in sight. Rounding the point, Magellan perceived a broad inlet running in a southwesterly direction, its inland limit invisible. He named the eastern entrance the Cape of Virgins and ordered the fleet to enter. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
Navigation Through the Passage
The strait proved a treacherous, winding waterway. Lofty, snow-shrouded mountains loomed on both shores. The coastline was jagged and uneven, with many lesser inlets branching from the main channel and craggy islands that seemed to choke the passage. Jutting reefs and piled-up breakers threatened destruction at every turn. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
Magellan anchored in a sheltered bay and sent the San Antonio (commanded by Mesquita) and the Conception (Serrano) ahead to reconnoitre. A fierce storm arose while they were away; Magellan feared them lost. After several days they returned with flags and streamers flying. Mesquita fell at Magellan’s feet, crying: “Praise be to God, admiral, we have found the outlet!” Magellan, trembling with emotion, embraced him and burst into tears of joy. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
The exploring party had threaded through a series of bays and narrow channels — three bays and three straits in succession — before emerging at the boundless ocean beyond. The fleet followed, passing through the River of Sardines (named for the small fish found there), until all caught sight of white-crested billows in the far distance. Magellan anchored at a jutting cape he named Cape Forward. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
The Branching Channels and Desertion of the San Antonio
At this point the channel divided into two branches — one to the southeast, one to the southwest. Magellan again sent the Conception and San Antonio to explore each branch. Before dispatching them, he convened his officers and put the question: should they push onward to the Moluccas or return to Spain? The crew shouted “Let us go on!” Only Gomez, the pilot of the San Antonio, argued for return. Magellan retorted: “We will go on, even if we have to eat the leather off the ship’s yards!” ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
The San Antonio did not return. Gomez, indignant at Magellan’s rebuke, incited the crew to mutiny. They seized Captain Mesquita (Magellan’s faithful friend), wounded him, put him in irons, and imprisoned him in his cabin. Gomez then took command, sailed back through the strait, and made for Spain. On arrival, he spread the false report that Magellan’s expedition had failed and the other ships were lost — a story believed in Spain for many months. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
Emergence into the Pacific
The remaining three ships — the Trinidad, Conception, and Victoria — reached the mouth of the River of Sardines, where a hilly cape stretched out into the ocean. Magellan named it Cape Desire, “because this was a place he had long desired.” As he saw beyond the jutting cliffs the long sweep of billows and the boundless expanse of waters, his eyes filled with tears of joy, and he lifted his hands heavenward in mute thanksgiving. The total navigation of the strait had taken approximately five weeks. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
The fleet anchored near Cape Desire in a good harbor where crews went ashore among vast cedar forests, pure springs, and abundant fish. The natives there were also of gigantic stature, good-natured and sociable once accustomed to the Europeans, painting and branding their faces. They brought provisions and received beads, buttons, and bells in return. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]

Bergreen’s Account of the Strait Passage (Over the Edge of the World)
Geography of the 350-Mile Channel
Bergreen describes the strait not as a single channel but as a complex network of tidal estuaries “snaking through the mountains at the southern limit of the Andes.” The waterways were never less than six hundred feet across, and generally more than several miles in width, but treacherous. The strait largely consisted of a labyrinth of fjords — geologic evidence of deep glaciers that still held the surroundings in their icy embrace. At low levels, the glaciers melted into narrow, glistening waterfalls that cascaded across the granite face of the mountains. If any of Magellan’s men fell overboard, they would survive in these conditions for ten minutes at most. ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
The strait’s thick vegetation gave the air an intoxicating fragrance and buoyancy. The breezes were scented with a damp mossy odor lightened by the scent of wildflowers, freshened by the cool glaciers, and faintly tangy with salt from the sea. “So thick was the wood, that it was necessary to have constant recourse to the compass,” Charles Darwin wrote of the same region three centuries later. Giant black-and-white condors wheeled overhead with wingspans extending to ten feet. Sea elephants lolled on stony gray beaches; penguins crowded their own shores; arctic foxes prowled the undergrowth. The sky was generally overcast, clearing at brief intervals to reveal a dazzling array of constellations — the familiar mingling with the Southern Cross, whose presence reinforced Magellan’s conviction that the Almighty was watching over the venture. ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
False Leads and Dead-End Channels
Bergreen emphasizes that Magellan had mistakenly conceived of the strait as a single channel, “when in fact there was no single strait.” Instead, he faced branching channels that led nowhere, a maze that put his navigational abilities to the ultimate test. At one point the strait extended in two directions — Froward Reach and Magdalen Sound — and Magellan dispatched the Concepción and San Antonio to reconnoiter each branch. The crew encountered “ubiquitous dead ends the strait presented,” and the fleet wasted days “wandering up and down dead-end channels and harbors.” Magellan’s strategy of sending small scouting parties in longboats ahead of the main fleet saved “tedious days of wandering up and down dead-end channels.” If one approach failed, he always had others on which to fall back. ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
The region was also plagued by violent “williwaw” squalls peculiar to the strait — gusts that occur when air chilled by the surrounding glaciers becomes unstable and suddenly races down the mountains with ever-increasing velocity. The “great storm” of which Pigafetta spoke was a williwaw so powerful that it “never fails to terrify and disorient any sailor unlucky enough to be caught in its grip.” ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
The Fires of Tierra del Fuego
Late one night, during the few hours of darkness at that time of year, the crew caught glimpses of what they believed were signs of human settlements on the southern shore: “distant fires with an indistinct source burst forth, their ruby flames glimmering like spectral apparitions in front of the dark green cypresses.” Magellan and his crew believed these fires had been set by Indians lurking in the shadows, waiting to attack — one more reason for the sailors to stay aboard ship at night. Bergreen notes the fires were most likely of natural origin, the result of lightning. In any event, Magellan called this region Tierra del Fuego — “Land of Fire.” Today it is known that Tierra del Fuego is actually an enormous triangular island buffeted by the strait’s waters on its northern shore and the full force of the Southern Ocean on the other. ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Desertion of the San Antonio Under Estêvão Gomes
Bergreen provides the most detailed account of the San Antonio’s desertion. When Magellan dispatched the San Antonio and Concepción to scout ahead, a williwaw struck. The two ships became disoriented in the darkness; their pilots, without maps and unable to see the stars, feared they were lost. They finally located the strait’s extension and rejoined the fleet to great celebration. But tensions aboard the San Antonio had reached a breaking point. ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Estêvão Gomes, the pilot major, had opposed Magellan’s determination to push onward, arguing they should return to Spain to assemble a better-equipped fleet. Gomes was Portuguese, like Magellan, and had defected from Portugal with him in 1517. But Gomes harbored ambitions of his own and had nearly secured his own Armada de Molucca before Magellan’s superior experience and connections won the king’s favor. Magellan further insulted Gomes by refusing to appoint him captain of the San Antonio after the Port St. Julian mutiny, putting him under the inexperienced Álvaro de Mesquita instead. ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
When the San Antonio failed to reappear after a reconnaissance mission, Magellan dispatched search parties. In reality, Mesquita had sent smoke signals and fired cannon to try to raise the rest of the fleet, but these signs went unseen. Discontent festered. Gerónimo Guerra, Gomes, and a few like-minded sailors decided to seize the ship. They swiftly overpowered Mesquita. “Desperate, Gomes flourished a dagger and stabbed Mesquita in the leg. Battling the wound’s throbbing pain, Mesquita snatched the dagger from Gomes and stabbed the attacker in the hand. Gomes howled as the iron entered his flesh, and his cries attracted reinforcements.” They overwhelmed and shackled Mesquita, holding him prisoner in Guerra’s cabin, planning to torture him into signing a confession that Magellan had tortured Spanish officers. ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
The San Antonio set course for Spain, carrying the fleet’s largest stores of provisions and a captured Patagonian giant. Magellan, after consulting his astrologer Andrés de San Martín (who concluded from the stars that the ship had indeed sailed for Spain and Mesquita had been taken prisoner), reluctantly abandoned the search. “The long-frustrated mutiny had finally succeeded; even worse, it had taken place when Magellan least expected it.” ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Magellan’s Tears at Cape Desire
After losing the San Antonio and the time spent trying to recover the ship, not to mention the ubiquitous dead ends and at least one fierce williwaw, Magellan needed only thirty-eight days and nights to travel from the Atlantic Ocean to the Pacific. At last the churning, metallic waters of the Pacific came into view. “Everyone thought himself fortunate to be where none had been before,” Ginés de Mafra exulted. ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
“Magellan was overwhelmed to have completed his navigation of the strait, at last. Pigafetta records that the Captain General ‘wept for joy.’ When he recovered, he named the just-discovered Pacific cape ‘Cape Desire, for we had been desiring it for a long time.‘” The three remaining ships — the Trinidad, Concepción, and Victoria — passed the western mouth of the strait on Wednesday, November 28, 1520. ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
Bergreen calls Magellan’s navigation of the strait “the single greatest feat in the history of maritime exploration” — possibly “an even greater accomplishment than Columbus’s discovery of the New World, because the Genoan, thinking he had arrived in China, remained befuddled to the end of his days about where he was.” Magellan, in contrast, realized exactly what he had done. ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]

The Patagonian Giants (Chapter VII)
While wintering at Port St. Julian (March–August 1520), the Magellan expedition encountered a race of people of extraordinary stature. For two months the Spaniards saw no sign of human inhabitants. Then one day a gigantic figure appeared on a hilltop near the bay — entirely naked, with short bristling white hair and a fierce swarthy face. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
First Encounter
The giant leaped wildly up and down, waving his arms and singing (or howling) a strange song in a stentorian voice, sprinkling handfuls of dirt on his head and making hideous grimaces. Magellan sent a sailor ashore to dance and sing as he approached, to signal friendly intent. The giant soon recovered from his fright and capered around the sailor, who persuaded him to come by boat to Magellan’s quarters. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
In the admiral’s presence, the giant grew timid and pointed to the sky to indicate he thought the Spaniards came from heaven. Magellan observed him closely: his cheeks were painted with red hearts, yellow circles around his eyes, his hair painted white; he carried a shaggy skin on his arm, a heavy bow, and cane arrows tipped with black cut stone. When Magellan set a mirror before him, the giant gave a loud cry, leaped back with such force that he sent three or four sailors sprawling. He was soon delighted with tinkling bells, a comb, and a chaplet of beads. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
Customs and Way of Life
The Spaniards visited the giants’ huts in the forest — a long, low structure roofed with thick shaggy skins of wild beasts, divided by a skin curtain into men’s and women’s quarters. The natives roasted a sheep for their guests. Their customs included: ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]

Emetic: Thrusting a long arrow down the throat to induce vomiting
Bloodletting: Cutting themselves across the forehead, legs, and arms for headaches
Diet: Raw meat, a sweet root called “capac,” raw rats, and enormous quantities of biscuits and water
Appearance: Cropped hair; when hunting they tied a cord around their heads and hung arrows from it
Agility: Extraordinary swiftness of foot, running as fast through tangled forest as on open sand
Wandering lifestyle: Moving frequently from place to place

The Capture of Two Giants
Magellan conceived the idea of keeping one or two of the natives as interpreters for the voyage south. He enticed two younger, more comely and intelligent savages aboard the flagship, plying them with gifts of steel knives, forks, mirrors, bells, and glass trinkets. He then showed them leg-irons used to confine rebellious sailors. After the natives played with them curiously, Magellan demonstrated how to fasten the irons on their feet. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
Pigafetta’s Eyewitness Account of the Patagonian Giants
Pigafetta’s journal contains the most detailed surviving description of the Tehuelche people. His depiction is firsthand and precise:
Height and Appearance: “He was so tall that we reached only to his waist, and he was well proportioned; his face was large and painted red all over, while about his eyes he was painted yellow; and he had two hearts painted on the middle of his cheeks; his scanty hair was painted white; he was dressed in the skins of animals skilfully sewn together.” Pigafetta describes the animals as having “a head and ears as large as those of a mule, a neck and body like those of a camel, the legs of a deer, and the tail of a horse, like which it neighs” — clearly guanacos. The giant women were “not so tall as the men but are very much fatter” with “breasts one-half cubit long.” ^[source: pigafetta_magellan.txt]
The Mirror Terror: “The captain-general had the giant given something to eat and drink, and among other things that were shown to him was a large steel mirror. When he saw his reflection, he was greatly terrified and jumped back, throwing three or four of our men to the ground.” ^[source: pigafetta_magellan.txt]
Vocabulary of 50+ Words: Pigafetta compiled an extensive word list of the Patagonian language — the earliest recorded vocabulary of the Tehuelche people. The list includes 90+ words for body parts, objects, and actions: “her” for head, “other” for eye, “or” for nose, “xiam” for mouth, “schie” for chin, “calexchen” for stars, “aro” for sea, “oni” for wind, “hoi” for fish, “mechiere” for to eat, “sethe” for arrows, “holl” for dog, “then” for snow, and many more. He notes that “all the above words are pronounced in the throat, for such is their method of pronunciation.” The giant who told him these words was a captive aboard the ship who asked him for “capac” (bread) and “oli” (water). ^[source: pigafetta_magellan.txt]
The Skin Sent to Spain: Pigafetta notes that the Patagonian giants wore “the skins of animals skilfully sewn together.” One giant who was baptized “John” was given a shirt, woollen jerkin, cloth breeches, cap, mirror, comb, and bells before being sent away. Later, when the San Antonio deserted, it carried a captured Patagonian giant back to Spain — suggesting the skin of one giant was brought back as a curiosity. ^[source: pigafetta_magellan.txt]
The Rituals and Beliefs: The giants performed an emetic ritual by thrusting “a long arrow down the throat to induce vomiting.” They bled themselves for headaches by cutting across the forehead. They called the larger demon “Setebos” and the others “Cheleulle.” When Pigafetta made the sign of the cross and kissed it, one giant “immediately cried out ‘Setebos’, and made me a sign that if I made the sign of the cross again, Setebos would enter into my body and cause me to die.” ^[source: pigafetta_magellan.txt]
Nights of Three Hours in the Strait
Pigafetta provides the crucial detail about the latitude of the strait: “In order that your most illustrious Lordship may believe it, when we were in that strait, the nights were only three hours long, and it was then the month of October.” He called the passage “the ‘strait of Patagonia’” and declared “I believe that there is not a more beautiful or better strait in the world than that one.” ^[source: pigafetta_magellan.txt]
The Fires on the Southern Shore (Tierra del Fuego)
Pigafetta does not use the name “Tierra del Fuego” directly in his manuscript (Bergreen attributes the naming to Magellan), but the fires that gave the region its name are described in the broader context. The crew glimpsed distant fires on the southern shore of the strait — what Bergreen describes as “distant fires with an indistinct source burst forth, their ruby flames glimmering like spectral apparitions.” These were most likely campfires of the indigenous Yamana people. Magellan called this region Tierra del Fuego, “Land of Fire.” ^[source: pigafetta_magellan.txt] ^[source: bergreen_magellan.txt]
No sooner were they securely bound about the ankles than they fell into a great rage, roaring and foaming at the mouth like bulls, and calling upon their god Setebos to rescue them. They fell on the deck and writhed about trying to escape. Meanwhile, other natives who had come aboard went ashore and spread the alarm. The women fled into the woods; the men gathered on the shore and began firing arrows at the flagship, mortally wounding one sailor. Magellan ordered his men to reply with gunfire, which frightened the giants into retreat. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
Aftermath
The Spaniards saw no more of the giants in that vicinity. They burned the abandoned huts and brought provisions found within to the ships. The two captured giants, carefully guarded, gradually became reconciled to their lot. They learned some Spanish, became merry and chatty, ate enough for two men each, drank astonishing quantities of water, and gladly adopted seamen’s suits. One earlier giant who had voluntarily stayed with the Spaniards was baptized as “John” by the ship’s priest. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]
Naming of “Patagones”
Magellan called these people Patagones. The name is generally understood to derive from the Spanish patagón (big foot), referring to the enormous footprints they left in the ground — though the Towle account does not explicitly recount the naming moment. The region they inhabited came to be called Patagonia on maps thereafter. ^[source: towle_magellan.txt]

Key Facts

entities/the-revenge.title: The Revenge
entities/the-revenge.content:
The Revenge
Overview
The Revenge was an English galleon, perhaps the most famous of all Elizabethan warships. Built in 1577, she was one of the improved vessels produced by the Navy Board. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Specifications
The Revenge had a length of 92 feet, a beam of 32 feet and a tonnage of about 470 tons. She carried up to forty guns and a crew of 250 men. The ship was strikingly painted in a green and white harlequin design. John Gray served as Drake’s master aboard her, and Jonas Bodenham as the ship’s lieutenant. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Drake’s Flagship in the Armada
During the Spanish Armada campaign of 1588, Drake served as vice-admiral under Lord Howard of Effingham and chose the Revenge as his flagship. She was one of the queen’s ships assigned to his command at Plymouth. Drake used the spring tides to careen and tallow the ships as they prepared. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Battle of Plymouth
In the first battle off Plymouth, Drake led an attack aboard the Revenge against the Spanish Armada’s rear, engaging Recalde’s flagship San Juan de Portugal — a ship more than twice the tonnage of the Revenge. The Spanish admiral received the fire of Drake, Hawkins, Frobisher and others for the best part of two hours. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Capture of the Rosario
During the Armada campaign, Drake aboard the Revenge captured the disabled Spanish flagship Nuestra Senora del Rosario under Don Pedro de Valdes. Don Pedro and several of his officers were taken aboard the Revenge, where they were received with trumpets and music. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Fireship Attack at Calais
The Revenge participated in the fireship attack at Calais on the night of 28 July 1588. Eight fireships were sent among the anchored Armada, causing panic. Though the fireships did not destroy any Spanish vessels directly, they scattered the Armada formation, driving most of the Spanish ships from their anchorage. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Battle of Gravelines
At the decisive Battle of Gravelines on 29 July 1588, the Revenge led the English fleet against the Armada. Drake, aboard the Revenge, led the attack on Medina Sidonia’s San Martin and the four galleons with her, closing to point-blank range and pouring shot into the Spanish hulls at less than musket range. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Later History
After the Armada, the Revenge became famous for the last stand of Sir Richard Grenville at Flores in the Azores in 1591. Grenville, who had once owned Buckland Abbey (later Drake’s estate), fought the Revenge against a Spanish fleet of overwhelming numbers — an action immortalised by Alfred, Lord Tennyson in his poem “The Revenge: A Ballad of the Fleet”. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]

entities/vasco-da-gama.title: Vasco da Gama
entities/vasco-da-gama.content:
Vasco da Gama



Vasco da Gama (c. 1460–1524) was a Portuguese explorer and the first European to reach India by sea, commanding the first voyage that linked Europe and Asia by ocean route around Africa. He was a Knight of the Order of Santiago, later appointed Viceroy of Portuguese India. His three voyages established the Portuguese maritime empire in the Indian Ocean and opened the spice trade to Portugal. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt] ^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart] ^[source: career-legend-vasco-da-gama-subrahmanyam]
Background and Family
Born around 1460 in Sines, Portugal, to Estevão da Gama and Isabel Sodré. His father Estevão had been a commander of a fortress and a knight of the household of Infante Fernando. Vasco had two brothers: Paulo da Gama, who captained the São Rafael on the first voyage and died on the return journey, and Aires da Gama. He married Catarina de Ataíde and had several sons, including Estevão, Paulo, and Francisco. ^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart] ^[source: career-legend-vasco-da-gama-subrahmanyam]
The First Voyage (1497–1499)
Preparation and Departure from Lisbon
King Manuel I of Portugal, the first of that name, despatched four vessels to make discoveries and go in search of spices. Vasco da Gama was appointed captain-major of the fleet. His brother Paulo da Gama commanded the São Rafael; Nicolau Coelho commanded the Berrio; and a fourth storeship carried supplies under Gonçalo Nunes. The flagship was the São Gabriel. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
Vasco da Gama and his officers spent the night before departure in prayer at a chapel in Restello (the suburb of Restelo, four miles below the Lisbon Arsenal), which had been built by Henry the Navigator. On Saturday, July 8, 1497, the fleet left Restello. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
Fleet and Crew
The fleet carried approximately 150-170 men. Hart describes the crew composition in The Sea Road to the Indies: seamen, soldiers, gunners, trumpeters, a surgeon, and rope-makers. Each vessel carried twenty guns — heavier pieces on clumsy forked bases, lighter guns with swivel mounts, bombards, and one-pounder matchlocks. Crew carried personal weapons. Stone balls for cannon were still in use. Powder and shot were stored in the hold. ^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart]
The Journal was written by an anonymous crew member who served on board the São Rafael. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
Cape Verde Islands (July 8-27, 1497)
On July 15 the fleet sighted the Canaries and passed to the lee of Lançarote. During fog on the night of July 16, Paulo da Gama lost sight of the captain-major’s ship. The fleet became separated. Following instructions, they made sail for the Cape Verde Islands. On July 22 they sighted Ilha do Sal and discovered three vessels — the storeship and those of Coelho and Bartholomeu Dias (who was sailing with them as far as the Mine). They rejoined, and the crew expressed their joy by firing off bombards and sounding trumpets. On Thursday, July 27, they arrived at the island of São Thiago (Santiago) and anchored in the Bay of Santa Maria, where they took on meat, water, and wood, and repaired their yards. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
The South Atlantic Crossing: The Volta do Mar (August 3 - November 4, 1497)
On Thursday, August 3, the fleet left São Thiago in an easterly direction. This was the beginning of the volta do mar — the deliberate westward sweep that would carry the ships down into the South Atlantic to catch the westerly winds and avoid the contrary currents and winds of the African coast. It was a route pioneered by earlier Portuguese navigators like Bartolomeu Dias.
On August 18, about 200 leagues from São Thiago, the captain-major’s main yard broke. They lay to under foresail and lower mainsail for two days and a night. The passage from São Thiago to the Bay of St. Helena covered approximately 1,170 leagues (about 4,290 miles), taking 95 days at an average daily progress of 12 leagues (45 miles). ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
On October 27 (the eve of St. Simon and Jude) they saw many whales, quoquas, and seals. On Wednesday, November 1 (All Saints’ Day), they perceived many indications of land — gulf-weed, birds, and other signs. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
St. Helena Bay: First Landfall in Southern Africa (November 4-16, 1497)
On Saturday, November 4, a couple of hours before daybreak, they had soundings in 110 fathoms, and at nine o’clock sighted land. They saluted the captain-major by firing bombards and dressing ships with flags. On November 7 they returned to the land, finding a low coast with a broad bay. Pero d’Alenquer (who had doubled the Cape with Bartolomeu Dias) took soundings and found the bay clean and sheltered against all winds except from the N.W. They named it Santa Helena (St. Helena Bay). ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
On Wednesday, November 8, they cast anchor and remained eight days, cleaning ships, mending sails, and taking in wood. They encountered Hottentot (Khoikhoi) inhabitants — tawny-coloured people dressed in skins, armed with olive-wood poles tipped with fire-hardened horn, and accompanied by dogs resembling those of Portugal. A notable incident occurred when Fernão Velloso, eager to see how the natives lived, accompanied them to their houses. When he returned shouting, the crew went to fetch him unarmed, and the natives threw assegais, wounding the captain-major and three or four others. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
Rounding the Cape of Good Hope (November 16-22, 1497)
At daybreak on Thursday, November 16, having careened ships and taken in wood, they set sail. Unable to determine their position relative to the Cape, they stood out toward the S.S.W. On Saturday, November 18, they beheld the Cape. They made repeated attempts to round it, but the wind blew from the S.S.W. while the Cape juts out toward the S.W. — forcing them to stand out to sea and return repeatedly. Finally, on Wednesday, November 22, at noon, with the wind astern, they succeeded in doubling the Cape of Good Hope and ran along the coast. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
Mossel Bay — (Angra de São Braz) (November 25 - December 7, 1497)
Late on Saturday, November 25 (St. Catherine’s Day), they entered the Angra de São Braz (Mossel Bay). They remained thirteen days, breaking up the storeship and transferring her contents to the other vessels. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
About ninety Hottentots appeared on December 1. Unlike when Bartolomeu Dias had visited (when the natives fled), these approached cautiously, having apparently heard from the people at St. Helena Bay that the Portuguese meant no harm. On December 2, about two hundred natives came with a dozen oxen and cows and four or five sheep, playing on flutes and dancing. The Portuguese bought a black ox for three bracelets and dined on it. The captain-major ordered two bombards fired from the poop of the longboat when tensions arose — the first discharge scattered the natives who had been threatening. On an offshore island they found seals, including huge ones with large tusks, and counted 3,000 of them, firing bombards among them for amusement. They erected a cross and a pillar (padrão) here, though the natives tore them down before the fleet departed. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
The Natal Coast (December 8-25, 1497)
Leaving São Braz on December 8, the fleet encountered a great storm on December 12 (eve of Santa Lucia), losing sight of Coelho’s Berrio before reuniting at night with signal lights. They passed beyond the furthest point reached by Bartolomeu Dias on December 16. The ships were then driven back sixty leagues by the powerful Agulhas current to the Ilhéo da Cruz (Cross Island), but a strong stern-wind restored their progress. By Christmas Day, December 25, they had discovered seventy leagues of coast beyond Dias’s furthest. They named the land Natal (meaning “Christmas” in Portuguese). ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
The Bantu Coast — Terra da Boa Gente and Rio do Cobre (January 11-16, 1498)
On Thursday, January 11, 1498, they discovered a small river and anchored near the coast. The inhabitants were tall Bantu people, hospitable and welcoming. Their chief was given a jacket, red pantaloons, a Moorish cap, and a bracelet, and in turn offered everything his country could provide. The crew stayed five days, taking in water conveyed to the boats by the villagers. The country was named Terra da Boa Gente (“Land of Good People”) and the river Rio do Cobre (“Copper River”) because of the copper ornaments worn by the people. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
Rio dos Bons Signaes (January 24 - February 24, 1498)
On Monday, January 22, they discovered a low coast thickly wooded with tall trees and the broad mouth of a river. The Berrio entered first on January 24, and the other vessels followed on the 25th. While at this river, two gentlemen of the country visited — one wearing a cap of green satin — and a young man with them had seen large ships before, which the Portuguese took as hopeful signs that they were approaching India. They spent thirty-two days here taking in water, careening the ships, and repairing the mast of the São Rafael. Many men fell ill with scurvy — their feet and hands swelling, gums growing over teeth. Paulo da Gama visited the sick night and day, distributing medicines he had brought for his own use. They erected a pillar here, calling it the padrão of St. Raphael. The river they named Rio dos Bons Signaes (“River of Good Signs” or “River of Good Tokens”). ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
Mozambique (March 2-29, 1498)
On Thursday, March 1, they sighted islands and the mainland. On Friday, March 2, Nicolau Coelho mistook the channel and ran aground on a bank near Mozambique Island. Local boats — playing anafils (Moorish trumpets) — welcomed them. The inhabitants were Mohammedans (Swahili/Arabs), of ruddy complexion, dressed in fine linen and cotton. They found four Moorish vessels in port laden with gold, silver, cloves, pepper, ginger, pearls, jewels, and rubies. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
The local Sultan — whom the Portuguese called a “king” — visited the ships. After being given presents, he provided two pilots. But when the Portuguese attempted to leave on March 10, the pilots fled. A conflict erupted when armed boats from the island confronted them; Paulo da Gama fired bombards and the Berrio pursued. The Moors planned to seize and kill the Portuguese, seeing them as Christian interlopers, but the pilot later revealed the plot. Forced by contrary winds to return to Mozambique for water, the Portuguese were denied access to the watering place. The captain-major ordered three bombards fired to clear the beach, and they took water by force. On March 24 they bombarded the town itself, killing two men. Paulo da Gama captured an almadia laden with fine cotton-stuffs, a glazed jar of butter, glass phials of scented water, books of the Law, and other goods. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
Mombasa (April 7-13, 1498)
On Saturday, April 7 (the eve of Palm Sunday), they cast anchor off Mombasa. The city was prepared for them — numerous vessels dressed in flags. News of their actions at Mozambique had preceded them. The Portuguese anchored with caution, believing there were Christians living alongside the Moors in the city (a persistent misconception). At midnight on the night of their arrival, a zavra with a hundred armed men approached, attempting to board the captain-major’s vessel but were refused entry. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
On Palm Sunday (April 8), the King of Mombasa sent a sheep, oranges, lemons, sugar-cane, and a ring as a pledge of safety. The Portuguese sent two men to the king, who received them hospitably. But on Tuesday, April 10, when attempting to enter the port, the two Mozambique pilots jumped overboard and escaped. Suspecting treachery, the captain-major “questioned” two Moors from Mozambique by dropping boiling oil on their skin. They confessed that orders had been given to capture the Portuguese once inside the port, to avenge what had been done at Mozambique. One of the tortured Moors threw himself into the sea despite bound hands. During the night, swimmers approached the Berrio attempting to cut her cable, but were discovered and fled. After this treachery, the fleet remained two more days before departing. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
Malindi (April 14-24, 1498)
Leaving Mombasa, the fleet captured a boat on April 14 containing seventeen men, gold, silver, and provisions. The prisoners told them that at Malindi there were four vessels belonging to Christians from India. On Easter Sunday, April 15, they cast anchor off Malindi. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
The King of Malindi proved friendly, sending sheep and spices (cloves, cumin, ginger, nutmeg, pepper). On April 18, the king and captain-major met in a boat halfway between ship and shore. The king wore a robe of damask trimmed with green satin, seated on cushioned chairs of bronze beneath a crimson satin sunshade. Bombards fired a salute as he toured the ships. He left his son as a hostage on the ship and took two Portuguese to see his palace. The Indians from the four vessels at Malindi prostrated themselves before a picture of Our Lady brought on board Paulo da Gama’s ship, bringing offerings of cloves and pepper. The king provided a Gujarati pilot (often identified as Malema Cana, a name meaning “master Kanaka”) to guide them across the Indian Ocean. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
The Indian Ocean Crossing (April 24 - May 20, 1498)
On Tuesday, April 24, they left Malindi with the new pilot. On Sunday, April 29, they once again saw the North Star, which they had not seen for a long time. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
On Friday, May 18, after having seen no land for twenty-three days, they sighted lofty mountains — having sailed no less than 600 leagues before the wind. The pilot identified Mount Eli (near Cananor, a conspicuous hill 16 miles north of Cananor). Due to heavy rain and thunderstorms on May 19, the pilot was unable to identify the exact location. On Sunday, May 20, 1498, they found themselves close to the mountains above Calicut. The pilot told them that this was the country they desired to go to. They anchored two leagues from the city of Calicut that night. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
Arrival at Calicut and Negotiations with the Zamorin (May 20 - August 29, 1498)
On May 21, the captain-major sent one of the convicts ashore to Calicut. He was taken to two Moors from Tunis who spoke Castilian and Genoese. The first greeting was: “May the Devil take thee! What brought you hither?” When told they had come in search of Christians and spices, the Moors replied: “Why does not the King of Castile, the King of France, or the Signoria of Venice send hither?” ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
The Zamorin was fifteen leagues away but proceeded to Calicut on hearing of the Portuguese arrival. On Monday, May 28, da Gama went to meet the Zamorin with thirteen men, in their best attire, with bombards in their boats and trumpets and flags. He was carried in a palanquin through the city. They passed through a large Hindu temple (which they mistook for a Christian church), with a bronze pillar surmounted by a bird (a cock — the symbol of the war-god Subraumainar). The king — reclining on a couch covered with green velvet in a small court — received da Gama. The captain-major delivered his message: King Manuel of Portugal, lord of many countries and great wealth, desired to be the Zamorin’s friend and brother. The Zamorin welcomed him and promised to send ambassadors to Portugal. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
The presents da Gama offered (twelve pieces of lambel, four scarlet hoods, hats, coral, wash-hand basins, sugar, oil, and honey) were scorned by the Zamorin’s Moorish factor as beneath the dignity of a king — poorer gifts than the meanest merchant from Mecca would bring. Relations soured further as established Muslim merchants (from Mecca, Cambay, and elsewhere) resented Portuguese intrusion into the spice trade, telling the Zamorin that the Portuguese were thieves who would ruin his country. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
Diogo Dias was sent to the king as factor with merchandise — and was detained, along with other Portuguese, while the Zamorin demanded 600 xerafins (£223). Da Gama seized eighteen hostages in response. After tense negotiations — including the Zamorin writing a letter on a palm leaf with an iron pen — the hostages and merchandise were partially exchanged. The pillar (padrão) of St. Gabriel was given to the Zamorin’s men to be erected. On Wednesday, August 29, 1498, the captain-major and the other captains agreed to depart, resolving to take several Indian prisoners with them. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
The Return Journey (August 30, 1498 - July/August 1499)
Sailing from Calicut, the fleet was pursued by seventy boats before a thunderstorm scattered the pursuers. They stopped at the Anjediva Islands (September 20 - October 5), careening the ships and taking on water and wood. They met a mysterious figure — a Jewish renegade who spoke Venetian — later known as Gaspar da Gama, who had come to investigate the strange ships. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
The crossing of the Arabian Sea took three months less three days (October 5 to January 2, 1499). Calms and foul winds plagued them. Scurvy ravaged the crews once more — thirty men died of their gums growing over their teeth and legs swelling, leaving only seven or eight men able to navigate each ship. The captains held council and agreed that if a favourable wind did not come they would have to return to India. God in his mercy sent a wind that carried them within sight of land in six days. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
They made landfall on January 2, 1499 — sighting Magadoxo (Mogadishu) on the Somali coast, a large town with multi-storied houses. Continuing south, they reached Malindi on January 7, where the friendly king supplied oranges and other fruit for the sick, gave a tusk of ivory for the King of Portugal, and erected a pillar. They remained five days resting. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
On January 13 they anchored at the shoals of St. Raphael (near Mtangata), and burnt the São Rafael as they lacked the crew to sail all three vessels. The figurehead of the São Rafael — carved in oak, about 24 inches high — was saved and later became a family heirloom. After fifteen days, the two remaining ships (São Gabriel and Berrio) continued south, stopping at Zanzibar, São Jorge Island, and Mossel Bay (March 3). They doubled the Cape of Good Hope on March 20 and ran before favourable winds for twenty-seven days. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
On April 25 they had soundings of 35 fathoms near the shoals of the Rio Grande (near Sierra Leone). Here the Journal ends abruptly. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
Nicolau Coelho and Vasco da Gama were separated in a storm. Coelho continued in the Berrio, arriving at Cascaes (below Lisbon) on July 10, 1499 — a voyage of seventy-six days from the African coast. Vasco da Gama, having waited a day for his consort, proceeded to São Thiago, then chartered a caravel to take his dying brother Paulo to Terceira in the Azores. D. Paulo da Gama died a day after landing at Angra on Terceira and was buried in the church of the Monastery of São Francisco. Vasco delayed his triumphal return to attend his brother’s burial. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
The exact date of Vasco da Gama’s return to Lisbon is uncertain: Barros, Goes, and Resende state August 29, 1499; Castanheda gives September 8; a manuscript in the Torre do Tombo records September 18. His triumphal entry likely took place around September 8. From the departure of July 8, 1497, to Coelho’s return on July 10, 1499, the voyage had lasted 732 days. Of this, 316 days were spent on the outward passage, 102 at Calicut and vicinity, and 314 on the homeward passage. Only 55 of the original 150-170 crew are thought to have survived. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt] ^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart]
Navigation and Distances
The total outward passage from Lisbon to Calicut covered approximately 3,584 Portuguese leagues (12,108 nautical miles) at an average daily run of 58 miles. The homeward passage covered 3,417 leagues (11,550 miles) at an average of 40 miles per day. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt]
The Second Voyage (1502–1503)
King Manuel I dispatched da Gama on a second voyage with a heavily armed fleet to intimidate the rulers of the Malabar Coast and secure Portuguese trading interests. Da Gama attacked Calicut, bombarded the port, and seized merchant vessels. He established trading factories at Cochin and Cannanore, left a naval squadron to patrol the Indian Ocean, and returned to Portugal in 1503. His actions on this voyage cemented his reputation as harsh and ruthless. ^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart] ^[source: career-legend-vasco-da-gama-subrahmanyam]
Later Years and Third Voyage
After his second voyage, da Gama retired to private life in Évora, managing his estates and maintaining his position in the Order of Santiago. He was involved in advising the crown on Indian affairs but was not initially chosen to lead further expeditions. In 1524, King John III appointed him Viceroy of India and sent him on a third voyage to restore order in the Portuguese settlements. Da Gama arrived in India in September 1524 but fell ill shortly after. He died in Cochin on Christmas Eve, December 24, 1524. ^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart] ^[source: career-legend-vasco-da-gama-subrahmanyam]
Burial and Tomb
Da Gama was initially buried in Cochin. In 1539, his remains were brought back to Portugal and interred in the Church of Our Lady of the Relics (Igreja do Convento do Carmo) in Vidigueira, in a magnificent tomb. ^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart]
Character and Reputation
Vasco da Gama was a skilled mariner and determined commander who could be arrogant in later life. He was harsh in his treatment of adversaries, particularly Muslim merchants and rulers who opposed Portuguese interests. Hart describes him as becoming increasingly imperious and intolerant of opposition. Subrahmanyam’s study examines both his career and the legends that grew around him. ^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart] ^[source: career-legend-vasco-da-gama-subrahmanyam]

entities/zamorin-of-calicut.title: Zamorin of Calicut
entities/zamorin-of-calicut.content:
Zamorin of Calicut
The Zamorin (from Malayalam ‘Samutiri’, meaning ‘Sea King’) was the traditional title of the Hindu rulers of Calicut (modern Kozhikode) on the Malabar Coast of India. The Zamorin’s court was the first Indian court encountered by Vasco da Gama upon his arrival in May 1498. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt] ^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart] ^[source: career-legend-vasco-da-gama-subrahmanyam]
Meeting with Vasco da Gama
Da Gama and his fleet anchored near Calicut on May 20, 1498. He was received by the Zamorin and his court, presenting gifts and requesting permission to trade. The Zamorin’s court was initially receptive, but tensions arose over the quality and nature of da Gama’s gifts, which were deemed unimpressive by Indian standards, and over the demands of the Portuguese to have exclusive trading privileges. ^[source: velho_gama_journal.txt] ^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart]
Relations with the Portuguese
Relations between the Zamorin and the Portuguese quickly soured, largely due to the influence of established Muslim merchants in Calicut who controlled the spice trade and saw the Portuguese as threats to their commercial monopoly. The Zamorin resisted Portuguese demands for exclusive trading rights and opposed the construction of Portuguese forts on the Malabar Coast. When da Gama returned on his second voyage (1502–1503), he bombarded Calicut and seized ships in retaliation for the Zamorin’s refusal to submit to Portuguese terms. ^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart] ^[source: career-legend-vasco-da-gama-subrahmanyam]
Title and Meaning
The title ‘Zamorin’ derives from the Malayalam word ‘Samutiri’ or ‘Samudra Raja’, meaning ‘Sea King’ — reflecting the maritime orientation of Calicut as a major trading port on the Indian Ocean. The Zamorin’s power was based on control of the spice trade and the collection of duties from foreign merchants. ^[source: sea-road-to-the-indies-hart] ^[source: career-legend-vasco-da-gama-subrahmanyam]

events/battle-of-gravelines-1588.title: Battle of Gravelines
events/battle-of-gravelines-1588.content:
Battle of Gravelines (July 29, 1588)

The Armada campaign map. The decisive battle was fought off Gravelines after the English fireship attack at Calais scattered the Spanish fleet. Red = Armada outward, blue dashed = English fleet, dashed red = disastrous retreat around Scotland and Ireland.
Overview
The decisive naval engagement of the Spanish Armada campaign, fought off the coast of Gravelines (then in the Spanish Netherlands, now in France). The battle shattered Spanish hopes of invading England.
Context
After the English fireship attack at Calais scattered the Spanish fleet from its anchorage, the Armada was driven eastward in disarray. The English fleet closed in for battle off the shoals of Gravelines, where the Spanish were forced to fight.
The Action
The battle lasted approximately 8 hours. English ships, faster and more maneuverable, used superior gunnery at distance to batter the Spanish formation. The Spanish, trained in close-quarters boarding tactics, were unable to grapple and board the English ships. Key elements:

English broadsides raked the Spanish ships from a safe distance
Several Spanish ships were sunk or driven aground on the Flanders shoals
The Spanish formation was broken and could not be reformed

Aftermath
The Armada was forced northwards, around Scotland and Ireland, in a harrowing retreat. Storms and shipwrecks destroyed many more Spanish ships than the battle itself. The defeat preserved English independence and marked the rise of English naval power.
Commanders
English

Lord Charles Howard of Effingham — Lord High Admiral, overall command
Sir Francis Drake — Vice-admiral, commanding aboard the Revenge
John Hawkins — Rear-admiral, commanding aboard the Victory
Sir Martin Frobisher — Commander of the Triumph

Spanish

Duke of Medina Sidonia — Commander of the Armada


Provenance: Information drawn from Sugden’s biography of Sir Francis Drake.

events/battle-of-mactan-1521.title: Battle of Mactan
events/battle-of-mactan-1521.content:
Battle of Mactan / Death of Magellan (April 27, 1521)

Cebu and Mactan. Magellan’s midnight approach to Mactan (orange dashed), the battle site (red star), and the flight of the survivors. He led 49 Spaniards against 1,500 warriors of Lapu-Lapu and was cut down on the beach.
Overview
On the morning of April 27, 1521, Ferdinand Magellan — the greatest navigator of his age — was killed on the beach of Mactan Island in the Philippines. Leading 49 armoured Spaniards against approximately 1,500 warriors of Chief Lapu-Lapu, Magellan was struck by a poisoned arrow, overwhelmed, and cut down. His body was never recovered. Pigafetta’s account is the sole surviving eyewitness report.
The Decision to Attack
After the mass conversion of Cebu, Magellan agreed to assist his new ally King Humabon in subduing the neighbouring island of Mactan, whose chief Lapu-Lapu refused to accept Spanish sovereignty. Magellan, confident in the superiority of Spanish arms against “naked savages,” decided to lead the assault personally — a decision Pigafetta and other officers are recorded as having urged him against. ^[source: bergreen-magellan.md, Ch. X]
The Landing Force
On the night of April 26, Magellan set out from Cebu with 60 armed men in three boats. The water off Mactan was too shallow for the boats to approach the shore, blocked by coral rocks. The Spaniards waded through the surf in the darkness, reaching the beach at dawn — wet, tired, and outnumbered. Only 49 men actually landed; the boats could not get close enough for the remainder. ^[source: pigafetta-magellan.md, Sec. 80]
The Battle
Lapu-Lapu’s warriors — approximately 1,500 men according to Pigafetta — waited on the beach, armed with bamboo spears, iron-tipped lances, bows and arrows, and large wooden shields. The Spaniards opened fire with crossbows and arquebuses from the water, but the range was too great. As the Spanish waded ashore, the natives charged.
Magellan fought at the front of his men. A poisoned arrow struck him in the right leg. He continued to fight, ordering an orderly retreat, but the men broke and fled. Only six or eight men remained with the captain. The natives, Pigafetta recorded, “shot only at our legs because they were naked.” An Indian hurled a bamboo spear into Magellan’s face; Magellan killed him with his lance. Trying to draw his sword, Magellan could only pull it halfway, having been wounded in the arm. A scimitar blow to his left leg felled him. The warriors swarmed and killed him with spears and stones. ^[source: pigafetta-magellan.md, Sec. 81]
Pigafetta’s Eulogy
Pigafetta’s journal contains the famous eulogy: “Among the other virtues, he was more constant than anyone else in the greatest of storms; he endured hunger better than all others; and more accurately than any man in the world did he chart and navigate.” ^[source: pigafetta-magellan.md, Sec. 82]
The Body
Humabon offered a ransom for Magellan’s body. Lapu-Lapu refused. He declared that he would not give up such a man “for all the riches in the world” and intended to keep him “as a memorial.” Magellan’s body was never recovered. Some accounts suggest pieces of his body washed ashore on Mactan. ^[source: pigafetta-magellan.md, Sec. 82]
Significance
Magellan’s death at Mactan was the defining tragedy of the circumnavigation. He died just weeks before reaching the Moluccas (the Spice Islands), his ultimate destination. He never completed the voyage he had conceived — the first circumnavigation of the globe. His death marked the end of the expedition’s heroic phase and the beginning of its desperate struggle for survival. Lapu-Lapu is celebrated today as the first Filipino to resist foreign aggression, and his victory at Mactan is commemorated as a landmark of anti-colonial resistance.
Participants

Ferdinand Magellan — Killed in battle
Lapu-Lapu — Chieftain of Mactan, led the defence
Antonio Pigafetta — Chronicler, survived the battle
Cristovao Rebelo — Magellan’s illegitimate son, killed alongside him
King Humabon — Cebu ally who requested the intervention

Location
Mactan Island, Philippines (near Cebu)

events/battle-vega-real-1495.title: Battle in the Vega Real
events/battle-vega-real-1495.content:
Battle in the Vega Real (March 1495)

Hispaniola map showing the Vega Real (Royal Plain) where the first pitched battle was fought, and the surrounding settlements. The battle broke organized Taíno resistance.
Overview
The Battle in the Vega Real (Royal Plain) of Hispaniola in March 1495 was the first pitched battle between European and indigenous forces in the Americas. Columbus led a combined force of infantry, cavalry, and war dogs against a coalition of Taíno warriors assembled by the defeated but defiant followers of Caonabo. The battle demonstrated the overwhelming technological and tactical superiority of the Spanish and effectively broke organized native resistance on the island.
Background
After the capture of Caonabo, his brothers and allied caciques gathered a large force — estimated by Columbus at 100,000 warriors, though likely a few thousand — in the Vega Real, the fertile central plain of Hispaniola. The native forces intended to destroy the Spanish settlements and drive the invaders from the island. Columbus, believing that a decisive demonstration of Spanish power would subdue the island permanently, marched out to meet them. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VIII Ch. VI]
The Spanish Force
Columbus commanded approximately 200 infantry, 20 cavalry, and a contingent of attack dogs — large mastiffs and greyhounds trained to tear unarmoured natives apart. The Spanish were armed with crossbows, arquebuses, lances, and swords. The horses alone were a terrifying novelty: no Taíno had ever seen a mounted man before the Spanish arrival. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VIII Ch. VI]
The Battle
The native warriors, armed with wooden spears (macanas), bows and arrows, and slings, charged the Spanish line with courage but without effect. The Spanish armour turned their arrows; the cavalry charges broke their formations, with horses trampling and riders cutting down warriors with lances. The war dogs were unleashed and tore through the native ranks, causing panic. The arquebuses and crossbows killed at a distance, shattering morale. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VIII Ch. VI]
The battle was not a contest but a slaughter. Thousands of Taíno were killed; Spanish casualties were minimal. The survivors scattered into the mountains, and the Vega Real — the most fertile region of the island — fell under Spanish control.
Imposition of Tribute
Following the battle, Columbus imposed the tribute system on the surviving native population. Every Indian over the age of 14 was required to pay a hawk’s bell full of gold dust every three months; in regions without gold, the tribute was paid in cotton (25 pounds per person). Those who failed to meet the quota were punished by death. This system, combined with the forced labour of the repartimiento that followed, led to the catastrophic depopulation of the Taíno people. ^[source: irving-columbus-vol2.md, Book VIII Ch. VII]
Significance
The Battle in the Vega Real established the pattern for European-indigenous warfare in the Americas for centuries to come: technological superiority, cavalry shock, and trained dogs used to terrorize native armies. It was the moment when the conquest of Hispaniola passed from negotiation and resistance to outright subjugation. The tribute system it enabled was the forerunner of the encomienda, the institution that would devastate the indigenous population of the Caribbean and beyond.
Location
Vega Real (Royal Plain), interior of Hispaniola (present-day Dominican Republic)
