sources/columbus-letter-de-insulis.title: De Insulis nuper inventis — The Letter of Christopher Columbus
sources/columbus-letter-de-insulis.content:
De Insulis nuper inventis — The Letter of Christopher Columbus
Context line — Columbus’s first written report of the 1492 voyage, announcing the discovery of islands in the “Indian Sea” to the Spanish sovereigns’ treasurer Luis de Santángel (addressed as Raphael Sanxis), in the Latin translation by Leander de Cosco; this file is a facsimile of the earliest illustrated edition.
Source
Christopher Columbus. De Insulis nuper inventis / The Letter of Christopher Columbus Announcing the Discovery of the New World. Latin text of the letter to Raphael Sanxis (Luis de Santángel), translated from the Spanish by Leander de Cosco (Aliander de Losco), dated 3 kalends of March A.D. 1493 (the year of Pope Alexander VI’s first year).
This edition: Facsimile of the earliest known illustrated printing, reproduced for John S. Kennedy, President of the Lenox Library (New York, 1890). Complete copy from the Lenox Library, with the outside sheet lacking in earlier reproductions (e.g. Pilinski).
Digital source: Anna’s Archive ZIP (OCLC 12397922; tree 32044086252996/), 40 OCR page files.
Text
wiki/raw/columbus-letter-de-insulis/raw.txt — 483 lines, ~16,400 characters, 40 OCR pages. The 1890 facsimile opens with an English publisher’s NOTE (June 1890); the body is the Latin letter in early printed orthography with pictorial woodcut headings. Body prose is readable despite OCR artifacts in title pages, illustration captions, and library stamps. Original page-level files preserved under sources/columbus-letter-de-insulis/32044086252996/.
Contents
Publisher’s Note (1890 facsimile)
John S. Kennedy’s English preface (Lenox Library, June 1890) explains that this is a fac-simile of the earliest edition known with pictorial illustrations of Columbus’s First Letter to the Spanish Sovereigns. It reproduces the complete work — identical to Pilinski’s facsimile but with the outside sheet that was missing from his copy. The Lenox copy is described as the only complete original known. Kennedy notes the approaching Four Hundredth Anniversary of the Discovery and the high prices commanded by contemporary editions; a few facsimile copies were prepared for private distribution to libraries.
Letter Header
Full title as printed: Epistola Cristoferi Colom (de Insulis in mari Indico nuper inventis), addressed to the magnificent lord Raphael Sanxis, treasurer of the most serene King Ferdinand of Spain. Translated from the Spanish idiom into Latin by the noble and learned Leander de Cosco, 3 kalends of March A.D. 1493, in the first year of the pontificate of Alexander VI.
Opening — Voyage Complete and Possession Taken
Columbus opens by assuring Santángel that he has completed the business of the province entrusted to him and will relate everything done and discovered on the voyage. On the thirty-third day after leaving Cadiz he entered the Indian Sea, where he found very many islands inhabited by countless people. He took possession of all of them for the most fortunate King, with proclamation and extended banners, none contradicting. The first island he named after the Divine Saviour (San Salvador), in whose aid he had reached it and the others.
First Landfall and Naming of Islands
The first island the Indians call Guanahani; Columbus gave new names to others — Santa Maria de la Concepción, Fernandina, Isabela, Juana (Hispaniola), and so on for the rest. On the island he had already called Juana he landed and coasted westward a considerable distance without finding cities or towns on the shore, only villages and country houses; the inhabitants fled when they saw the Spaniards. He continued inland expecting to find a city or village, but after going far found nothing new; winter was setting in and he wished to turn south. He returned to a port he had marked and sent two men inland for three days; they found innumerable people and dwellings, small and without any government, and returned.
Coast of Juana and Discovery of Hispaniola
From Indians he had taken aboard he learned that Juana was an island; he therefore sailed east along its coast for 322 leagues to its eastern end. From there he found another island to the east, 54 leagues distant, which he immediately named Hispaniola. He entered it and sailed north along its coast as he had sailed east along Juana — 178 leagues. He reports that Juana and the other islands there are exceedingly fertile.
Description of Hispaniola — Natural Riches
Hispaniola is surrounded by many safe and wide harbours, not comparable to any he had seen. Many great and wholesome rivers flow through it; many lofty mountains. All the islands are beautiful and distinguished by diverse shapes; full of the greatest variety of trees reaching to the stars. He saw them so green and lovely as in May in Spain; some flowering, some fruiting, some in other states; nightingales singing and many kinds of birds in February when he walked among them. On the said island are seven or eight kinds of palm trees of exceptional beauty. There are marvellous pines, fields, vast meadows, varied birds, varied honey, varied metals — except iron.
Hispaniola — Landscape, Ports, and Natives
On the part he named Hispaniola are great and beautiful mountains, vast fields, groves, very fertile plains, and forests suitable for building. The convenience of ports, abundance of rivers, and healthfulness of the people surpass belief unless seen. The trees, pastures, and fruits differ greatly from Juana’s. Hispaniola abounds in diverse aromatics, gold, and metals. The inhabitants of all the islands he saw go naked as they are born, except some women who cover themselves with a leaf, foliage, or a cotton veil. They carry no arms and know nothing of them; they are not ill-formed but timid and full of fear. They have reed spears hardened in fire with a wooden tip sharpened to a point.
Native Character and Conduct
When Columbus sent two or three men to villages, the Indians fled in crowds until they saw the Spaniards meant no harm; then they were simple and good-faith, very liberal with what they had — no one refused what was asked, but invited the Spaniards to ask. They showed love to all. Columbus forbade his men to give worthless trifles for gold or cotton. They know no idolatry; they firmly believe that all power and good things are in heaven, and that Columbus and his ships came from heaven — especially after he was received at Barcelona and sent back. They are not slow or dull but of very sharp intelligence; men who have crossed the sea explain everything with wonder, having never seen clothed peoples or ships.
Taking of Informants and Native Welcome
Columbus seized some Indians by force so they might learn from the Spaniards and teach what was known in those parts; this succeeded quickly — by signs and words both sides understood. Some Indians now travel with him, believing he descended from heaven. Wherever the fleet arrived, the first to see them cried out and others repeated: “Come, come, you will see heavenly people.” Men, women, young and old then visited with great crowds, bringing food and drink with incredible love and kindness.
Canoes and Inter-Island Commerce
Each island has many dugout canoes, narrow and long like Spanish birremes but swifter, rowed only with oars. Some are large, some small, some medium. Many birremes rowed by eighteen oarsmen, with which they cross to all the innumerable islands and carry on trade and commerce among themselves. Columbus saw some birremes or skiffs carrying seventy or eighty rowers. There is no difference in appearance, customs, or language among all these islands — all understand one another — which makes it easy for the King to bring them to holy Christian faith.
Size of Hispaniola and Neighbouring Islands
Columbus reports having sailed 322 leagues east from Juana on a straight west-to-east course and can say Juana is larger than England and Scotland together — not counting the two provinces beyond the 322 leagues toward the west that he did not visit. One is called India (where people are born with tails); the other is Hispaniola, which in circumference is greater than all Spain from Cologne to Cape St. Vincent. In Hispaniola he solemnly took possession for the King and committed all its dominion to him. At a most convenient and beautiful place he took possession of a large village named for the Nativity of the Lord and immediately ordered a fort built (which should now be finished) with men, arms, and more than a year’s provisions. He left a caravel to be built and skilled men for the rest.
Native Government, Appearance, and Caribs
The King’s benevolence toward Columbus is incredible; the peoples are very amiable and benign. The natives have no kings except princes who may have twenty subjects; women appear to work more than men. He saw no monsters as many thought; the people are not black like Ethiopians but have flat, hanging hair and live where the sun’s heat is great — about twenty-six degrees from the equator. On one island called Carib (second from Hispaniola on the route to India) a fiercer people live who eat human flesh; they have many birremes and raid other islands. They differ in wearing long hair like women and using bows and reed spears. Other Indians fear them greatly. There is also an island where women alone live (visited on the route from Hispaniola to India), who use bows and spears and arm themselves with copper plates. Another island beyond Hispaniola is said to have people without hair and abundant gold.
Gold, Spices, and Request for Ships
Columbus promises that as much gold will be supplied as the King and Queen wish, as well as spices, cotton, mastic (as found at Chios), aloes, rhubarb, and other aromatics — as much as their majesties may command. Those left in the fort have already found these or will find them; Columbus stayed nowhere else except as winds compelled, except at the Nativity village until the fort was secured. If ships had come as reason required, even greater things would have followed. He attributes the discovery not to human merit but to holy Christian faith and the piety and religion of the sovereigns.
Closing — Religious Exhortation and Date
He urges the King, Queen, princes, and all Christendom to give thanks to God for the victory and to celebrate solemn festivals. Dated from the Galley, Lisbon, the day before the Ides of March (14 March 1493). Signed: Cristofor Colom, Prefect of the Ocean Fleet.
Epigram (R.L. de Corbaria, Bishop of Monte Palusis)
Latin verses addressed to the Invincible King of Spain: no land remained to add to Spanish triumphs until this region beneath eastern waves shall increase Betic titles; grace is due to Columbus and greater grace to God who prepares new kingdoms for pious and strong kings.
Illustrations (1890 facsimile woodcuts)
The illustrated edition includes pictorial headings and woodcuts interleaved with the letter, captioned in Latin (e.g. Oceanica Classis, Infula Hispana, royal arms of Ferdinand and Isabella, Granada). Several OCR pages are illustration-only with minimal extractable text.

sources/corbett-drake-tudor-navy.title: Drake and the Tudor Navy — Julian S. Corbett
sources/corbett-drake-tudor-navy.content:
Drake and the Tudor Navy — Julian S. Corbett
Bibliographic Information

Author: Julian Stafford Corbett (Julian S. Corbett), 1854–1922
Full title: Drake and the Tudor Navy with a History of the Rise of England as a Maritime Power
Form: In two volumes
First printed: February 1898 (Longmans, Green, and Co.)
This impression: New Impression, April 1917 (earlier cheaper edition September 1899; reprinted September 1912)
Publisher: Longmans, Green, and Co., London
Library copy noted in OCR: University of Virginia call DA86.22.D7 C75 1917 V.1
Source files: wiki/raw/corbett-drake-tudor-navy-v1/raw.txt (Vol. I, 444 OCR pages); wiki/raw/corbett-drake-tudor-navy-v2/raw.txt (Vol. II, 508 OCR pages)
Quality note: OCR from two Anna’s Archive ZIPs (hashes c883d311… / tree x001645269/; cd5d5ff2… / tree x001931749/). Readable naval narrative; running headers, plate lists, and library marks appear. Distinct from John Sugden’s modern biography sir-francis-drake-sugden.

About the Author and Edition
Corbett was the leading English naval historian of the late Victorian and Edwardian period, later associated with official and strategic writing on sea power. This work is not a pure personal life of Drake but a two-volume history of the rise of England as a maritime power, with Drake as the central agent of that rise. The 1917 impression reprints the 1898 text; the Preface to the Second Edition answers J. K. Laughton’s criticism on the development of line-ahead tactics in 1588. An epigraph from Sir Walter Raleigh on trade and command of the sea opens the argument. A portrait of Drake from Buckland Abbey is among the front matter illustrations.
Summary
Volume I carries Drake from Crowndale near Tavistock through Hawkins’s third voyage and San Juan de Ulúa, the early Navy service, Nombre de Dios and the Spanish Main, the war-party years, the circumnavigation (three chapters), knighthood, and a closing study of Elizabeth’s Navy. Volume II opens with the Indies voyage of 1585, San Domingo and Cartagena, operations on the Spanish coast, Drake’s plan of campaign against the Armada, the Channel actions through Portland, the Isle of Wight, and Gravelines, then the Lisbon expedition, Drake’s disgrace, the last voyage, and a Conclusion. Appendices in both volumes collect authorities, documents, and technical notes (birth and parentage; San Juan de Ulúa reports; Armada and Indies voyage authorities; Elizabethan tonnage measurement; etc.). Corbett’s thesis—later a target of twentieth-century revision—is that Drake and the Tudor seamen forged a new naval art and England’s claim to maritime supremacy.
Scope and Approach
Corbett writes operational and institutional naval history: ship types, gunnery, fleet tactics, administration, and the political “war party” around Elizabeth, Burghley, Walsingham, and Leicester, as much as pure biography. He treats the long “neither peace nor war” of Anglo-Spanish relations as the sixteenth century’s distinctive international form. The Preface to the Second Edition defends his reading of 1588 tactics against Laughton. Sugden’s later popular biography explicitly names the “Corbett tradition” of Drake as founder of English naval supremacy as one pole it seeks to move beyond; this page documents that older standard work for the wiki corpus.
Contents
Volume I
Introduction / The Naval Art in the Middle of the Sixteenth Century — Sets the technical and strategic baseline of mid-Tudor sea fighting before Drake’s generation transforms it.
Chapter I: Drake’s Early Years — Birth at Crowndale near Tavistock; the farm’s passage from Tavistock Abbey to the Russells; Devon and Reformation milieu; family ties that lead toward the Hawkins connection and the sea.
Chapter II: John Hawkins — Three streams of national sentiment—religious passion foremost among them—that gather toward rupture with Spain and the House of Burgundy. Hawkins’s career as the hinge of Drake’s early service and of England’s first sustained push into the Atlantic slave and contraband trades.
Chapter III: San Juan de Ulúa — Hawkins’s third voyage as the step that “could never be retraced.” Camden’s report that seafaring men fretted for war; Drake’s and his master’s turn to irreconcilable hostility toward Spain; English and Spanish responsibility weighed in Corbett’s balance.
Chapter IV: Drake’s First Service in the Navy — Sixteenth-century hostilities short of open war; Drake’s early official employment; the legal and diplomatic grey zone of reprisal and “distraint” at sea.
Chapter V: Nombre de Dios — The new stream of daring that Corbett sees entering Elizabeth’s Navy through Drake; the 1572 Panama enterprise; Nombre de Dios as the opening of a distinctive English style of oceanic war.
Chapter VI: The Spanish Main — After the ease of the Nombre de Dios stroke, Drake attempts the capital of the Spanish Main itself; islands of San Bernardo; night entry toward Cartagena; raids and intelligence along the treasure coasts.
Chapter VII: Drake and the War Party — Lost years after Drake empties a Plymouth church until he reappears in Ireland in spring 1575; conjectural movements; return to a political atmosphere eager for peace after the Ridolfi crisis; alignment with the court faction pushing harder measures against Spain.
Chapter VIII: The Voyage of Circumnavigation — Secret aims of Drake’s exalted promoters; Spanish suspicions that the “Alexandria currants” cover story is false; departure and the Atlantic leg of 1577–78.
Chapter IX: The Voyage of Circumnavigation (continued) — Crisis in St. Julian’s Bay; the Doughty tragedy; Drake as a matured, harsher leader; the passage toward the Strait and the Pacific.
Chapter X: The Voyage of Circumnavigation (continued) — The voyage “made”: Golden Hind ballasted with silver; Anton’s question on the return route; Drake’s chart of four ways home (including Moluccas and the Cape); the homeward design.
Chapter XI: Knighthood — England’s year of waiting; Wynter’s return and reception; reports of Magellan’s Strait and of Doughty’s death; Drake’s reappearance and the queen’s recognition—knighthood as official seal on the new oceanic prestige.
Chapter XII: The Navy of Elizabeth — Drake on the Royal Commission into the Navy Office; complaints of mismanagement and dishonesty; Sir Thomas Cotton and other critics; institutional reform as the counterpart to Drake’s personal glory.
Volume I Appendices (selected) — A. Birth, parentage, and early years; B. Authorities for Hawkins’s third voyage, with Spanish official report on San Juan de Ulúa; C. further documentary notes on Drake’s early services (as listed in the volume TOC).
Volume II
Chapter I: The Indies Voyage 1585 — Navy reorganisation not completed before England stands on the brink of war; forces beyond even Elizabeth’s genius for delay; Drake’s commission and the West Indies expedition as the opening of open large-scale oceanic offensive.
Chapter II: San Domingo and Cartagena — Beyond official instructions, Drake pursues the real object of the expedition; plan of operations (with expected timings and plunder) drawn for Burghley’s information; sack and ransom of Santo Domingo and Cartagena as the campaign’s centrepiece.
Chapter III: Operations on the Spanish Coast — Home ovation and the revelation of the Babington Plot; assassination of Elizabeth and Mary Stuart’s cause; Cadiz and the Spanish littoral operations that “singe the King of Spain’s beard” and disrupt Armada preparations.
Chapter IV: Drake’s Plan of Campaign — End of the first stage of the war; criticism of Cartagena’s evacuation set against the brilliance of the preliminary campaigns; Elizabeth’s handling of the next stage; Drake’s strategic design for meeting the Armada at sea.
Chapter V: Attempts to Attack the Armada — The Plymouth fleet as the culmination of the long transition—Howard’s royal great-ships and pinnaces plus a formidable auxiliary squadron; efforts to strike the Armada before or as it completes its concentration.
Chapter VI: The Fleets in Contact — Combined fleet back at Plymouth (12 July); revictualling and readiness; false home reports that the Armada lies scattered; the first real contact and the Channel chase begins.
Chapter VII: Portland and the Isle of Wight — Fleets lying-to off Plymouth; Sidonia succouring injured ships; Howard’s council of war; Recalde and Salvador; Valdés’s foremast lost; fighting about Portland and the Isle of Wight as the Armada still advances largely intact.
Chapter VIII: The Battle of Gravelines — English seamen’s disappointment with mere Channel cannonades; anxiety ashore as the Armada seems to defy the best seamen; fireships, the Flanders shore, and Gravelines as the decisive fleet action; Corbett’s long view that three centuries later can call it one of the decisive military exploits of the world even when contemporaries felt dazed disappointment.
Chapter IX: The Lisbon Expedition — After Gravelines, the Counter-Armada / Portugal voyage; aims under Dom Antonio; Corunna and Lisbon; the campaign that undoes much of Drake’s political capital.
Chapter X: Drake’s Disgrace — The country counts an irreparable loss: Drake’s fall from the pre-eminence won by Armada service and earlier exploits; jealousy of “natural leaders” of the realm in arms; court and public judgment after Lisbon.
Chapter XI: The Last Voyage — Relief of Brest as nearly the last blow to the Spanish cause in France; languid war after Walsingham’s death (1590); Burghley’s cautious control; the final Drake–Hawkins Indies voyage; failure, sickness, and Drake’s death in the Caribbean.
Conclusion — Corbett’s closing assessment of Drake’s place in the rise of England as a maritime power and of the Tudor Navy’s transformation across the reign.
Volume II Appendices (selected) — A. Authorities for the Indies voyage, 1585; B. Authorities for the Armada campaign; C. Elizabethan tonnage measurement; D. Authorities for the Indies voyage, 1595; Index.
Relation to Other Drake Sources in This Wiki

sir-francis-drake-sugden — Modern (1990/2006) rounded biography; explicitly distances itself from the “Corbett tradition” of Drake as architect of naval supremacy and from purely privateering readings.
This Corbett page is the classic two-volume operational-naval treatment (1898; 1917 impression) and should be cited when the wiki needs the older strategic narrative, Armada tactics debate (vs Laughton), or institutional Navy chapters.

Sources

Corbett, Julian S. Drake and the Tudor Navy with a History of the Rise of England as a Maritime Power. 2 vols. London: Longmans, Green, and Co., first printed February 1898; New Impression 1917.

sources/crescentio-nautica-mediterranea.title: Nautica Mediterranea — Bartolomeo Crescentio
sources/crescentio-nautica-mediterranea.content:
Nautica Mediterranea — Bartolomeo Crescentio
Bibliographic Information

Author: Bartolomeo Crescentio (Crescenti), Romano — papal engineer (Ingegniero Pontificio), active in the service of Cardinal Aldobrandini and the Papal States
Full title: Nautica Mediterranea: Nella quale si mostra la fabrica delle galee, galeazze, e galeoni, e di qual si voglia altra sorte di naviglio, insieme con tutte le sue parti, misure, e proportion (Nautical Mediterranean: in which is shown the construction of galleys, galleasses, galleons, and of whatever other kind of vessel, together with all their parts, measures, and proportions)
Original imprint: Della Nautica Mediterranea di Bartolomeo Crescentio Romano. Rome, first printed 1602
This file: An Internet Archive/Google digitisation (identifier nauticamediterra00cres), converted to EPUB by automatic OCR (Ebook-lib 0.17.1, 2023)
Source file: wiki/raw/crescentio-nautica-mediterranea.txt (662 OCR pages, ~880,000 characters)
Language: 17th-century Italian (original orthography, with heavy OCR degradation); source page in English

About the Author and Edition
Bartolomeo Crescentio was an Italian engineer in the service of the Papal States, styling himself “Ingegniero Pontificio.” He dedicated the work to the Illmo et Reverendissimo Signor Cardinale Aldobrandino (Cardinal Aldobrandini), Camerlengo of the Holy Church and governor-general of Ferrara and of the whole Ecclesiastical State. The opening address recounts the work’s slow composition: the Nautica Mediterranea was first given to the press some six years before completion, then long interrupted while the author was “impiegato” in various voyages and affairs, in the service of the Pope and of the Cardinal. Crescentio’s frame is classical — he opens on Plato’s ascent from the species to the genus, on Hero of Alexandria and the marriage of Platonic geometry with the Mechanics of Archimedes — and applies it to the practical geometry of the Mediterranean galley.
Summary
The Nautica Mediterranea is a systematic practical-geometry treatise on the design, building, rigging, and navigation of the Mediterranean war galley and its consorts, arranged in three books. It opens with the choice of place for building the armada, the qualities of timber (elm, oak, poplar, chestnut, larch), and the enumeration of the galley’s parts — from the keel (carena), frames (stamenali), and futtocks through the planking, the ferzi (the diagonal ribs over which the hull is planked), and the fastening system of treenails and iron. The first book carries the running theme of the parts of the galley, their measures and proportions. The second book turns to navigation: the compass (bussola) and its variation, the errors of charts — the Mediterranean and Lisbon charts “abbagliate” (blinded) by the false arrangement of meridians and parallels — the riformation of the rose, the poles and the tropic circles, and the longitudinal problem. The third book takes up the astronomical and practical rules of the mariner: the meridian, the two tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, the declination of the sun, the rising and setting of the stars, and the removal of “il prolisso colo de gl’Aprologhi” (the prolix error of the aphorisms) and of mariners’ errors.
Scope and Approach
Crescentio writes as a practising military engineer, not a historian: the work is prescriptive, technical, and heavily diagrammatic — the OCR pages are dense with the letter-references (A, B, C, D) of geometric figures. He is sharply critical of the current state of Mediterranean navigation, dismissing the errors of the common charts and of the mappi (plane charts) “abbagliate” by a false arrangement of meridians, and reporting the compass-variation rules of Gio. Battista della Porta, “commune amico nostro,” the Neapolitan natural philosopher. He addresses himself to working mariners, stating his intent to be understood by them rather than to dazzle the learned, and in the third book records that he taught a young mariner his rules to test whether his manner of writing was clear enough to be followed.
Contents

The structure below is reconstructed from the surviving OCR. Because this digitisation is a degraded Google/Internet Archive optical scan of an early-modern Italian book (heavy ligatures, f/s confusion, broken letter forms), individual chapter headings are frequently garbled or lost; the three-book division and running subjects are clear, but the exact chapter titles and boundaries could not all be recovered. This page therefore records the book structure at the level the scan supports.

Front Matter and Dedication
Dedication to Cardinal Aldobrandino — Crescentio addresses the Cardinal, Camerlengo of the Holy Church and governor of Ferrara and the Ecclesiastical State, on the Platonic ascent from the particular to the general as the path by which the Ancients found all the sciences, and applies it to the reduction of the heavens and the measures of the globe to the small sphere of water and earth.
Address to the Reader — Signed by “Bartolomeo Crescentio Ingegniero Pontificio”; recounts that the work was first given to the press six years before, then long interrupted while the author served the Pope and the Cardinal in voyages and affairs; notes the friendship and correspondence of Gio. Battista della Porta.
“Quello che si ha da trattare in questo libro” — A table of the subjects to be treated in the book, framed as the author’s perpetual intent to be useful to others by procuring rules whereby man may preserve himself in safety on land and sea.
Libro Primo (Book One) — The Fabrica (construction) of the Galley
Capitolo Primo: Che luoghi si debbano eleggere per fabricar l’armata navale — Which places should be chosen for building the naval armada; the site must be sufficient for the senale (dockyard), the port, and the maestranza (workmen), with timber and victuals brought to it.
The running text then proceeds through the qualities of timber (olmo elm, quercia oak, faggio beech, chiuppo poplar, tiglio linden), the enumeration of the galley’s parts — carena (keel), impiatori, bracciuoli, bancacci, fodero (planking), the four matere stamenali (frame timbers), cordone, cinta, parme, contevali, contouali, the ferzi and their setting, the corsia (gangway), coperta (deck), tapere, raggioli, gioghi, corde, crocette, calaveme, draganti, baccalari, banchi, battagliuole — and on through the ship’s furniture: catene (chains), chiavi, sartie (shrouds), schiffo, alberi (masts), antenne (yards), gomeni, aguglie, metalame, pulegge (blocks), quarnari; then the making of the tacking and hoisting gear, the varodano (windlass) and the centura, the hoisting of the oar-crew from one galley to another, the parts of the sail, and the measures and proportions of each part of the vessel.
Libro Secondo (Book Two) — Navigation, the Compass, and the Errors of Charts
The second book turns from the fabric to the sailing of the vessel. It treats the compass (bussola) and its variation, the errors of the Mediterranean charts and of the Lisbon charts (“Le Carte di Lisbona sono pure abbagliate come le Mediterranee” — the charts of Lisbon are as blinded as the Mediterranean ones), the false arrangement of meridians and parallels on the mappi (plane charts), the riformatione della rota (reformation of the compass rose), the taking of the hours by night, the Gregorian reform and the need to add ten days to the computation, the poles, the two tropics, and the problem of longitude — recording della Porta’s rule for finding degrees of longitude by sailing under a fixed parallel.
Libro Terzo (Book Three) — Astronomical and Practical Rules of the Mariner
The third book gathers the mariner’s astronomical rules. It treats the meridian and the description of its limb, the two tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, the equinoctial and its cross, the declination of the sun, the rising and setting of the fixed stars by which the mariner reckons, and the correction of the errors of the common aphorisms and of mariners’ practice. Crescentio states his intent to be understood by working mariners, and records teaching a young mariner his rules as a test of their clarity.
Scan Completeness Audit
The digitisation runs continuously from the title page through the dedication, the address to the reader, the table of subjects, and the three books, ending with the last leaves of the third book. The 662 OCR pages are ordered and gapless, but the scan is a degraded optical character recognition of an early-modern Italian book: about 55 pages carry an explicit “low accuracy” banner, and many others are garbled or fragmented (the letters are broken, f and s are confused in the long-s orthography, and diacritics are scattered). Roughly 160,000 words of usable Italian text survive, enough to identify the work, its author, its three-book structure, and its principal subjects, but not enough to recover every chapter heading exactly. This source is usable for broad doctrine and structure; individual passages should be treated with caution and checked against a clean edition before quotation.
Relation to Other Sources in This Wiki

This is the Mediterranean, galley-building counterpart to the Iberian and English naval texts in the corpus: it complements oliveira-arte-da-guerra-do-mar (the Portuguese Arte da Guerra do Mar, 1555) on the galley as a fighting vessel and its construction, and the navigation texts (maritime-technology-navigation, cartography-age-of-discovery) on the state of Mediterranean charts, the compass, and the longitude problem in the age of Gama, Magellan, and Drake.
It should be cited where the wiki needs the Mediterranean shipbuilder’s own account of galley construction, measures, and rigging, or the era’s criticisms of the plane charts and the compass before the age of precise navigation.

Sources

Crescentio, Bartolomeo. Della Nautica Mediterranea di Bartolomeo Crescentio Romano. Rome, 1602.

sources/fiske-discovery-of-america-vol1.title: The Discovery of America, Vol. I — John Fiske
sources/fiske-discovery-of-america-vol1.content:
The Discovery of America, Vol. I — John Fiske
Bibliographic Information

Author: John Fiske (1842–1901), American historian and philosopher
Full title: The Discovery of America, with Some Account of Ancient America and the Spanish Conquest
Edition: In Two Volumes, Vol. I. Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, copyright 1892 (The Riverside Press, Cambridge)
This file: A Project Gutenberg e-text (EBook #27253, released 13 November 2008), supplied here as an EPUB
Source file: wiki/raw/fiske-discovery-of-america-vol1.txt (~464,000 words / ~2.7 million characters, clean digital text)
Language: English (author’s original spelling maintained; transcriber’s note states obvious printer’s errors were corrected)

About the Author and Work
John Fiske (1842–1901) was an American historian, philosopher, and popular lecturer whose histories of colonial America and the age of exploration reached a wide Victorian readership. The Discovery of America (1892) is the culminating work of his “Spanish conquest” trilogy, following The War of Independence and The Critical Period of American History. It opens with an epigraph from Emerson — “Then I unbar the doors; my paths lead out / The exodus of nations; I disperse / Men to all shores that front the hoary main” — signalling the work’s framing of the discovery of America as the great dispersal of peoples. The work is in two volumes; the volume treated here (Vol. I) carries the narrative from ancient America through Columbus’s first landfalls.
Summary
The first volume opens with an account of the aboriginal inhabitants of the New World as they appeared to the first civilized Europeans, and surveys the question of their origin, the antiquity of man in America, and the archaeological evidence (shell-mounds, the Trenton gravel, the Calaveras skull) that Fiske marshalled for a long human occupation of the continent. It then takes up the pre-Columbian voyages — most fully the Norse voyages to Vinland and the Greenland settlement — and weighs the evidence for and against them as genuine discoveries. From there it turns to Europe and Cathay: the state of geographical knowledge in medieval Europe, the place of Cathay in the European imagination, and the practical problem of reaching the Indies. Two chapters then trace the two competing routes — the Portuguese eastward search around Africa, and the Spanish westward search across the Atlantic that produced Columbus’s voyages — before closing with the finding of strange coasts and the first encounters with the New World.
Scope and Approach
Fiske writes as a synthetic popular historian of the late nineteenth century, combining archaeological, geographical, and narrative materials into a continuous account. He is concerned with the chain of discovery as a whole — the Norse and legendary pre-Columbian voyages, the growth of European geographical knowledge, and the Portuguese and Spanish efforts — rather than with Columbus alone. His framing is a teleology of civilization: the discovery of America appears as the natural culmination of European maritime and geographical progress, and he repeatedly assesses the significance of each voyage within that larger story.
Contents
Front Matter
Preface and Contents — Fiske lays out the plan of the two-volume work and the arrangement of chapters; Illustrations list the maps and plates.
Chapter I — Ancient America
Fiske describes the aboriginal peoples as they appeared to the first civilized Europeans — “a race of men quite unlike any of the races with which they were familiar in the Old World.” He reviews the question of their origin, the antiquity of man in America, the shell-mounds or middens, the Glacial Period, and the archaeological discoveries (Trenton gravel, Ohio and Minnesota, the Calaveras skull) bearing on Pleistocene man, and surveys the cultural state of the American aborigines before European contact.
Chapter II — Pre-Columbian Voyages
The Norse voyages to Vinland, the Greenland colony, and the question of whether Norse or other mariners reached America before Columbus; Fiske examines the saga evidence and the claims of the earlier voyagers.
Chapter III — Europe and Cathay
The growth of European geographical knowledge, the place of Cathay and the Indies in the medieval imagination, and the intellectual preparations for the age of discovery.
Chapter IV — The Search for the Indies: Eastward or Portuguese Route
The Portuguese effort to reach the Indies by rounding Africa — the progress of Portuguese navigation along the African coast that culminated in the route to India.
Chapter V — The Search for the Indies: Westward or Spanish Route
The Spanish project of reaching Cathay by sailing westward — the enterprise of Columbus, and the demonstration that the route was feasible with the ships and instruments then at command.
Chapter VI — The Finding of Strange Coasts
The first encounters with the New World — the discovery and description of strange coasts, and the beginning of the Spanish conquest that the second volume carries forward.
Scan Completeness Audit
The source is a complete, clean Project Gutenberg digital text of Vol. I, running from the title page and preface through all six chapters. There are no missing pages, OCR errors, or scan gaps: the text is fully legible and searchable, and all chapter titles and boundaries are intact. This source is fully usable for quotation.
Relation to Other Sources in This Wiki

This is the synthetic nineteenth-century narrative counterpart to the contemporary sources in the corpus. It complements the Irving volumes (irving-columbus, irving-columbus-vol2, irving-columbus-vol3, irving-columbus-vol4) on the life and voyages of Columbus, and pairs with its companion volume fiske-discovery-of-america-vol2 which continues the narrative (the “Mundus Novus,” the conquests of Mexico and Peru, Las Casas).
It should be cited where the wiki needs the mature Victorian synthesis of the discovery of America, the pre-Columbian and Norse voyage evidence as received in the late nineteenth century, or the framing of the discovery within the wider European maritime expansion that the wiki’s other sources (Gama, Magellan, Drake) document.

Sources

Fiske, John. The Discovery of America, with Some Account of Ancient America and the Spanish Conquest. Vol. I. Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, 1892.

sources/fiske-discovery-of-america-vol2.title: The Discovery of America, Vol. II — John Fiske
sources/fiske-discovery-of-america-vol2.content:
The Discovery of America, Vol. II — John Fiske
Bibliographic Information

Author: John Fiske (1842–1901), American historian and philosopher
Full title: The Discovery of America, with Some Account of Ancient America and the Spanish Conquest
Edition: In Two Volumes, Vol. II. Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, copyright 1892 (The Riverside Press, Cambridge). Title page carries the Emerson epigraph: “Then I unbar the doors; my paths lead out / The exodus of nations…”
This file: A University of Michigan/HathiTrust-style page scan (identifier 39015050320152, ex libris Herbert Graves Partridge, M.D.), supplied as a ZIP of 678 single-page OCR text files
Source file: wiki/raw/fiske-discovery-of-america-vol2.txt (678 pages, ~1.16 million characters)
Language: English; source page in English

About the Author and Work
This is the second and concluding volume of John Fiske’s The Discovery of America (1892). Where Vol. I carried the narrative from ancient America and the pre-Columbian voyages through Columbus’s first landfalls, Vol. II carries it forward from the confirmation of a “New World” through the Spanish conquests of Mexico and Peru, and closes with the great question of the moral consequence of the discovery — the enslavement and destruction of the native peoples, personified in the figure of Las Casas. It is the volume in which Fiske’s Victorian moral and civilizational framework bears most heavily on the story of the Spanish Empire in the New World.
Summary
The second volume opens with “Mundus Novus” — the recognition, building on the name of Amerigo Vespucci’s reported voyages, that the lands across the Atlantic constituted a new world rather than the eastern edge of Asia. It treats the early career of the Cabots and the northern voyages, then turns to the central dramas of the Spanish conquest: the conquest of Mexico under Cortés, the ancient civilization of Peru and the conquest of Peru under Pizarro, and the career of Bartolomé de las Casas, the Dominican who became the great opponent of Indian enslavement. It closes with “The Work of Two Centuries,” surveying the two centuries of Spanish colonization and its consequences in the New World.
Scope and Approach
Fiske writes as a synthetic popular historian, uniting the narrative of the Spanish conquests with an account of the ancient civilizations they destroyed (the Aztecs, the Incas) and a sustained moral reckoning with the Spanish treatment of the native peoples. He opens the volume’s last chapters on a theme of fate and moral consequence: as he writes of Las Casas, “with the first arrival of civilized Europeans in this New World there should have come that plague of slavery which was so long to pollute and curse it.” The work is thus both a history of discovery and conquest and a meditation on the costs of that conquest.
Contents
Front Matter
Contents (Chapters VII–XII with full page reference tables) and Illustrations list the maps and plates of the second volume.
Chapter VII — Mundus Novus
The confirmation of a new world: Fiske opens on Wagner’s musical foreshadowing of catastrophe and applies it to the discovery — “the introduction of a few notes from some leading melody foretells the inevitable catastrophe.” He treats the few facts known about John Cabot, the merchants of Bristol and the voyage of Thomas Lloyd, John Cabot’s landfall supposed to be Cathay (June 24, 1497), the later career of Sebastian Cabot, what part of North America the Cabots visited, the Newfoundland fisheries and Baccalaos, and the career of Amerigo Vespucius — his letters, the four voyages described in them, his landfall near Cape Honduras, his voyage up the coast toward Florida and around it, and his appointment as pilot-major of Spain. Fiske weighs what the word “new world” originally meant, the oceanic and continental theories, and the maps (Ruysch 1508, the Lenox globe, the globe of Orontius Finæus 1531) that registered the new knowledge.
Chapter VIII — The Conquest of Mexico
The effects of increased geographical knowledge upon the romantic spirit; the romantic dreams of the Spanish explorers; prehistoric Mexico and the wild notions about the “Toltecs” and “Chichimecs”; the Nahua tribes, Tollan and the Serpent Hill, the fabulous “Toltec empire”; the Aztecs and the founding of the city of Mexico; and the conquest under Hernando Cortés.
Chapter IX — Ancient Peru
The general view of the South American peoples, from the elevated table-lands of New Mexico and Arizona to the mountain fastnesses of Bolivia; the culture of the Cordilleras; Chiriqui, the Chibchas, the Caribs and Maypures, the Araucanians, and the Quichua-Aymara tribes; the method of recording by quipus; the lists of Incas; Lake Titicaca and the cyclopean ruins at Tiahuanacu; and the civilization of the Incas as it stood before the Spanish arrival.
Chapter X — The Conquest of Peru
The chain of circumstances that led to the discovery and conquest of Peru, rooted in the island of Hispaniola and the colonizing of the isthmus of Darien; the relations of the Admiral Diego Columbus to the crown; the provinces of Terra Firma granted to Ojeda and Nicuesa; the expeditions, the death of La Cosa, the death of Ojeda; the expedition of Enciso and the first appearance of Balboa; the deposition of Enciso and the sufferings of Nicuesa; and the conquest of the Incas under Francisco Pizarro.
Chapter XI — Las Casas
The plague of slavery: ancient slavery, the beginnings of modern slavery, Azurara’s narrative, the beginnings of Indian slavery under Columbus, repartimientos and their origin, Nicolas de Ovando and his treatment of white and red men in Xaragua; the birth and family of Las Casas; and the Dominican’s long campaign against the enslavement of the Indians.
Chapter XII — The Work of Two Centuries
Hispaniola as the centre of Spanish colonization; the first voyage of Vespucius; Mandeville’s Fountain of Youth and the Land of Easter; Pineda’s discovery of the Mississippi (1519); the effect of Magellan’s voyage in turning exploration northward; Cape Horn; the Congress of Badajos; the search for a Northwest Passage; and Fiske’s concluding survey of the two centuries of Spanish work and its consequences in the New World.
Scan Completeness Audit
The source is a complete University of Michigan page scan of Vol. II, running continuously from the title page through all six chapters to the end matter. The 678 pages are ordered and gapless; 18 pages are blank or near-blank (0–17 characters) — these are the blank front leaves, plate interleaves, and end blanks typical of a book scan, not missing content. Page 676 carries a bookseller’s device (A.B. Clarke & Co., Booksellers) and pages 677–678 the end blanks. The OCR is generally legible; the engraved plates appear as near-empty pages (the plates themselves are images, not OCR text). This source is fully usable; the text is complete and identifiable for quotation.
Relation to Other Sources in This Wiki

This is the concluding volume of Fiske’s synthesis, pairing with fiske-discovery-of-america-vol1 (ancient America, pre-Columbian voyages, the Portuguese and Spanish routes, the first landfalls).
It complements the Irving volumes (irving-columbus and its continuations) on Columbus himself and the Spanish conquest narrative, and the contemporary primary sources of the age of discovery (Gama, Magellan, Drake) by supplying the mature Victorian account of the Spanish conquests of Mexico and Peru, the career of Las Casas, and the moral reckoning with the destruction of the native peoples.
It should be cited where the wiki needs the Spanish-conquest narrative, the ancient civilizations of Mexico and Peru as received in the late nineteenth century, or the Las Casas story.

Sources

Fiske, John. The Discovery of America, with Some Account of Ancient America and the Spanish Conquest. Vol. II. Boston and New York: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, 1892.

sources/irving-columbus-vol2.title: A History of the Life and Voyages of Christopher Columbus (Vol. II)
sources/irving-columbus-vol2.content:
A History of the Life and Voyages of Christopher Columbus — Vol. II
Author: Washington Irving
Full title: A History of the Life and Voyages of Christopher Columbus (Volume II)
Publication: 1828 (G. & C. Carvill, New York; parallel: A. & W. Galignani, Paris)
Source file: irving_columbus_carvill_v2.txt
Quality note: OCR-scanned text. Body text readable; occasional page-header artifacts.
Summary
This volume covers Columbus’s second voyage, the discovery of Jamaica, the administration of Hispaniola, the third voyage (discovery of Trinidad and South America), the rebellion of Roldan, and the events leading to his arrest. In the four-volume edition this corresponds to Books VII–XIV.
Chapter-by-Chapter Detail
BOOK VII — Second Voyage: Eastern Exploration (1494)
Chapter I: Voyage to the East End of Cuba — Columbus sails from Isabella (April 24, 1494), touches Monte Christi, and anchors at La Navidad to seek Guacanagari. Crosses to eastern Cuba (Point Maysi), enters Puerto Grande (Guantanamo). Finds deserted villages.
Chapter II: Discovery of Jamaica — Sights Jamaica’s blue mountains. Anchors at St. Ann’s Bay. Met by numerous canoes. Notes Jamaica’s size, fertility, dense population.
Chapter III: Return to Cuba — Queen’s Garden — Crosses back to Cuba. Navigates the labyrinth of small islands he names the Queen’s Garden (Jardines de la Reina). Treacherous shallows.
Chapter IV: Coasting Southern Cuba — Continues through the Queen’s Garden archipelago. Coast trends southwest, raising hopes of approaching Asia.
Chapter V: Return along Southern Cuba — Turns back. Retraces course through the maze of islands. Ship runs aground. Emerges into province of Ornofay.
Chapter VI: Coasting South Side of Jamaica — Crosses to Jamaica coast. Lands at a large village. Cacique presents gifts.
Chapter VII: Return to Hispaniola — Sails to southern Hispaniola (Cape Tiburon). Endures storms. Arrives at Isabella September 1494 after five months away.
BOOK VIII — Government and Rebellion (1494–1495)
Chapter I: Character of Bartholomew Columbus — Returns to find colony suffering famine and disease. Reunited with brother Bartholomew, newly arrived from Spain. Portrait of Bartholomew as loyal, capable, severe.
Chapter II: Misconduct of Pedro Margarite — Margarite abuses authority, plunders natives, abandons post, returns to Spain with Fray Boil to spread damaging reports.
Chapter III: Ojeda Besieged by Caonabo — Carib cacique Caonabo attacks fortress of Santo Tomas. Ojeda defends with small force. Beginning of organized native resistance.
Chapter IV: Ojeda Surprises Caonabo — Ojeda lures Caonabo with a ruse involving polished manacles. Captures him. Brings him to Isabella in chains.
Chapter V: Torres Arrives from Spain — Antonio de Torres brings provisions and reinforcements. Columbus sends Indian slaves back to Spain. Torres returns with dispatches.
Chapter VI: Battle in the Vega — Columbus marches into the Vega Real with 200 infantry, 20 cavalry, and dogs. Natives routed by horses, firearms, and dogs.
Chapter VII: Imposition of Tribute — Columbus imposes tribute: every Indian over 14 must pay gold (a hawk’s bell full) every three months, or cotton. System proves unworkable.
Chapter VIII: Aguado Sent to Investigate — Disaffected colonists spread accusations. Sovereigns dispatch Juan de Aguado with authority to investigate Columbus.
Chapter IX: Aguado at Isabella — Aguado acts arrogantly, hears complaints. Columbus, ill, endures the insult. Tempest sinks ships in harbour.
Chapter X: Discovery of the Mines of Hayna — Rich gold mines discovered in southern Hispaniola. Promises wealth but intensifies labour demands.
BOOK IX — Return to Spain (1496–1497)
Chapter I: Return with Aguado — Columbus builds new caravel (Santa Cruz), refits Niña. Appoints Bartholomew adelantado. Sails April 1496 with Aguado. Long, arduous crossing.
Chapter II: Reception at Burgos — Arrives to waned popularity. Appears before Ferdinand and Isabella at Burgos. Defends conduct. Proposes third voyage. Received graciously but with diminished enthusiasm.
BOOK X — Third Voyage (1498)
Chapter I: Discovery of Trinidad — Sails from San Lucar (May 30, 1498) with six vessels. Sends three to Hispaniola, steers south with three. July 31, sights three peaks. Names Trinidad. Approaches South American coast.
Chapter II: Gulf of Paria — Enters Gulf of Paria. Observes powerful Orinoco currents. Deduces continent, not island. Trades with pearl-bearing natives.
Chapter III: Return to Hispaniola — Explores islands of Margarita and Cubagua. Attempts westward but blocked by shoals. Sets course for Hispaniola, ill with gout and ophthalmia.
Chapter IV: Speculations on Paria — Develops cosmological theory: believes Orinoco is one of four rivers of Paradise. Concludes Earthly Paradise lies in this region.
BOOK XI — Adelantado’s Administration (1498–1499)
Chapter I: Expedition to Xaragua — Columbus arrives August 1498 to turmoil. Bartholomew governs firmly. Expedition to province of Xaragua, ruled by female cacique Anacaona.
Chapter II: Military Posts — Insurrection of Guarionex — Chain of fortified posts established. Cacique Guarionex rises in rebellion in the Vega.
Chapter III: Tribute at Xaragua — Bartholomew returns to collect tribute. Tense but outwardly peaceful negotiations with Anacaona.
Chapter IV: Conspiracy of Roldan — Francisco Roldan, chief magistrate, organizes conspiracy. Gathers discontented colonists, establishes rebel camp. Accuses Columbus brothers of tyranny.
Chapter V: Interview with Roldan — Adelantado attempts to negotiate. Roldan refuses to submit. No resolution.
Chapter VI: Second Insurrection of Guarionex — Guarionex leads second uprising. Defeated again. Flees to Ciguay mountains.
Chapter VII: Campaign in Ciguay — Adelantado pursues Guarionex through forests and mountains. Captures him. Ends organized native resistance.
BOOK XII — Rebellion and Disorder (1499–1500)
Chapter I: Confusion in the Island — Columbus returns from third voyage to chaos. Roldan’s rebellion spread to Xaragua. Admiral, weakened by illness, struggles.
Chapter II: Negotiation with Rebels — Columbus opens negotiations. Offers amnesty and free passage to Spain. Ships depart carrying rebels who will accuse Columbus.
Chapter III: Arrangement with Rebels — Formal agreement: amnesty, Roldan reinstated as alcalde mayor. Temporarily pacifies colony but undermines authority.
Chapter IV: Second Mutiny — Rebels mutiny again. Columbus forced into second round of concessions, including land grants and native labour.
Chapter V: Grants to Roldan — Formalizes encomiendas to Roldan and followers. Rewarding rebellion. Several sail for Spain with accusations.
BOOK XIII — Arrest (1500)
Chapter I: Representations at Court — Columbus’s enemies succeed at court. Bobadilla empowered to examine conduct. Given wide authority.
Chapter II: Bobadilla Arrives — Bobadilla arrives at St. Domingo, assumes command violently, seizes prisoners, broadcasts accusations.
Chapter III: Columbus Summoned — Columbus at Fort Conception hears news. Considers it unauthorized. Decides to cooperate.
Chapter IV: Arrest and Chains — Columbus and brothers arrested. Sent to Spain in chains. Columbus refuses to have irons removed. Famous voyage in chains.
BOOK XIV — Aftermath (1500–1502)
Chapter I: Sensation in Spain — Columbus arrives at Cadiz in chains. Public outrage. Summoned to court at Granada. Queen Isabella outraged. Columbus received with favour. Promises of redress.
Chapter II: Contemporary Voyages — Survey of voyages by Ojeda, Nino, Pinzon, Lepe, Bastides, Cabot, Cabral, and Corte Real. Context of the Age of Discovery.
Chapter III: Ovando Appointed — Nicholas de Ovando appointed to supersede Bobadilla. Massive fleet of 30 ships, 2,500 souls. Ovando’s character and instructions.
Chapter IV: Holy Sepulchre Proposition — Columbus proposes crusade to recover Jerusalem. Elaborate letter to sovereigns. His religious fervour and mystical speculation.
Chapter V: Fourth Voyage Preparations — Columbus granted ships for fourth voyage. Delays from Fonseca. Departure preparations. Last letter from sovereigns.
See Also

sources/irving-columbus-vol3.title: A History of the Life and Voyages of Christopher Columbus (Vol. III)
sources/irving-columbus-vol3.content:
A History of the Life and Voyages of Christopher Columbus — Volume III
Author: Washington Irving
Full title: A History of the Life and Voyages of Christopher Columbus (Vol. III)
Publication: 1828 (this edition: John Murray, London, 1828)
Source file: irving_columbus_v3.txt
Quality note: OCR-scanned text (Google Books, University of Chicago Library copy). Body text is clean and readable; occasional page-header artifacts and line-break hyphenation issues.
Summary of Contents
Volume III covers Columbus’s return to Hispaniola in August 1498 and the descent into factional chaos that ultimately led to his arrest and return to Spain in chains. The volume spans Books XII through XVII. It opens with the rebellion of Francisco Roldan in the province of Xaragua, traces the machinations of Columbus’s enemies at the Spanish court, and details the appointment and violent conduct of Francisco de Bobadilla, who arrested Columbus and his brothers and sent them to Spain. Book XIV covers the public sensation this caused, Columbus’s rehabilitation at court, and the contemporary voyages of Ojeda, Pinzon, Lepe, Cabot, Cabral, and Corte Real. The book then follows Columbus’s fourth and final voyage — along the coasts of Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama (Veragua) — his shipwreck on Jamaica, the desperate canoe voyage of Diego Mendez for help, and the mutiny of Porras. The volume closes with an account of the administration of Nicolas de Ovando in Hispaniola, the massacre at Xaragua, the fate of Anacaona, and the war with the native province of Higuey.
Chapter-by-Chapter Detail
BOOK XII — Confusion in the Island; Rebellion of Roldan; Negotiation with the Rebels; Arrival of Ojeda
Chapter I: Confusion in the Island. Proceedings of the Rebels at Xaragua — Opens with Columbus’s arrival at St. Domingo on August 30, 1498, exhausted and ill, to find the island in chaos. Describes the ruin of the colony: famine, neglect of cultivation, and the depopulation of native villages. Francisco Roldan, the rebel, has taken possession of Xaragua with his followers, living licentiously among the natives. Three caravels detached from Columbus’s squadron at the Canary Islands drift to Xaragua by currents, and Roldan deceives their captains into supplying him with arms and military stores while his men secretly recruit defectors among the crews.
Chapter II: Negotiation of the Admiral with the Rebels. Departure of Ships for Spain — Columbus opens negotiations with Roldan through emissaries. Roldan sends a list of grievances to Columbus. The admiral’s attempts to reconcile the rebels. Several ships depart for Spain carrying Columbus’s dispatches and representations of the state of the colony.
Chapter III: Arrangement with the Rebels — Columbus and Roldan reach a provisional agreement. Terms are proposed for the return of Roldan and his followers to obedience. The rebels agree to submit, and the foundations of a settlement are laid.
Chapter IV: Another Mutiny of the Rebels; and Second Arrangement with them — The agreement breaks down. Roldan’s followers renew their insubordination. A second negotiation results in a modified arrangement, with Columbus making further concessions to secure peace.
Chapter V: Grants made to Roldan and his Followers. Departure of several of the Rebels for Spain — To definitively end the rebellion, Columbus grants Roldan and his principal followers lands and privileges, including assignments of Indians. Several of the rebels depart for Spain, where their accounts will fuel the campaign against Columbus at court.
Chapter VI: Arrival of Ojeda with a Squadron at the Western part of the Island. Roldan sent to meet him — Alonso de Ojeda arrives on the western coast of Hispaniola with a squadron, having obtained a license for discovery. He begins independent operations and encroaches on Columbus’s jurisdiction. Columbus dispatches Roldan (now reconciled) to confront Ojeda and assert the admiral’s authority.
Chapter VII: Manoeuvres of Roldan and Ojeda — Roldan and Ojeda engage in a series of manoeuvres and negotiations. Ojeda attempts to win over Roldan’s followers and establish his own authority. Roldan skillfully outmaneuvers Ojeda, who is eventually forced to depart from the island. Ojeda’s return to Spain with reports damaging to Columbus.
Chapter VIII: Conspiracy of Guevara and Moxica — A new conspiracy against the Adelantado, Bartholomew Columbus, is hatched by Hernando de Guevara and Adrian de Moxica. The plot is discovered and suppressed. Moxica is captured and meets his death; Guevara is imprisoned.
BOOK XIII — Representations at Court against Columbus; Bobadilla Sent; Columbus Arrested and Sent to Spain in Chains
Chapter I: Representations at Court against Columbus. Bobadilla empowered to examine into his conduct — Columbus’s enemies at the Spanish court succeed in undermining his reputation. Every returning vessel brings complaints against Columbus and his brothers, painting them as arrogant, oppressive foreigners. Ferdinand’s growing displeasure. The sovereigns dispatch Francisco de Bobadilla as commissioner with full powers to investigate Columbus’s conduct and, if necessary, assume the government.
Chapter II: Arrival of Bobadilla at San Domingo. His violent Assumption of the Command — Bobadilla arrives at San Domingo in 1500. Without any prior investigation, he publicly reads his commission, seizes the fortress, takes command of the colony, and orders the seizure of Columbus’s property. He invites depositions against Columbus and his brothers, drawing testimony from the very men who had rebelled against them.
Chapter III: Columbus summoned to appear before Bobadilla — Columbus receives Bobadilla’s summons while at the fortress of Conception. He returns to San Domingo expecting to refute the charges. Bobadilla, having already prejudged the case, orders Columbus arrested and placed in chains.
Chapter IV: Columbus and his Brothers arrested and sent to Spain in Chains — Columbus is imprisoned, along with his brothers Bartholomew and Diego. Bobadilla claps them all in irons. The governor of the caravel refuses to remove the chains despite Columbus’s age and infirmity. Columbus is shipped to Spain as a prisoner, maintaining a dignified composure throughout the passage.
BOOK XIV — Sensation in Spain; Columbus at Court; Contemporary Voyages; Ovando Appointed; Fourth Voyage Prepared
Chapter I: Sensation in Spain on the Arrival of Columbus in Irons. His appearance at Court — The arrival of Columbus in chains at Cadiz creates a public outcry. Isabella and Ferdinand, shocked at Bobadilla’s excessive zeal, order Columbus released and invite him to court. Columbus appears before the sovereigns at Granada, where he is received with kindness and assured of his reinstatement — promises that will ultimately be only partially fulfilled.
Chapter II: Contemporary Voyages of Discovery — A survey of the voyages undertaken by other navigators during the period of Columbus’s troubles. Covers: the expedition of Pedro Alonzo Nino along the Pearl Coast; the voyage of Vicente Yanez Pinzon, who discovers Cape St. Augustine and the Amazon; the expedition of Diego Lepe, who explores farther south along the Brazilian coast; the voyage of Rodrigo Bastides along the coast of Tierra Firme; the northern explorations of Sebastian Cabot in the service of England, discovering Newfoundland and Labrador; and the Portuguese voyages of Vasco de Gama to India and Pedro Alvarez Cabral, who discovers Brazil by accident while sailing for Calicut.
Chapter III: Nicholas de Ovando appointed to Supersede Bobadilla — Ferdinand, jealous of Columbus’s privileges and alarmed by the growing importance of the New World, decides not to restore Columbus to the government. Instead, he appoints Nicolas de Ovando as governor of Hispaniola, superseding Bobadilla. Ovando sails with a large fleet of thirty ships and 2,500 men.
Chapter IV: Proposition of Columbus relative to the Recovery of the Holy Sepulchre — During his long stay in Granada awaiting the restoration of his offices, Columbus returns to a long-held religious vow: to lead a crusade for the recovery of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem. He proposes to finance the expedition from the wealth of the New World. The sovereigns receive the proposal politely but take no action.
Chapter V: Preparations of Columbus for a Fourth Voyage of Discovery — Stung by the Portuguese success of Vasco de Gama and Cabral’s voyages to India, Columbus conceives a new expedition to find a strait through the lands west of the Caribbean that would open a direct route to the Indian Ocean. He obtains royal permission, and preparations begin for a fourth voyage of discovery.
BOOK XV — The Fourth Voyage: Mosquito Coast, Costa Rica, Veragua, Settlement on the Belen
Chapter I: Departure of Columbus on his Fourth Voyage. Refused Admission to the Harbour of San Domingo. Exposed to a violent Tempest — Columbus departs Cadiz on May 9, 1502, with four small caravels and 150 men, accompanied by his brother Bartholomew and his son Fernando. He is now about 66 years old and in declining health. Arriving off San Domingo, he requests shelter from an approaching hurricane but is refused entry by Ovando. Columbus’s squadron rides out the storm; the treasure fleet that had sailed from San Domingo is devastated.
Chapter II: Voyage along the Coast of Honduras — Columbus sails westward from Hispaniola, touches at the Bay Islands, and reaches the coast of Honduras. He explores the coast, encountering native trading canoes that hint at advanced civilizations to the west.
Chapter III: Voyage along the Mosquito Coast, and Transactions at Cariari — The squadron sails along the Mosquito Coast (present-day Nicaragua). They land at the port of Cariari, where they have notable interactions with the native inhabitants, who are more hostile and organized than those encountered previously.
Chapter IV: Voyage along Costa Rica. Speculations concerning the Isthmus at Veragua — The ships continue along the coast of Costa Rica. Columbus becomes convinced, based on native reports and the westward trend of the coast, that he is approaching a strait or isthmus leading to another ocean. He begins to believe this is the region of Veragua (present-day Panama).
Chapter V: Discovery of Puerto Bello and El Retrete. Columbus abandons the Search after the Strait — Columbus discovers Puerto Bello (Portobelo) and continues to El Retrete. After extensive exploration and failing to find any passage through the continent, he reluctantly abandons the search for a strait and decides to return to Veragua.
Chapter VI: Return to Veragua. The Adelantado explores the Country — The squadron returns to the coast of Veragua. Bartholomew Columbus (the Adelantado) leads an inland expedition, exploring the country and making contact with the native chief Quibian, from whom they learn of nearby gold mines.
Chapter VII: Commencement of a Settlement on the River Belen. Conspiracy of the Natives. Expedition of the Adelantado to surprise Quibian — Columbus decides to establish a settlement on the River Belen (Belem) in Veragua. The local natives, led by Quibian, conspire to attack the Spaniards. Bartholomew Columbus leads a preemptive expedition to capture Quibian.
Chapter VIII: Disasters of the Settlement — The settlement at Belen suffers a series of catastrophes. Quibian escapes captivity and organizes a fierce assault on the Spanish. Several of Columbus’s men are killed. The settlement is besieged and conditions deteriorate rapidly.
Chapter IX: Distress of the Admiral on board of his Ship. Ultimate Relief of the Settlement — Columbus, confined aboard his ship by illness and unable to assist the settlement directly, endures great anxiety. Eventually, the beleaguered garrison is relieved and the survivors are evacuated.
Chapter X: Departure from the Coast of Veragua. Arrival at Jamaica. Stranding of the Ships — The battered squadron departs Veragua. One caravel is abandoned as unseaworthy. Columbus, making for Hispaniola, is forced by adverse winds and currents to run for Jamaica. The two remaining ships, riddled by shipworms, are deliberately beached on the coast of Jamaica to prevent them from sinking.
BOOK XVI — Shipwreck in Jamaica; Diego Mendez’s Canoe Voyage; Mutiny of Porras
Chapter I: Arrangement of Diego Mendez with the Caciques for Supplies of Provisions. Sent to San Domingo by Columbus in quest of Relief — The Spanish castaways are stranded on Jamaica. Diego Mendez volunteers to travel through the island, making agreements with caciques for regular provisions. He secures a canoe and sets off with Bartholomew Fiesco to cross the open sea to Hispaniola to obtain rescue ships from Ovando.
Chapter II: Mutiny of Porras — While waiting for relief, a mutiny breaks out among the stranded crew, led by Francisco de Porras. The mutineers seize ten canoes and attempt to paddle to Hispaniola on their own, but are forced back by contrary winds and currents. They establish a separate camp and plunder the natives, turning them against Columbus.
Chapter III: Scarcity of Provisions. Stratagem of Columbus to obtain Supplies from the Natives — Provisions grow scarce. The natives, alienated by the depredations of Porras’s mutineers, become reluctant to supply food. Columbus, knowing a lunar eclipse is approaching, predicts it to the natives as a sign of divine displeasure, successfully frightening them into resuming deliveries of provisions.
Chapter IV: Mission of Diego de Escobar to the Admiral — Ovando, the governor of Hispaniola, receives Diego Mendez but delays sending relief. He dispatches Diego de Escobar in a small caravel with a message of reassurance, but Escobar only reconnoiters and returns without taking any of the castaways aboard, leaving Columbus and his men in despair.
Chapter V: Voyage of Diego Mendez and Bartholomew Fiesco in a Canoe to Hispaniola — The full account of Mendez and Fiesco’s perilous canoe voyage across the 150-mile channel from Jamaica to Hispaniola. They endure thirst, storms, and exhaustion. Mendez successfully lands and makes his way to Ovando.
Chapter VI: Overtures of Columbus to the Mutineers. Battle of the Adelantado with Porras and his Followers — Columbus attempts to negotiate with Porras and his men. When overtures fail, Bartholomew Columbus leads the loyal Spaniards against the mutineers in a pitched battle on the beach. Porras is defeated and captured. The mutineers are pardoned by Columbus, restoring order among the castaways.
BOOK XVII — Administration of Ovando; Massacre at Xaragua; War with Higuey
Chapter I: Administration of Ovando in Hispaniola. Oppression of the Natives — Describes Ovando’s governorship after his arrival with a large fleet of adventurers. The disastrous experience of gold-seekers who arrive expecting easy riches and perish in misery. The introduction of the repartimiento system, which reduces the native population to forced labor in the mines and fields, causing massive depopulation and suffering. Ovando’s policies are contrasted with Columbus’s earlier attempts to protect the natives.
Chapter II: Massacre at Xaragua. Fate of Anacaona — Ovando, suspecting the female cacique Anacaona of plotting rebellion, leads an expedition to Xaragua. Under the guise of a friendly festival, the Spanish fall upon the unarmed native nobles and massacre them. Anacaona is captured, subjected to a mock trial, and executed. The province of Xaragua is devastated.
Chapter III: War with the Natives of Higuey — The native province of Higuey, at the eastern end of Hispaniola, resists Spanish domination under its powerful cacique Cotabanama. Following the massacre of eight Spaniards at the island of Saona, Ovando sends a military force to subdue Higuey. Describes Cotabanama’s physical prowess and the tactics of the native resistance.
Chapter IV: Close of the War with Higuey. Fate of Cotabanama — The Spanish pursue Cotabanama and his people into the mountains with relentless brutality. Cotabanama is eventually captured and executed. The war ends with the complete subjugation of Higuey. The native population of the island is thoroughly broken, marking the effective end of organized indigenous resistance in Hispaniola.
