sources/irving-columbus-vol4.title: A History of the Life and Voyages of Christopher Columbus (Vol. IV)
sources/irving-columbus-vol4.content:
A History of the Life and Voyages of Christopher Columbus — Vol. IV
Author: Washington Irving
Full title: A History of the Life and Voyages of Christopher Columbus
Publication: 1829 (this edition: Baudry, Paris)
Volume: IV (contains Book XVIII and Appendix)
Summary of Contents
This is Volume IV of Irving’s biography, containing the concluding Book XVIII (the final years and death of Columbus) followed by a substantial Appendix of 34 or more documentary, biographical, and geographical supplements. The volume covers Columbus’s return from his fourth voyage, his final applications to the crown, his death in 1506, and a concluding character study. The Appendix gathers a wide range of supporting material: genealogical records, biographical sketches of contemporaries and chroniclers, essays on pre-Columbian voyages and geographical theories, and documentation on the Columbus family.
Chapter-by-Chapter Detail
BOOK XVIII — Final Years and Death
Chapter I: Departure for St. Domingo, Return to Spain (1504) — Covers Columbus’s departure from Hispaniola (St. Domingo) after his fourth voyage, his difficult return passage across the Atlantic, and his arrival back in Spain. Treats the condition of the Admiral upon his return — physically worn and burdened by the loss of his official positions and the collapse of his governorship.
Chapter II: Illness at Seville, Application to the Crown, Death of Isabella — Describes Columbus’s residence in Seville following his return, the deterioration of his health, and his efforts to petition the Spanish sovereigns for restoration of his titles and revenues. Documents the death of Queen Isabella in November 1504, which removed Columbus’s most steadfast patron at court and severely weakened his position in negotiations with King Ferdinand.
Chapter III: Columbus Arrives at Court, Fruitless Application for Redress — Columbus’s journey to the court of King Ferdinand, his audience with the king, and the failure of his petitions for reinstatement as governor and restoration of his privileges. Covers the legal and political obstacles raised against his claims and the Crown’s reluctance to restore his former authority in the Indies.
Chapter IV: Death of Columbus (1506) — The final illness and death of Christopher Columbus at Valladolid on May 20, 1506. Describes his last days, his testamentary arrangements, and the immediate aftermath of his death. Notes the presence of his sons Diego and Fernando at his deathbed and the modest circumstances of his passing.
Chapter V: Observations on the Character of Columbus — A concluding, retrospective chapter offering Irving’s observations on Columbus’s personal qualities: his religious devotion, his perseverance in the face of adversity, his administrative strengths and weaknesses as governor, his temperament, his intellectual formation, and his place in history. Draws on the testimony of contemporaries such as Las Casas, Peter Martyr, and Fernando Columbus.
Appendix — Contents (34+ Items)
The Appendix to Volume IV contains a collection of supplementary essays, biographical notices, documentary records, and critical discussions. The following entries are included:
No. I: Transportation of the Remains of Columbus to Havana — An account of the removal of Columbus’s remains from Valladolid to Seville, their subsequent transfer to Santo Domingo (Hispaniola), and their final translation to Havana, Cuba, following the cession of Hispaniola to France in 1795.
No. II: Descendants of Columbus — A genealogical account of Columbus’s descendants: his sons Diego and Fernando, the line of Dukes of Veragua, and the subsequent history of the Columbus family through successive generations.
No. III: Fernando Columbus — A biographical sketch of Fernando (Ferdinand) Columbus, the Admiral’s second son, natural historian, scholar, and bibliophile. Covers his education, his travels, his collection of books (the Biblioteca Colombina in Seville), and his biography of his father.
No. IV: Lineage of Columbus — A discussion of the genealogical origins of the Columbus family, tracing ancestry and disputing various claims about the family’s nobility and background.
No. V: Birthplace of Columbus — An examination of the evidence concerning Columbus’s birthplace in the Republic of Genoa, addressing the rival claims of various Genoese localities.
No. VI: The Colombos — A historical note on the Colombo (Colombo) family of Genoa, their maritime traditions, and their relationship to Christopher Columbus.
No. VII: John of Anjou Expedition — An account of the expedition of John of Anjou, Duke of Lorraine, and his naval operations in the Mediterranean (1459-1462), in which the young Columbus is said to have participated.
No. VIII: Capture of the Venetian Galleys — A narrative describing the naval battle off Cape St. Vincent (1476) in which Columbus participated, involving a Genoese squadron and the capture of Venetian galleys.
No. IX: Amerigo Vespucci — A biographical notice on Amerigo Vespucci, the Florentine navigator after whom America was named. Examines his voyages, his writings, and the controversy over his role in the discovery of the South American mainland.
No. X: Martin Alonso Pinzon — A biographical sketch of Martin Alonso Pinzon, the Spanish mariner and co-discoverer who commanded the Pinta on Columbus’s first voyage. Treats his rivalry with Columbus and his subsequent career.
No. XI: The Pilot Who Died in the House of Columbus — An examination of the story, reported by Las Casas, of an unknown pilot who, having previously reached lands in the west, died in Columbus’s house in Madeira or the Azores and whose papers and charts influenced Columbus’s plans. Discusses the credibility of this account.
No. XII: Martin Behem — A biographical essay on Martin Behaim (Behem), the German cosmographer and globe-maker who corresponded with Columbus and constructed the famous terrestrial globe of Nuremberg (1492). Discusses his influence on contemporary geography.
No. XIII: Voyages of the Scandinavians — A survey of the early Norse voyages to North America: the discoveries of Bjarni Herjolfsson, Leif Erikson, and subsequent Norse expeditions to Vinland, Greenland, and Markland. Discusses the extent of knowledge of these voyages in Columbus’s time.
No. XIV: Circumnavigation of Africa by the Ancients — An essay on ancient accounts of the circumnavigation of Africa, including the Phoenician expedition under Pharaoh Necho (reported by Herodotus) and the voyage of Hanno the Carthaginian. Discusses what ancient geographers knew of the African continent.
No. XV: St. Brandan’s Island — A discussion of the legendary Island of St. Brendan (San Borondón), the mythical island in the Atlantic associated with the sixth-century Irish monk’s voyage. Traces its appearance on medieval maps and its persistence in geographical imagination.
No. XVI: Island of the Seven Cities — An essay on the legend of the Island of the Seven Cities (Antilia), the mythical Atlantic island supposedly settled by seven Portuguese bishops fleeing the Moorish conquest. Discusses its role in shaping expectations about discovery.
No. XVII: Discovery of Madeira — An account of the rediscovery and colonization of the Madeira archipelago by Portuguese navigators under Prince Henry the Navigator in the early fifteenth century.
No. XVIII: Las Casas — A biographical sketch of Bartolome de las Casas, the Spanish Dominican friar, historian, and defender of the indigenous peoples of the Americas. Discusses his Historia de las Indias, his Brevísima relación de la destrucción de las Indias, and his use of Columbus’s journals and papers.
No. XIX: Peter Martyr d’Anghiera — A biographical notice on Peter Martyr (Pietro Martire d’Anghiera), the Italian-born humanist, historian, and diplomat at the Spanish court whose De Orbe Novo (Decades of the New World) provides a contemporary account of the early discoveries.
No. XX: Gonzalo Fernandez de Oviedo — A biographical sketch of Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo y Valdés, the Spanish historian and naturalist who served as official chronicler of the Indies. Discusses his Historia General y Natural de las Indias and his relationship to Columbus.
No. XXI: The Cura de Los Palacios — A biographical note on Andrés Bernáldez, the curate of Los Palacios, whose chronicle Historia de los Reyes Católicos includes valuable contemporary testimony about Columbus and the early voyages.
No. XXII: Navigatione del Re — A discussion of the Navigatione del Re (or Navigation of the King), a work or document concerning Portuguese royal navigation and discovery projects during the reign of King John II.
No. XXIII: Antonio de Herrera — A biographical notice on Antonio de Herrera y Tordesillas, the official Spanish chronicler of the Indies whose Historia General de los Hechos de los Castellanos en las Islas y Tierra Firme del Mar Océano (commonly known as the Décadas) is a major source for early Spanish exploration.
No. XXIV: Bishop Juan Rodriguez de Fonseca — A biographical sketch of Juan Rodríguez de Fonseca, the Spanish ecclesiastic and royal administrator who served as head of the Casa de Contratación and as Columbus’s persistent adversary in court.
No. XXV: Situation of the Terrestrial Paradise — An essay examining Columbus’s belief, expressed during his third voyage, that the Orinoco River region was the location of the Terrestrial Paradise (Garden of Eden). Discusses the patristic and medieval geographical theories that informed this conviction.
(Additional appendices beyond No. XXV exist in the collection but their exact sequence and numbering are not fully recorded in the available source. The total Appendix contains at least 34 numbered items.)

sources/irving-columbus.title: A History of the Life and Voyages of Christopher Columbus (Vol. I)
sources/irving-columbus.content:
A History of the Life and Voyages of Christopher Columbus
Author: Washington Irving
Full title: A History of the Life and Voyages of Christopher Columbus
Publication: 1828 (this edition: A. & W. Galignani, France)
Source file: irving_columbus_full.txt
Quality note: OCR-scanned text (Anna’s Archive / Google Books). Body text is clean and readable; occasional page-header artifacts and line-break hyphenation issues.
Summary of Contents
This is Volume I of Irving’s biography, covering Columbus’s life from his birth in Genoa through the successful return from his first voyage and preparations for the second. It ends with the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494), which divided the newly discovered territories between Spain and Portugal. The work draws heavily on the documents collected by Martin Fernandez de Navarrete, as well as Fernando Columbus’s biography of his father, and contemporary chroniclers such as Peter Martyr, Oviedo, Las Casas, and Herrera.
Chapter-by-Chapter Detail
BOOK I — Early Life and First Applications
Chapter I: Birth, Parentage, and Education of Columbus — Covers Columbus’s birth in Genoa, his family background (his father Domenico Colombo was a wool-comber), and his early education at the University of Pavia. Describes his early inclination toward the sea and his apprenticeship in the Mediterranean.
Chapter II: Early Life of Columbus — Follows Columbus’s early seafaring career: voyages in the Mediterranean under the elder Colombo (his relative), service on a Genoese squadron, a shipwreck off the coast of Portugal, and his arrival in Lisbon around 1470. Describes his marriage to Felipa Perestrello and his access to his father-in-law’s nautical charts and papers.
Chapter III: Progress of Discovery under Prince Henry of Portugal — Surveys the Portuguese Age of Discovery under Prince Henry the Navigator: the exploration of the African coast, the discovery of Madeira and the Azores, the development of the caravel, and the gradual Portuguese push southward. Sets the context for Columbus’s own ambitions.
Chapter IV: Residence of Columbus at Lisbon — Ideas concerning Islands in the Ocean — Describes Columbus’s life in Lisbon, his study of classical and medieval geography (Aristotle, Seneca, Pliny, Marco Polo, Mandeville), and his growing conviction that undiscovered lands lay to the west. Discusses the legend of Antilia and the Island of St. Brendan.
Chapter V: Grounds on which Columbus founded his belief of the existence of undiscovered lands in the West — Details the three categories of evidence Columbus assembled: (1) natural/physical signs (unusual currents, floating vegetation, carved sticks washed ashore); (2) classical authority (Aristotle, Seneca, Strabo); (3) reports from mariners of islands sighted to the west.
Chapter VI: Correspondence of Columbus with Paulo Toscanelli — Covers Columbus’s correspondence with the Florentine astronomer and cosmographer Paolo Toscanelli, who sent him a map and letter supporting the westward route to Asia. Also discusses Portuguese discoveries under King John II, including the exploration of the African coast.
Chapter VII: Propositions of Columbus to the Court of Portugal — Describes Columbus’s formal application to King John II of Portugal, the submission of his plan to a royal council, its rejection (partly due to the competing project of the Cape route), and the navigator’s secret dispatch of a caravel to test Columbus’s theory without him.
Chapter VIII: Departure of Columbus from Portugal, and his Application to other Courts — Columbus’s departure from Portugal in 1485 after the secret-caravel incident. His journey to Genoa to present his plan, then to Venice (both rejected). His decision to try the Spanish court, and his arrival in Spain.
BOOK II — Negotiations with Spain
Chapter I: First Arrival of Columbus in Spain — Columbus’s arrival at the Franciscan monastery of La Rábida near Palos, his meeting with Fray Juan Perez de Marchena, who became his advocate. His first appearance at the court of Ferdinand and Isabella.
Chapter II: Characters of Ferdinand and Isabella — A portrait of the Spanish monarchs: Ferdinand’s political acumen and Isabella’s religious devotion and strong will. Their recent unification of Castile and Aragon and their completion of the Reconquista.
Chapter III: Propositions of Columbus to the Court of Castile — Columbus’s arrival at Cordova in 1486, his presentation to the sovereigns, and the appointment of a commission headed by Hernando de Talavera to examine his proposals.
Chapter IV: Columbus before the Council at Salamanca — The famous academic conference at Salamanca, where Columbus defended his theories before the learned men of Spain. The theological and scientific objections raised, and the ambiguous outcome.
Chapter V: Further Applications at the Court of Castile — Columbus follows the Court in its Campaigns — Columbus’s long years of waiting (1487–1491), following the Spanish court from camp to camp during the war against Granada. His growing frustration, the repeated delays, and his near-abandonment of the project.
Chapter VI: Application to the Duke of Medina Celi — Return to the Convent of La Rábida — Columbus’s brief negotiation with the Duke of Medina Celi, who offered to finance the voyage himself. His return to La Rábida, where Fray Juan Perez interceded with Queen Isabella on his behalf.
Chapter VII: Application to the Court at the time of the Surrender of Granada — Columbus’s recall to court after the fall of Granada in January 1492. The final rejection by the Talavera commission, Columbus’s departure from court, and his interception by Luis de Santangel, who persuaded Isabella to reconsider.
Chapter VIII: Arrangement with the Spanish Sovereigns — The historic agreement at Santa Fe: the Capitulations of April 1492, granting Columbus the titles of Admiral, Viceroy, and Governor, and one-tenth of all discoveries. The financing of the expedition (partly from the Santa Hermandad, partly from Santangel’s loan).
Chapter IX: Preparations for the Expedition at the Port of Palos — Columbus’s return to Palos, the royal order compelling the town to provide two caravels. The reluctance of the seamen, the recruitment of the Pinzon brothers, and the final fitting of the three ships: the Santa Maria, the Pinta, and the Niña.
BOOK III — The First Voyage
Chapter I: Departure of Columbus on his First Voyage — The departure from Palos on August 3, 1492. The course to the Canary Islands, the repair of the Pinta’s rudder, and the final departure from Gomera on September 6.
Chapter II: Continuation of the Voyage — Variation of the Needle — The voyage westward into unknown waters. The discovery of magnetic declination (variation of the compass needle), which alarmed the sailors. Columbus’s skill in managing the crews’ fears.
Chapter III: Continuation of the Voyage — Various Terrors of the Seamen — The growing panic among the crews as weeks passed without sight of land. Fears of contrary winds, the Sargasso Sea, sea monsters, and never being able to return. The mutinous murmurs and Columbus’s attempts to reassure them.
Chapter IV: Continuation of the Voyage — Discovery of Land — The final days: signs of land (birds, floating branches, carved wood). The sighting of land by Rodrigo de Triana on October 12, 1492. The landing on Guanahani (San Salvador).
BOOK IV — The Discovery
Chapter I: First Landing of Columbus in the New World — The ceremonial landing on San Salvador, taking possession for Spain. First contact with the Taino people, their appearance and customs, and Columbus’s impression that he had reached islands off Asia.
Chapter II: Cruise among the Bahama Islands — The voyage through the Bahamas, discovering and naming Santa Maria de la Concepcion, Fernandina, and Isabella. Encounters with the native people and observations of their culture.
Chapter III: Discovery and Coasting of Cuba — The arrival at Cuba on October 28. The expedition’s exploration of the Cuban coast, the search for gold and the Grand Khan of Asia. The sending of an embassy inland.
Chapter IV: Further Coasting of Cuba — Continued exploration of the Cuban coast. Attempts to communicate with the natives and the search for cities of gold. Columbus’s decision to turn east toward what he hoped was Japan.
Chapter V: Search after the supposed Island of Babeque — Desertion of the Pinta — The search for the golden island of Babeque (according to native reports). The desertion of the Pinta under Martin Alonso Pinzon, who sought gold independently.
Chapter VI: Discovery of Hispaniola — The arrival at Hispaniola (December 5). Contact with the Taino chief Guacanagari. Favorable reports of gold in the island’s interior.
Chapter VII: Coasting of Hispaniola — Navigation along the northern coast of Hispaniola. Further trade with natives, acquisition of gold ornaments, and growing confidence that this was a land of great wealth.
Chapter VIII: Shipwreck — The wreck of the Santa Maria on Christmas Eve 1492. The beaching and dismantling of the ship. Guacanagari’s assistance in saving the crew and stores.
Chapter IX: Transactions with the Natives — Columbus’s growing friendship with Guacanagari. Reports of a powerful chief (Caonabo) in the interior. The decision to establish a settlement.
Chapter X: Building of the Fortress of La Navidad — The construction of the fortified settlement of La Navidad from the timbers of the wrecked Santa Maria. The selection of 39 volunteers to remain as the first European colony in the New World.
Chapter XI: Regulation of the Fortress of La Navidad — Departure of Columbus for Spain — Columbus’s instructions to the colonists, his farewell, and the departure of the Niña for Spain on January 4, 1493.
BOOK V — Return and Preparations for the Second Voyage
Chapter I: Coasting towards the Eastern End of Hispaniola — Meeting with Pinzon — Affair with the Natives — The voyage along the coast, the reunion with Pinzon and the Pinta. An armed encounter with natives at the Gulf of Samana.
Chapter II: Return Voyage — Violent Storms — Arrival at the Azores — The Atlantic crossing, a violent storm that nearly sank the Niña, the separation from the Pinta, and the arrival at the island of Santa Maria in the Azores.
Chapter III: Transactions at the Island of St. Mary’s — Portuguese hostility at the Azores, a brief detention of Columbus’s men by the Portuguese governor, and Columbus’s diplomatic resolution of the incident.
Chapter IV: Arrival at Portugal — Visit to the Court — Forced by weather to land at Lisbon. Columbus’s audience with King John II of Portugal, the king’s chagrin at losing the western discovery to Spain, and a near-violent confrontation between the two nations.
Chapter V: Reception of Columbus at Palos — Columbus’s triumphant return to Palos on March 15, 1493. The rejoicing of the townspeople and the arrival of the Pinta shortly after.
Chapter VI: Reception of Columbus by the Spanish Court at Barcelona — Columbus’s journey to Barcelona, his ceremonial reception by Ferdinand and Isabella, and the presentation of the trophies of the New World (gold, exotic plants, parrots, and Taino people).
Chapter VII: Sojourn of Columbus at Barcelona — Attentions paid him by the Sovereigns and Courtiers — Columbus’s weeks of honor at Barcelona, the royal favor, the preparation of his coat of arms, and the jealousy of some courtiers.
Chapter VIII: Papal Bull of Partition — Preparations for a Second Voyage of Columbus — Pope Alexander VI’s bulls (May 1493) dividing the non-Christian world between Spain and Portugal. The massive preparations for a second expedition of 17 ships and 1,500 men.
Chapter IX: Diplomatic Negotiations between the Courts of Spain and Portugal — The diplomatic dispute between Spain and Portugal over the new discoveries. The Portuguese claim based on earlier treaties and the Spanish reliance on the papal bulls.
Chapter X: Further Preparations for the Second Voyage — Character of Alonso de Ojeda — Difference of Columbus with Soria — The continued outfitting of the fleet. The introduction of Alonso de Ojeda, a young nobleman who would become a significant figure. Columbus’s conflicts with Juan de Soria over supplies and personnel.
(Source ends here with the Treaty of Tordesillas settlement, June 1494, and the end of Volume I.)
See Also

sources/irving-companions-columbus.title: Voyages and Discoveries of the Companions of Columbus
sources/irving-companions-columbus.content:
Voyages and Discoveries of the Companions of Columbus
Author: Washington Irving
Full title: Voyages and Discoveries of the Companions of Columbus
Publication: Carey & Lea, Philadelphia, 1831 (copyright deposit Southern District of New York, 31 December 1830; printers L. Ashmead & Co.)
Source file: wiki/raw/irving-companions-columbus/raw.txt (362 OCR pages, ~556 KB)
Quality note: OCR-scanned text (Anna’s Archive / University of California library copy, tree b3114252/). Body prose is readable; running headers, library stamps, broken hyphenation, and end-matter publisher ads appear in the extract. Chapter titles below follow the book’s own CHAPTER headings and section title pages where present.
Summary of Contents
A companion volume to Irving’s Life and Voyages of Christopher Columbus, this book narrates the early Spanish expeditions of the men who followed Columbus into the Caribbean and along the coasts of Tierra Firme: Alonso de Ojeda (three voyages), Diego de Nicuesa, Vasco Núñez de Balboa (including the discovery of the South Sea), and Juan Ponce de León (including the Florida venture and the Fountain of Youth legend). Irving frames the work as a chivalric sequel to the fall of Granada: Spanish cavaliers, deprived of the peninsular wars, carry armour and crusading spirit into the caravel. An epigraph from Peter Martyr (Decad. III c.4, Lock’s translation) opens the book. The narrative draws on the same chroniclers Irving used for Columbus—Peter Martyr, Oviedo, Las Casas, Herrera, and related archives—and ends with Ponce’s death in 1514 after the Florida expedition.
Chapter-by-Chapter Detail
Introduction
Irving opens by linking the capitulation of Granada to the sudden surplus of martial energy among Spanish youth. Columbus’s treaty with the sovereigns is signed, he says, almost with the same pen that closed the Moorish wars; many of the early commanders of the New World had first drawn steel under Ferdinand and Isabella in Andalusia. Chivalry leaves the land and launches upon the deep, mingling romantic enterprise with seaman’s craft and mercenary scheme. The introduction sets the moral and social key for the companion biographies that follow.
Alonzo de Ojeda — First Voyage (1499)
Chapter I: Departure of Ojeda from Spain — Birth and character of Alonso de Ojeda: youth near Tavistock is not his story—he is the Spanish cavalier formed under the Granada campaigns, patronized by Bishop Fonseca. Fitting of the 1499 expedition; association with Juan de la Cosa and the Florentine Amerigo Vespucci; departure for the coast of Paria and Tierra Firme.
Chapter II: Arrival at Paria — Coasting of Terra Firma — Landfall and early contact on the Pearl Coast and neighbouring shores. Native trade, signs of gold, and the first detailed coasting of the mainland opposite the islands Columbus had already touched.
Chapter III: Transactions with the Natives — Exchange, misunderstandings, and armed clashes with coastal peoples. Ojeda’s personal boldness and the mixed motives of discovery, conversion, and plunder.
Chapter IV: Continuation of the Voyage — Further west along the mainland; mapping of bays and capes; reports that will feed European curiosity and Spanish claims.
Chapter V: Discovery of Coquibacoa — English Adventurers — Approach to Coquibacoa; encounter or rumour of English adventurers in the region, which later stiffens Spanish resolve to plant a fighting commander on this outpost. Ojeda sets up Castilian arms as signs of possession.
Chapter VI: Coasting of Coquibacoa — Closer survey of the province later granted to Ojeda; native polities, resources, and the strategic value of the coast.
Chapter VII: Discovery of the Island of Curaçao, and Return to Spain — Islands off the coast including Curaçao; meagre commercial return of the voyage; arrival back by June 1500. Ojeda gains celebrity more than wealth; Fonseca secures him further favour.
Alonzo de Ojeda — Second Voyage (1502)
Continuous narrative section (no numbered CHAPTER headers in the extract). After the first voyage’s thin profits, Fonseca obtains for Ojeda a grant of six leagues in southern Hispaniola and the government of Coquibacoa, with leave to fit up to ten ships at his own expense, trade beyond the Paria pearl reservation (one-fifth to the crown), and colonize Coquibacoa. A stated motive is to check English intrusion by a resolute commander who will plant the arms of Castile everywhere. Partners Juan de Vergara and García de Campos help finance the armament. The section follows the second voyage’s operations, the attempt to settle and exploit Coquibacoa, and the voyage’s ruinous outcome—another failure of fortune for a man Irving presents as brave, popular, and financially heedless.
Alonzo de Ojeda — Third Voyage (from c. 1508–1509)
Chapter I: Ojeda applies for a Command — Rival Candidate Diego de Nicuesa — Years of obscurity after a ruinous lawsuit; a poorly recorded 1505 return toward Coquibacoa; Ojeda poor in purse but proud in spirit on Hispaniola by 1508. King Ferdinand, excited by Columbus’s reports of Veraguan gold (the supposed Aurea Chersonesus), resolves to plant regular colonies on Tierra Firme with cheaper agents than the Columbus family. Ojeda and Diego de Nicuesa emerge as rival candidates for mainland commands.
Chapter II: Feud between Ojeda and Nicuesa — Court and island politics of the split command: Ojeda toward the eastern Tierra Firme (Urabá / New Andalusia region) and Nicuesa toward Veragua / Castilla del Oro. Character contrast—Ojeda the hard fighter, Nicuesa the generous cavalier—and the seeds of later disaster when their spheres and personalities collide at sea and on shore.
Chapter III: Ojeda’s Expedition to the Gulf of Urabá — Fitting out; departure; approach to the Gulf of Urabá and the hostile shores that had already bloodied earlier ventures.
Chapter IV: Arrival at Carthagena — Conflict with the Natives — Landfall near Cartagena; sharp fighting with coastal Indians; display of Spanish arms and the cost of establishing a foothold.
Chapter V: Foundation of San Sebastian — Attempt to plant the colony of San Sebastián on the Gulf of Urabá; fortification, famine, disease, and native pressure.
Chapter VI: Disasters of the Colony — Starvation, desertion, and the collapse of Ojeda’s settlement scheme; appeals for relief and the unravelling of the third voyage’s hopes.
Chapter VII: Ojeda’s Voyage to Hispaniola for Succour — Ojeda leaves the remnant to seek aid; sea perils and the political coldness of island authorities toward a ruined governor.
Chapter VIII: Fate of Ojeda — Closing of Ojeda’s arc: poverty, pride, and the end of the most restless of Columbus’s fighting companions as Irving shapes him—always forward in battle, never solvent in fortune.
Diego de Nicuesa
Chapter I: The Voyage of Diego de Nicuesa — Shipwreck and Subsequent Disasters — After parting from Ojeda at Cartagena, Nicuesa coasts westward in a caravel with brigantines under Lope de Olano ordered to keep near. Stormy weather off Veragua; the caravel is driven about; morning finds the squadron gone. Nicuesa enters a river that falls with the rains; the caravel grounds and falls over. The chapter opens the long catalogue of wreck, hunger, and scattered survivors that define Nicuesa’s Veragua venture.
Chapters II–VII (Nicuesa continuation) — Successive disasters of the Veragua / Nombre de Dios region: search for Olano and the missing vessels; starvation marches; attempts to found or hold Nombre de Dios; quarrels among officers; the contrast between Nicuesa’s generosity and the ruthless logic of survival. Irving tracks the colony’s misery until Nicuesa’s authority is broken and his personal fate is sealed—traditionally the tragic counterpart to Ojeda’s hard-edged failure, the “gallant and generous” commander destroyed by the same coast that would later make Balboa.
Vasco Núñez de Balboa
Section restart with a new Chapter I after the Nicuesa narrative (char offset ~227102 in the extract). Irving retells Balboa’s rise among the Darién settlers—the stowaway-turned-leader, the founding energy at Santa María la Antigua, and the political skill that outmanoeuvres higher-born rivals.
Middle chapters (Balboa narrative) — Consolidation of power at Darién; alliances and wars with neighbouring caciques; intelligence of a great sea to the south and of gold-rich lands beyond the mountains; the disciplined march across the isthmus; the famous first sight of the South Sea (Pacific); the formal taking of possession; coastal reconnoitring and the return with reports that reorient Spanish ambition from the Caribbean shore to the ocean beyond Panama.
Chapter XXVIII: Trial of Vasco Núñez — Pedrarias Dávila conceals exultation at the stratagem that has ensnared his confiding rival. He visits Balboa in prison with hypocritical concern, blaming the Treasurer Alonso de la Puente, while privately urging the Alcalde Mayor Espinosa to full rigor. The charge of treasonable conspiracy to cast off allegiance and rule independently on the borders of the Southern Sea rests heavily on confessions of Andrés Garabito and on overheard talk among officers on Isla Rica. Irving’s tone is openly hostile to Pedrarias and elegiac toward Balboa—the discoverer of the South Sea destroyed by colonial intrigue.
Closing Balboa chapters — Judicial process, condemnation, and execution; the moral coda Irving draws on envy, crown jealousy, and the waste of the man who first claimed the Pacific for Castile.
Juan Ponce de León
New section (~char 454213): Ponce’s career after Puerto Rico—ambition, reports of islands to the north, and the mixture of gold-seeking and legendary curiosity that sends him toward Bimini and Florida.
Chapter VII: The Fountain of Youth (1512) — Assembly of the Florida / Bimini tradition as Irving received it: Indian reports of a spring that restores youth; Ponce’s cruise among the Lucayan and Florida shores; naming and claiming of Florida; the blend of exploratory fact and romantic motif that made the fountain a durable European legend.
Chapter VIII: Death of Ponce de León (1514) — Return, second effort, wounding in conflict with Florida natives, and death in 1514. Irving closes the companion volume with the last of this generation of Columbian satellites—conquerors and dreamers whose routes stitched the early Spanish Main and the approaches to the Pacific.
Sources

Irving, Washington. Voyages and Discoveries of the Companions of Columbus. Philadelphia: Carey & Lea, 1831.

sources/marco-polo-1671.title: Marci Pauli Veneti de Regionibus Orientalibus (1671)
sources/marco-polo-1671.content:
Marci Pauli Veneti de Regionibus Orientalibus (1671)
Context line — Marco Polo’s account of his travels through Asia (1271–1295), in the 1671 Latin edition edited by Andreas Müller from an older manuscript in the Brandenburg Electoral Library; the work Columbus read when planning his westward voyage to reach Cathay and Cipango.
Source
Marco Polo (1254–1323). Marci Pauli Veneti de Regionibus Orientalibus (also titled De Conditionibus et Consuetudinibus Orientalium Regionum). Latin translation from the Spanish/Italian tradition, edited by Andreas Müller (Greiffenhagius), Prepositus Berolinensis.
Publication: Ex officina Georgii Schulzii, [Germany], 1671 (OCLC 12357493).
Editor’s note: Müller states this edition follows an older Latin manuscript in the Electoral Library at Berlin, supplied by Johann Vorst, differing from earlier printed versions (including Pilinski’s). Dedicated to Otto von Schwerin, counsellor to the Elector of Brandenburg.
Digital source: Anna’s Archive ZIP (Princeton/Widener scan; tree 32101080071085/), 414 OCR page files.
Text
wiki/raw/marco-polo-1671/raw.txt — 19,891 lines, ~727 KB, 414 OCR pages. Body Latin prose is highly readable; early pages carry library stamps and title-page noise; running headers, footnote sigla, and occasional OCR breaks in proper names appear throughout. Original page-level files preserved under sources/marco-polo-1671/32101080071085/.
Contents
Dedication and Editor’s Preface
Dedication to Otto von Schwerin — Andreas Müller dedicates the new edition to the Brandenburg court counsellor, acknowledging patronage and expressing gratitude.
Præfatio to the Chorographiam — Müller’s long scholarly preface on the value of geography for sacred and profane history; surveys ancient and medieval geographers (Ptolemy, Strabo, Scylax, Hanno, Marco Polo among them); argues that Marco Polo’s book is among the most useful yet most neglected and corrupted works in geographic literature, because it alone describes the extreme Orient and extreme North in such detail that later maps of those regions derive largely from it; explains his editorial method and the Berlin manuscript source.
De M. Paulo Ven. Judicia
A collection of testimonies and judgments about Marco Polo drawn from other authors — citations from Ramusio, Münster, Adam Olearius, and others on Polo’s reliability as a witness to Tartar affairs, the location of Prester John, the size of the Tartar empire relative to all Christian and Saracen kingdoms combined, and related geographic disputes.
Liber Primus — The Journey Out and Western Asia (66 chapters)
Chapters I–X: The Polo brothers and first embassy

I — How Nicholas and Maffeo Polo, brothers, set out for the East (1253, during Baldwin’s rule at Constantinople)
II — Their arrival at the court of the Great Khan
III — How graciously the Great Khan received them
IV — The Khan sends them to the Roman Pontiff to request Christian teachers
V — How they awaited the election of a new Pope
VI — Their return to the Tartar Emperor
VII — How the Venetians were received by the Tartar Emperor
VIII — How Marco Polo became favoured at the Tartar court
IX–X — After several years they obtain leave and return to Venice

Chapters XI–XX: Armenia, Turkey, Persia

XI–XIII — Lesser Armenia, Turkey, Greater Armenia
XIV–XVIII — Zorzania, Mosul, Baldach (Baghdad), Tauris, a mountain miraculously moved
XIX–XX — Persia, Yasdi, Camandu and Reobarle

Chapters XXI–XLIV: Persia to the Desert of Lop

XXI–XXVII — Campestrian plains, Cormos, regions between Cremos and Cobinam, Cobinam, Timochaim and the sun-tree
XXVIII–XXIX — A notable tyrant and his assassination
XXX–XLIII — Sopurgam, Balac, Taicam, Scaffem, Balafcia, Badakhshan, Chefmur, Vocam and its high mountains, Samarcand, Carcham, Cotam, Peim, Ciartiam
XLIV — The city of Lop and the great desert

Chapters XLV–LXVI: Tartary and the Great Khan’s predecessors

XLV–L — Sachion, Camul, Chinchinthalas, Sucbur, Campition, Ezina and another great desert, Tarocoram and the origin of Tartar dominion
LI–LIII — How the Tartars elect a Great Khan; Chinghis Khan’s campaigns against Unc Khan
LIV–LX — Catalogue of Tartar kings and their burial customs; general manners and customs of the Tartars; arms and clothing; idolatry and errors; industry; judgments and justice
LXI–LXVI — Erigimul and Singui, Egrigaia, Teuduch (Gog and Magog), Ciandu and its park, idolatrous monks

Liber Secundus — Kublai Khan’s Cathay (70 chapters)
Chapters I–XX: Kublai Khan’s power and court

I–V — The power and magnificence of Kublai Khan; his war against his uncle Naiam; Naiam’s defeat and suffocation
VI–VIII — Kublai restrains Jews and Saracens; rewards soldiers; his person, wives, sons, and attendants
IX–XIII — The palace at Cambalu (Beijing), description of the city, suburbs and merchants, the Khan’s great retinue, magnificent feasts
XIV–XX — New Year celebrations, wild beasts sent as tribute, hunting with tame leopards, hawking, magnificent tents

Chapters XXI–LXX: Administration and provinces of Cathay

XXI–XXVIII — Twelve prefects of provinces, couriers and messengers, provision against famine, wine substitute in Cathay, stones that burn like wood, rivers Pulisangin and Caramoran and their bridges
XXIX–XL — Kingdom of Tainfu, fortress Chingui, Caromoran river, provinces Chunchi, Achalechmangi, Sindinfu, Tebet, Caniglu, Caraiam, a forest region, great battle between Tartars and Nay
XLI–L — Province Arcladam, the tomb of a king at Mien, Bangala, Cangigu, Amu, Tholoman, Gingui, cities Cacaufu/Canglu/Ciangli
LI–LXX — Caromoran river and cities, province Mangi and its justice, Baian’s conquests, Conigangui, Panchi, Chain, Singui, Caigui, Cingianfu, Cingingui, the noble city Quinsay (Hangzhou), revenues of Quinsay, Tampingui, Fugui, Quelinfu, Unquen

Liber Tertius — India, the Islands, and the Far North (50 chapters)
Chapters I–XII: Zipangu and Southeast Asia

I — What kinds of ships are used in India
II–VII — The island of Zipangu (Japan); Kublai’s failed expedition; shipwreck; Tartar escape; idolatry and cruelty of Zipangu; various islands and their fruits
VIII–XII — Province Ciamba, island Java, Boëach, island Petan

Chapters XIII–XXVII: India and the Apostle Thomas

XIII–XXII — Kingdoms Ferlech, Basman, Samara, Dragoiam, Lambri, Fanfur; islands Necuram, Angania, great Seilan (Ceylon)
XXIII–XXVII — Kingdom Maabar (India Major); kingdom Var and its customs; the city where the body of St Thomas the Apostle is preserved (with miracle of the rice and the apparition)

Chapters XXVIII–L: Further India, Africa, and the Arctic

XXVIII–XXXVI — Kingdom Coilon, Comari, Eli, Melibar, Tana, Cambaet, two islands where men and women live separately, Scoira
XXXVII–XL — Great island Madagascar, the great bird Ruc (roc), island Zanzibar
XLI–XLIII — Province Abassia (Ethiopia), a man forcibly circumcised by a Sultan
XLIV–L — Various beasts; province Aden; a region where Tartars live; a region of mud and ice; the region of darkness; province of the Rucheni (Russians)

Indexes (Editorial Apparatus)
Index Primus Historicus — Alphabetical recension of all observations and memorable matters noted by the author throughout the three books, with book and chapter references.
Index Secundus Chronographicus — Chronological table of events mentioned in Polo’s travels (Polo brothers’ departures, Kublai’s wars, Zipangu expedition, Venetian return, etc.).
Index Tertius Itinerarius — Itinerary of places traversed and distances annotated by the author, organized by book and chapter with league measurements between cities (Venetia, Constantinopolis, Soldadia, Bochara, etc.).
Et Historica de Chataja (Müller’s Commentary)
Andreas Müller’s extended philological and geographic commentary on Cathay — not Marco Polo’s original text but the editor’s scholarly apparatus. Treats: etymology of Chataja / Cathay; synonyms (Temgagi, Tangut); the Great Wall; caravan routes and customs posts; comparison with Arabic, Persian, and later European authors on China; Sinic script and place-names; Müller’s corrections to earlier editors (Hornius, Trigault, etc.). Runs to several dozen sections with cross-references to the three books.
Appendices and Errata
Historia lapidis — Short treatise on a stone (when, where, and under what occasion it was found), with indices of contents.
Extantiora Errata Typographica — List of typographical errors in the edition.
See Also

christopher-columbus — Columbus studied Marco Polo when planning his westward route to Asia
genoa-lisbon — Columbus’s correspondence with Toscanelli and his copy of Marco Polo
cuba-columbus — Columbus interpreted Cuba as Cipango from Polo’s descriptions
cartography-age-of-discovery — Polo’s geography in Cantino and later maps
fiske-discovery-of-america-vol1 — Fiske on pre-Columbian voyages and Polo in the discovery context

sources/oliveira-arte-da-guerra-do-mar.title: A Arte da Guerra do Mar — Padre Fernando Oliveira
sources/oliveira-arte-da-guerra-do-mar.content:
A Arte da Guerra do Mar — Padre Fernando Oliveira
Bibliographic Information

Author: Padre Fernando Oliveira (also written Fernão de Oliveira, Fernand’ Oliveira), c.1507–c.1581, Portuguese Dominican friar, grammarian, navigator, and humanist
Full title: A Arte da Guerra do Mar (The Art of War at Sea)
Original imprint: Arte da guerra do mar novamente escrita per Fernand’oliveyra, & dirigida ao muyto manifico senhor, o senhor dom Nuno da Cunha capitão das galees do muyto poderoso rey de Portugal dom Johão o terceiro. Vista & amitida pellos senhores deputados da sancta inquisição. Em Coimbra, M. D. LV. (Coimbra, 1555)
This edition: Ministério da Marinha (Portuguese Navy Ministry), Colecção Documentos series, Lisbon; printed by Bertrand (Irmãos), Lda., Lisbon
Editorial matter: “Nota explicativa” (editorial preface) and “Comentários preliminares” (preliminary commentary) by Comandante Quirino da Fonseca, from the 1937 edition
Library copy noted in OCR: Michigan State University scan, call label FLARE 31262075342039
Source file: wiki/raw/oliveira-arte-da-guerra-do-mar.txt (196 OCR pages, 6,045 lines)
Language: Body text in 16th-century Portuguese orthography; modern Portuguese editorial commentary; source page in English

About the Author and Edition
Padre Fernando Oliveira was a Portuguese Dominican friar, philologist, and navigator — author of the first printed Portuguese grammar (Gramática da Linguagem Portuguesa, 1536) — whose restless, frankly opinionated life carried him from Lisbon to Castile, Italy, France, and England. The preliminary commentary (by Quirino da Fonseca, after the study of Henrique Lopes de Mendonça) recounts his clandestine departure from the Tagus in the galley armada of the Baron de La Garde, his service among French galleys against English ships off Dover, his sojourn in Protestant England, and his later trouble with the Inquisition. The Arte da Guerra do Mar, printed at Coimbra in 1555 and dedicated to Dom Nuno da Cunha, captain of the galleys of King John III, was chosen to open the Navy Ministry’s Colecção Documentos series as the oldest known treatise on naval strategy and tactics in print: “Tem este livro a destacá-lo o facto de ser o mais antigo tratado de estratégia e táctica naval de que há memória em letra de forma” (the book is distinguished by being the oldest treatise of naval strategy and tactics of which there is record in print).
Summary
The work is divided into two parts. The first part, “da intenção e apercebimento da guerra” (on the purpose and preparation of war at sea), treats the justification, justice, and conduct of war; the office of the Admiral; the shipyards (taracenas) and their provisioning; timber for ships and when to cut it; magazines and their supply; victuals; the men of the sea; the captains of the sea and their authority; the choosing and settling of soldiers; and the exercise of soldiers. The second part, “das frotas armadas, e das batalhas maritimas, e seus ardis” (on armed fleets, maritime battles, and their stratagems), treats ships for the armadas and the number of men for them; provisioning of stores, munitions, and rigging; the time to sail and the change of seasons; signs of storms and variation of the weathers; the winds, their regions and names; necessary advices for navigation; tides, currents, and the sea’s movements; how the armadas set sail; battles at sea and the stratagems needed in them; the place for fighting; the loss of the ships that went with the king of Bélez; the ordnances of war at sea; some general rules of war; and the conclusion of the work. Throughout, Oliveira draws on classical authorities (Vegetius, Pliny, Quintilian, Justin) and on his own sea service to prescribe the practical conduct of a naval war.
Scope and Approach
Oliveira writes a prescriptive and technical treatise rather than a narrative history: he lays down the offices, provisioning, seamanship, and battle order required to equip and fight an armada, mixing classical citation with firsthand knowledge of Portuguese and French galleys and caravels. He opens the Prologue by declaring that no earlier author, so far as he knew, had written any art or documents of war at sea — “Da qual nenhum autor, que eu sayba, escreuco antes dagora arte nem documentos” — the claim that makes the work foundational in the history of naval theory. The Navy Ministry edition frames him as “uma das figuras mais completas da Renascença” in Portugal (one of the most complete figures of the Renaissance in Portugal), restless, eclectic, and ahead of his time in opinion.
Contents
Editorial Front Matter
Nota explicativa — The Navy Ministry explains the Colecção Documentos series, chosen to open with the Arte da Guerra do Mar as the oldest printed treatise of naval strategy and tactics, and sketches Oliveira’s biography (first Portuguese grammar, cleric and scholar, rebel and outspoken).
Comentários preliminares (by Comandante Quirino da Fonseca, from the 1937 edition) — A biographical study of Oliveira: his schooling, his grammar of the Portuguese language, his service as master to the sons of the chronicler of India João de Barros and of other noble houses, his mysterious commission to Italy, his flight with the galleys of the Baron de La Garde, the fight against English ships off Dover, his stay in Protestant England and correspondence with the Count of Castanheira, his return to Lisbon and the bookseller’s shop of João Fernandes, and the suspicion of the Inquisition that his frankness drew upon him.
Fac-simile do frontespício da edição de 1555 — Facsimile of the 1555 title page.
Prologo (com exordio, e escusa do autor)
Prologue with exordium and the author’s apology — Oliveira addresses the “muyto manifico señor” (Dom Nuno da Cunha), drawing on Quintilian on the art of pleasing hearers, defends the active life of travel against mere idleness, praises the Portuguese for conquering and discovering new lands and spreading the faith by “a guerra do mar,” and declares that no author before him, so far as he knew, had written an art or documents of it; he excuses the novelty and smallness of his present to his patron.
Parte Primeira — “da intenção e apercebimento da guerra no mar”
Capítulo I: Que he necessario fazer guerra (That it is necessary to make war) — Opens on the authority of Plato and the laws of Crete that men should be kept prepared as in continual war; holds that since men disobeyed God they live in natural discord, and that war is sometimes necessary to defend the land.
Capítulo II: De quem pode fazer guerra (Of who may make war) — On the lawful maker of war, the prince and the commonwealth that defends its land and people.
Capítulo III: Que he necessario fazer guerra no mar (That it is necessary to make war at sea) — The necessity of war at sea for a maritime realm, the defence of coasts, and the keeping of the sea as part of the land’s safety.
Capítulo IIII: Qual he guerra justa (Which war is just) — The conditions of a just war, on the authority of the doctors of the Church, defense against injury, and the recovery of what is justly due.
Capítulo V: Da tenção e modo da guerra (Of the intention and manner of war) — The right intent and orderly manner of waging war.
Capítulo VI: Do officio do Almirante (Of the office of the Admiral) — The Admiral’s duty: to have ships ready in the taracenas to answer sudden surprises, and to keep all the navy’s provisions in order.
Capítulo VII: Das taracenas e seu prouimento (Of the shipyards and their provisioning) — The taracenas (royal shipyards) must hold ships made and ready, with cordage, nails, pitch, oakum, and all tackle; on ropes of hemp and of cotton, and on their qualities.
Capítulo VIII: Da Madeyra pera as naos (Of timber for the ships) — Which woods suit ships, differing by the lands in which they grow; on cork (souaro/sobreiro), larch, chestnut, and other timbers, their strength, resistance to rot and to the sea, and how to choose sound trees.
Capítulo IX: De quando se cortaraa a madeyra (Of when the timber shall be cut) — On the season and manner of cutting timber — before the sap and humours rise — so that the wood keeps its strength, and on sparing the cork woods and favouring the growth of pines.
Capítulo X: Dos armazens e seu provimento (Of the magazines and their supply) — The armazéns must be furnished with shot, powder, and artillery, and the men trained in their use, that the Portuguese may defend themselves with equal arms against the Moors; on the arms used on both sides.
Capítulo XI: Das victualhas (Of the victuals) — On provisioning biscuit, wheat, rice, maize, and roots as bread, on beans and pulses (after Pliny), oil, vinegar, candles, and all things needful for an armada.
Capítulo XII: Dos homens do mar (Of the men of the sea) — On mariners, rowers, and their numbers and qualities; on pilots and the perils of bad ones.
Capítulo XIII: Dos capitães do mar e do seu poder (Of the captains of the sea and their power) — The captain as the head of the company of war, “de capite palaura latina” (from the Latin word caput, head); the authority to govern and to punish soldiers without process of court; a captain-major in every fleet obeyed as the prince.
Capítulo XIV: De como deuem ser escolhidos, e assentados os soldados (Of how the soldiers ought to be chosen and enrolled) — On choosing soldiers of good blood, breeding, and honour over worthless and low fellows, that arms defend the land rather than ruin it; on the shame and virtue that win victories.
Capítulo XV: Do exercicio dos soldados (Of the exercise of the soldiers) — On keeping soldiers occupied — making wood and water, gathering stores, embarking artillery — lest idleness breed vice; on the danger of those who only win their living by arms and rail at God.
Parte Segunda — “das frotas armadas, e das batalhas maritimas, e seus ardis”
Capítulo I: Dos nauios pera as armadas (Of the ships for the armadas) — The captains charged with an armada must ask the Admiral or his officers for all things needful: ships suited to the sea and to the war, in kind, quantity, and number; long voyages over the great sea require great ships; on ships of oars and of sail, and on the caravel’s mixing of lateen sail and round hull.
Capítulo II: Do numero da gente pera os nauios (Of the number of men for the ships) — The complement of mariners and ship’s boys (grumetes) for ships of ten, twenty, and thirty tons; the master, pilot, and the company of a galley — pilot (patrão), fifteen mariners, and five bowmen, with the oar-crew; the office of the comitre.
Capítulo III: Da esquipação dos mantimentos, munições e enxerceas (Of the equipping of stores, munitions, and rigging) — The captain provides victuals of every kind with surplus, and arms the ship fittingly; on guns, chambers, and how to keep powder and pieces dry and ready against tempest.
Capítulo IV: Do tempo de nauegar as armadas, e mudança dos tempos (Of the time for the armadas to sail, and the change of seasons) — The captain consults with discreet and experienced friends on the time of departure; on the seasons favourable and dangerous for sailing.
Capítulo V: Dos sinaes das tempestades, e varição dos temporaes (Of the signs of storms and the variation of the weathers) — On reading the sky and stars for weather; the stars that show signs of rain and storm (the erratics, the asses of Cancer with their manger), and the need for humble knowledge among mariners.
Capítulo VI: Dos ventos e suas regiões, e nomes (Of the winds, their regions, and names) — A treatise on the winds: the four principal winds (east, west, north, south) and their regions, their names and properties, and the compendium of their quarters.
Capítulo VII: Dalguns auisos necessarios pa nauegar (Of some necessary advices for navigation) — To know the lands one sails toward and what winds will serve; on “demorar” (the bearing of lands), the height of the pole, and the sun’s declination about the equinoctial line.
Capítulo VIII: Das marees, correntes e aguagens do mar (Of the tides, currents, and the sea’s waters) — On the times of high and low water for entering ports with bars and channels; after Pliny, on the greater tides of the full moon and of summer, and on the head of the waters lagging two or three tides behind the lunations.
Capítulo IX: De como as armadas faram vela (Of how the armadas shall set sail) — The order of making sail: masters, pilots, and mariners aboard from the fleet’s assembly; the captain-major flies the prince’s banner at the mainmast (or on the starboard of the poop for oared ships) that he may be known and followed.
Capítulo X: Das batalhas do mar/e alguns ardis necessarios nellas (Of battles at sea, and some stratagems needed in them) — A terrible thing is the sea battle before human eyes, offering death without refuge amid confusions and anguish; on determining matters of war with moderation and diligence, and on the stratagems and deceits used to seize the occasion.
Capítulo XI: Do lugar pera pelejar (Of the place for fighting) — When combat comes the captain takes the best place; after Vegetius, place commands a great part of victory, and those in an importune place suffer a double labour.
Capítulo XII: De como se perderão os nauios que foram com elrey de Belez (Of how the ships that went with the king of Bélez were lost) — A narrative of the loss of the ships that went with the king of Bélez against the Turks: there was no proportion between the strength of the two sides, and the Portuguese lacked trained gunners (few knew how to fire an arquebus) while the enemy was well furnished.
Capítulo XIII: Das ordenanças da guerra do mar (Of the ordnances of war at sea) — Order in battle avails more than multitude; the ordnances are the nerves of the army and the rest of the captain; the formation of the sea squadrons is simple and straight (or but little curved), since the other forms — wedges, wedges-and-rounds, squares — do not avail at sea save to break and cut.
Capítulo XIV: Dalgumas regras geraes da guerra (Of some general rules of war) — General rules gathered for ready use: wise and faithful industry in the officers, use and dexterity in the men, plenty in provisioning, caution and diligence in action.
Capítulo XV: Da conclusam da obra (Of the conclusion of the work) — The conclusion: great importance of the documents of war at sea, especially in Portugal where the livelihoods of many depend on that sea; a call to prepare for the storms to come, to provision the taracenas and magazines, to exercise men in arms, to keep fleets ready, to know the seasons of navigation, and to be alert.
Colophon
Composto e impresso em BERTRAND (IRMÃOS), LDA., LISBOA — printers’ colophon of this edition.
Scan Completeness Audit
The 196 OCR pages run without gap from the title page through the editorial preface, the Quirino da Fonseca commentary, the facsimile of the 1555 title page, the Prologue, both parts (fifteen chapters each), and the Bertrand colophon, ending on the Michigan State University library barcode (FLARE 31262075342039). The small or blank pages correspond to title pages, facsimile divider pages, and plate/blank leaves within the volume — most notably the facsimile title page of the 1555 edition and the facsimile divider pages announcing the first and second parts — and do not represent missing text. The body chapters are all present, each opening on its own page in the original orthography.
Relation to Other Sources in This Wiki

This is the oldest printed naval-strategy treatise in the corpus (1555), a Portuguese primary source, the counterpart in naval theory to the navigational and voyage texts (velho-gama-journal, roteiro-vasco-da-gama) and the later English naval-historical works (corbett-drake-tudor-navy, sir-francis-drake-sugden).
It should be cited where the wiki needs the 16th-century Portuguese doctrine of fleet preparation, battle order, and the justification of war at sea, or the era’s own statement of the maritime vocation of Portugal.

Sources

Oliveira, Padre Fernando. A Arte da Guerra do Mar. Coimbra, 1555; reprinted by the Ministério da Marinha, Colecção Documentos, with preliminary commentary by Comandante Quirino da Fonseca, Lisbon: Bertrand (Irmãos), Lda.
Local ordered OCR extract: raw/oliveira-arte-da-guerra-do-mar.txt
Anna’s Archive source ZIP in the period archive folder (Michigan State University scan, FLARE 31262075342039)

sources/pigafetta-magellan.title: The First Voyage Around the World, 1519–1522 — Pigafetta's Journal
sources/pigafetta-magellan.content:
The First Voyage Around the World, 1519–1522
Author: Antonio Pigafetta, patrician of Vicenza and Knight of Rhodes
Editor/Translator: Theodore J. Cachey Jr.
Publisher: University of Toronto Press, 2007 (Lorenzo Da Ponte Italian Library)
Source file: pigafetta_magellan.txt (94,000 words)
Summary
The only surviving eyewitness account of Magellan’s circumnavigation. Pigafetta’s journal runs 213 numbered sections covering the entire voyage from the August 1519 departure through the Victoria’s return in September 1522, followed by extensive editorial notes and bibliography. The journal includes detailed ethnographic observations, vocabulary lists of indigenous languages, navigational data, and the sole first-hand report of Magellan’s death at Mactan. The Cachey edition provides a scholarly introduction, chronology, and apparatus.
Section-by-Section Breakdown
Dedicatory Letter (Sections 1–4)
Pigafetta addresses Philipe Villiers de l’Isle-Adam, Grand Master of Rhodes, explaining his motivation for joining the expedition — a desire to see the wonders of the world — and his purpose in writing the account. He describes obtaining permission from both Charles V and Magellan to sail as a supernumerary.
Organization and Departure (Sections 5–9)
The fleet’s night watch system — three watches (first, modora, and third), the captain-general’s secrecy about the route, the departure from Seville on August 10, 1519 (St. Lawrence’s day), the descent of the Guadalquivir River, and the final departure from Sanlucar on September 20. The fleet reached the Canary Islands on September 26.
Atlantic Crossing (Sections 10–14)
The Canary Islands — one island where fresh water is obtained from a daily cloud. Departure on October 3, passing Cape Verde. Observations of sharks (tiburoni) caught with iron hooks. St. Elmo’s fire appearing during storms, described as the Holy Body appearing in the form of light at the masthead. Sea birds, including the “bird without an anus” and a bird whose female lays eggs on the male’s back.
Brazil (Sections 15–22)
Landfall at Verzin (Brazil) after crossing the equator and losing the North Star. Description of Brazil as vast and bounteous, larger than Spain, France, and Italy combined. Ethnographic observations: ritual cannibalism of enemies, body painting with fire, the men smooth-shaven. Trade: hatchets and knives for young daughters as slaves. Mass celebrated twice on shore, the natives kneeling in imitation. Vocabulary list of 16 Tupi words.
The Patagonian Coast (Sections 23–30)
Departure from Brazil after 13 days. Islands of geese and sea-wolves (seals) — the geese could not fly, the sea-wolves had heads like calves. Arrival at Port St. Julian at 49.5° south. The first Patagonian giant encountered — so tall the Spaniards reached only to his waist. The mirror incident: the giant terrified by his own reflection. Giant women described as very fat with breasts half a cubit long. Further encounters with armed giants. Giant customs: vomiting by swallowing an arrow when sick, their vocabulary of 25+ words recorded by Pigafetta.
Mutiny and Loss of the Santiago (Sections 31–32)
Five months at Port St. Julian. The mutiny (described briefly — the editor’s notes expand). The loss of the Santiago during a coastal exploration — all crew saved “as by a miracle, not even getting wet.”
Discovery of the Strait (Sections 33–40)
A river of fresh water at 51°, the ships nearly lost. On October 21 (Feast of the Eleven Thousand Virgins), the strait discovered. The entrance cape named Cape of the Eleven Thousand Virgins. The branching channels: the San Antonio and Concepcion sent to explore one branch, the Trinidad and Victoria the other. The San Antonio’s desertion. The discovery that the strait continues to the southwest. The river of Sardines. Nights of only three hours. The fires glimpsed on the southern shore (hence Tierra del Fuego). A 45-word vocabulary of the Patagonian language.
The Pacific Crossing (Sections 41–45)
Departure from the strait on November 28, 1520. Three months and twenty days without fresh food or water. The harrowing description: eating biscuit reduced to powder “full of worms,” drinking yellow water stinking with rat urine, eating ox-hide leather softened in the sea, sawdust, and rats sold for half a ducado each. Nineteen men died of scurvy (gums swollen, unable to eat). Pigafetta’s observations of the Southern Cross and the Magellanic Clouds (two cloudy clusters of many small stars). Navigation data.
Guam — The Islands of Thieves (Sections 46–49)
Discovery of Guam on March 6, 1521. The natives swarming the ships, stealing everything they could touch — hence the name Islas de los Ladrones. Theft of the skiff. A punitive expedition ashore killing several natives. Ethnographic description: naked people with long tangled hair, palm-leaf houses on wooden beams, no lords, coconut and palm wine economy.
The Philippines — Samar and Massawa (Sections 50–68)
Arrival at Samar on March 16, 1521, after 300 leagues from Guam. First contact at Massawa (Limasawa). Detailed descriptions of coconuts — Pigafetta’s famous passage: “Just as we have bread, wine, oil, and milk, so these people get everything from those trees.” Nine men in a boat approach, trade, names of islands learned. The first mass on Philippine soil — Easter Sunday, March 31, 1521. The cross planted. Fencing tournament. The king of Massawa and his brother, the king of Cebu.
Cebu (Sections 70–76)
Arrival at Cebu on April 7. The fleet entering port with all sails lowered and all flags flying — a deliberate show of force. The king’s demand for tribute, Magellan’s refusal: the interpreter declaring that “since his master was the captain of so great a king, he did not pay tribute to any lord in the world.” The peace agreement. Trade established — gold for iron.
Conversion of Cebu (Sections 77–78, further sections)
The king’s visit to the flagship. The agreement to accept Christianity. Mass baptisms: the king baptized as “Charles,” the queen as “Joan,” approximately 800 souls. The destruction of native idols. A miraculous healing — the queen’s sick son given water blessed by Christ’s image.
The Battle of Mactan and Magellan’s Death
Magellan’s fatal decision to intervene in a local conflict. Chief Lapu-Lapu of Mactan refusing to submit. The midnight departure of 49 Spaniards in three boats. The landing at dawn, wading through water to the beach. Lapu-Lapu’s force of approximately 1,500 warriors. Magellan’s last stand: a poisoned arrow in the leg, a spear in the left arm, a scimitar blow to the leg, overwhelmed under a rain of spears and stones. Lapu-Lapu refusal to return the body. Pigafetta’s account is the only surviving eyewitness report.
The Sebu Massacre (Sections following)
After Magellan’s death, King Humabon’s betrayal. A feast on shore — 27 Spaniards killed, including the newly elected leaders. The burning of the Concepcion. The desperate flight from the Philippines.
Borneo and the Spice Islands
The voyage through the Malay archipelago. Arrival at Palawan and Brunei (Borneo). The diplomatic complications — Pigafetta describing the elaborate court ceremonies. Arrival at the Moluccas (Spice Islands) in November 1521. The friendly Sultan Almansor of Tidor. Trade agreement for cloves. The decision to leave the leaky Trinidad behind.
The Return (Sections for the Victoria’s voyage)
The Victoria under Elcano loading cloves at Tidor. Departure December 21, 1521. The Indian Ocean crossing — no stops, starvation. Rounding the Cape of Good Hope. The stop at Cape Verde Islands where 13 men were sent ashore for provisions and left behind when the Portuguese became suspicious. The Victoria’s arrival at Sanlucar de Barrameda on September 6, 1522. Only 18 survivors of the original 237. Pigafetta among them.
Final Sections
Pigafetta’s concluding remarks. The dedicatory close to the Grand Master. The preserved manuscript of the account.
Editorial Apparatus
The Cachey edition includes a bio-bibliographical note (Pigafetta’s life, the manuscript history), a chronology from March 1518 to September 1522, notes section with annotations on each section, bibliography, and index. The introduction discusses the text’s place in Renaissance travel literature.
See Also

bergreen-magellan — Bergreen’s Over the Edge of the World, based partly on this journal
ferdinand-magellan — Entity page

Word Lists and Linguistics
A distinctive feature of Pigafetta’s journal is the inclusion of four graded word lists recording the languages of the peoples encountered — the earliest written specimens of each. The lists grew progressively longer as his method improved: a short list of 8 Tupi-Guarani words from Brazil; approximately 90 words of Tehuelche (Patagonian giants); approximately 160 words of Philippine languages (what Pigafetta called “the language of the heathen” to distinguish it from Malay); and a remarkable 426-450 word vocabulary of Malay. The Malay vocabulary is one of the oldest written specimens of the Malay language, with the earliest surviving manuscripts dated to around 1500–1550. Scholars have described Pigafetta’s transcription of East Indian toponyms and his Malay vocabulary as “extremely accurate.” The Cachey edition notes that the four word lists “cumulatively constitute a kind of implicit anthropological portrait of the East Indian societies encountered.” ^[source: pigafetta_magellan.txt, Cachey editorial notes]
Cartography
The earliest manuscripts of Pigafetta’s journal included 23 hand-painted maps of the regions visited. The maps follow the narrative sequentially, with pairs of charts positioned at key transitions in the journey (the passage through the Strait, the Pacific crossing, the Moluccas). Pigafetta raised the treatment of cartography to a new level compared to earlier travel writers such as Columbus and Vespucci. ^[source: pigafetta_magellan.txt, Cachey editorial notes]
Literary Reception and Influence
Pigafetta’s narrative had a surprisingly long literary afterlife. His description of the Patagonian deity “Setebos” was picked up by Richard Eden’s 1555 English translation and later used by William Shakespeare in The Tempest, where Caliban’s god is named Setebos. The Colombian novelist Gabriel García Márquez, in his Nobel Prize acceptance speech, referenced Pigafetta’s account of the Patagonian giant who confronted a mirror and was terrified by his own reflection. The Cachey edition positions Pigafetta’s narrative within the lingua e letteratura cortigiana (courtly language and literature) that flourished in the Italian High Renaissance, noting that it “represents a particularly mature expression of courtly Italian Renaissance travel writing.” ^[source: pigafetta_magellan.txt, Cachey editorial notes]

Source file: sources/roteiro-vasco-da-gama/roteiro.txt (6,906 lines, OCR’d from scanned Portuguese original)
Summary
The Portuguese original of the Roteiro (ship’s journal) of Vasco da Gama’s first voyage to India (1497–1499), edited by the noted Portuguese historian Alexandre Herculano. This is the text in its original language, containing the same journal attributed to Álvaro Velho that forms the sole surviving first-hand account of the expedition. The Google Books scan was OCR’d with Portuguese language recognition (251 pages).
Contents
The Roteiro follows the same narrative as the English Hakluyt Society translation:

Departure from Lisbon and the Atlantic crossing
The Cape of Good Hope and the East African coast
Mozambique, Mombasa, and Malindi
The Indian Ocean crossing
Calicut — the Zamorin’s court, trade negotiations
The return voyage

The original Portuguese text includes place names, navigational data, and ethnographic observations in their 15th-century Portuguese orthography.

sources/sea-road-to-the-indies-hart.content:
Sea Road to the Indies
Author: Henry H. Hart
Publisher: Macmillan, New York, 1950
Source files: sources/sea-road-to-the-indies-hart/ (320 OCR page files)
Summary
A narrative history of the Portuguese voyages of discovery, from Prince Henry the Navigator through Vasco da Gama and his successors. Hart traces the development of Portuguese maritime exploration through the 15th and early 16th centuries, culminating in the discovery of the sea route to India around the Cape of Good Hope.
Contents
Prologue: The Forerunners (pp. 1–12)
Part I: Background and Preparation

Chapter I — Portugal (pp. 13–26): The kingdom’s geography, history, and maritime tradition
Chapter II — Prince Henry the Navigator (pp. 27–42): Henry’s life, his school at Sagres, and the early discoveries
Chapter III — Early Deep-Sea Ventures (pp. 43–63): The Atlantic islands, the African coast, caravel development

Part II: The Cape Route

Chapter IV — Bartholomeu Dias and the Discovery of the Cape of Good Hope (pp. 64–78): Dias’s 1487–88 voyage rounding the southern tip of Africa
Chapter V — The Mission of Pero de Covilhã (pp. 79–93): The overland spy mission to India and Ethiopia

Part III: Vasco da Gama, the Capitão-Mor

Chapter VI — The Building of the Armada (pp. 94–107): Construction and outfitting of the São Gabriel, São Rafael, Berrio, and the storeship
Chapter VII — Vasco da Gama’s Early Life (pp. 108–115): Gama’s background, family, career before 1497
Chapter VIII — The Ships’ Companies (pp. 116–120): Crew lists, officers, duties
Chapter IX — The Departure (pp. 121–126): The fleet’s departure from Lisbon, July 1497
Chapter X — The Sailing of the Fleet (pp. 127–157): The Atlantic crossing, St. Helena Bay, rounding the Cape
Chapter XI — Africa (pp. 158–172): The East African coast — Mozambique, Mombasa, Malindi
Chapter XII — Malabar and Calicut (pp. 173–188): The Indian coast, arrival at Calicut
Chapter XIII — The Portuguese in Calicut (pp. 189–195): Negotiations with the Zamorin, tensions with Muslim merchants
Chapter XIV — The Voyage Home (pp. 196–201): The difficult return crossing
Chapter XV — The Return of Vasco da Gama (pp. 202–206): Arrival in Lisbon, the king’s reception
Chapter XVI — Portugal, 1499–1502 (pp. 207–214): Preparations for the second armada
Chapter XVII — The Voyage of Pedro Álvares Cabral (pp. 215–219): Cabral’s discovery of Brazil and voyage to India

Part IV: The Second and Third Voyages

Chapter XVIII — Lisbon in 1502 (pp. 220–233): The city and court
Chapter XIX — The Narrative of the Second Voyage (pp. 234–241): Gama’s second voyage, the violent confrontation at Calicut
Chapter XX — Portugal, 1503–1524 (pp. 242–251): The intervening years
Chapter XXI — India, 1502–1524 (pp. 252–258): Portuguese India under Almeida and Albuquerque
Chapter XXII — The Third Voyage of Vasco da Gama, His Vice-royalty and Death (pp. 259–265): Gama’s final voyage and death in Cochin
Chapter XXIII — The Burial Place of Vasco da Gama (pp. 266–270): Gama’s tomb and its history

Part V: Assessment

Chapter XXIV — Vasco da Gama the Man (pp. 271–273): Character sketch
Chapter XXV — The Contribution of Vasco da Gama and His Discovery of the Sea Road to the Indies (pp. 274–278): Historical significance

Appendices

Note: The Descendants of Vasco da Gama (pp. 279–283)
Bibliography (pp. 284–292)
Index (pp. 293–305)
