sources/sir-francis-drake-sugden.title: Sir Francis Drake — John Sugden
sources/sir-francis-drake-sugden.content:
Sir Francis Drake — John Sugden
Bibliographic Information

Author: John Sugden
Title: Sir Francis Drake
First published: 1990 by Barrie & Jenkins (UK) / Henry Holt (US)
Revised editions: 1996 (Pimlico, with new preface); 2006 (revised Pimlico edition, with postscript)
Publisher (2006 edition): Pimlico, Random House, London
ISBN (ePub): 9781448129508
Copyright: John Sugden 1990, 1996, 2006
Source file: sugden_drake.txt (23,038 lines)

About the Author
John Sugden has degrees from three British universities and was formerly a lecturer and senior research fellow. The recipient of numerous awards, his most notable prior work was Nelson: A Dream of Glory (Cape, 2004). He is based in Cumbria. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Summary
A comprehensive modern biography of Sir Francis Drake covering his entire life — from obscure Devon yeoman origins, through his apprenticeship under John Hawkins, his early independent voyages to the Spanish Main, his circumnavigation of the globe (1577–1580), his knighthood and rise to prominence at the Elizabethan court, his command role in the defeat of the Spanish Armada (1588), the disastrous Portugal expedition (1589), his final voyage and death off Puerto Bello (1596), and his posthumous reputation across four centuries. The book draws extensively on both Spanish and English archival sources and attempts a rounded treatment of Drake as a businessman, property magnate, civic leader, parliamentarian and magistrate, as well as a bold sea rover. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Scope and Approach
In his preface, Sugden explains that the book was written as an up-to-date popular biography that would rescue Drake from two competing academic traditions: (1) the older Corbett tradition that exalted Drake as the founder of England’s naval supremacy, and (2) the reaction that viewed him narrowly through the lens of privateering. Sugden sought to present a rounded biography of the man, emphasising his social rise from poverty to international significance — the means by which Drake advanced in Elizabeth’s England, his search for patrons, his efforts to legitimise growing status through public service and property acquisition, and his endeavours to establish a heritable line. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
The book is intended for the general reader rather than the specialist, and modernises spelling and punctuation from primary sources while preserving integrity. Dates are given Old Style. The 2006 edition includes a substantial Postscript reviewing research published in the preceding fifteen years (c. 1990–2005). ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Contents
Chapters

‘By God’s Faith!’ — Drake’s origins in the Tavy valley near Tavistock, Devon; his grandparents John and Margery Drake; his father Edmund’s flight to Kent after indictments for robbery; the family’s connection to the Hawkins family; the religious milieu of Reformation England. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Beyond the Line — Drake’s early years at sea; his apprenticeship; the maritime world beyond European jurisdiction where Spain’s claims were unenforceable. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
The Troublesome Voyage of John Hawkins — Drake’s participation in John Hawkins’s third slaving voyage, culminating in the disastrous battle of San Juan de Ulúa (1568), where Drake lost his ship and barely escaped, an event that fuelled his lifelong enmity toward Spain. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Drake’s War — Drake’s early privateering voyages to the Spanish Main (1570–1571); the beginning of his personal war against Spanish shipping and settlements. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
‘The Mouth of the Treasure of the World’ — The 1572–1573 expedition to Panama; the attack on Nombre de Dios; the alliance with the Cimarrons (runaway African slaves); the ambush of the silver train on the Camino Real. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
‘Despite … All the Spaniards in the Indies’ — The conclusion of the 1572–1573 Panama voyage; Drake’s return to Plymouth with substantial treasure; his growing reputation. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Services Ashore and Afloat — Drake’s service in Ireland under the Earl of Essex (1575–1576); the Rathlin Island massacre; his acquisition of patronage at court. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
The South Seas Project — The planning and secret preparation of Drake’s circumnavigation; the investors and court intrigue; Elizabeth’s tacit support without written commission. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
The Atlantic Voyage — The departure from Plymouth (December 1577); the voyage down the Atlantic; the execution of Thomas Doughty at Port San Julián. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
War Comes to the Pacific — The passage through the Strait of Magellan; the separation of the fleet; Drake’s discovery of Cape Horn; the Golden Hind’s lone entry into the Pacific; raids on Spanish ports along the Chilean and Peruvian coasts. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
The World Encompassed — The capture of the Spanish treasure ship Cacafuego; the voyage north up the California coast; the landing at Nova Albion (Drake’s Bay, California); the claim of the region for England; the crossing of the Pacific; the Moluccas; the return via the Cape of Good Hope to Plymouth (September 1580). ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
The Golden Knight — Drake’s knighthood aboard the Golden Hind; the legal and diplomatic fallout of the circumnavigation; Spanish protests; Drake’s investment of his fortune and acquisition of Buckland Abbey. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
‘What Has Become of Drake?’ — Drake’s years ashore (1581–1585); his service as Mayor of Plymouth; his parliamentary career; the Plymouth waterworks (Drake’s Leat); his first marriage to Mary Newman and second to Elizabeth Sydenham. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Playing the Dragon — The West Indies raid of 1585–1586; the sacking of Santo Domingo, Cartagena, and St. Augustine; the failure to find the Spanish treasure fleet; the rescue of the Roanoke colonists. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
‘A Fearful Man to the King of Spain!’ — Drake’s raid on Cadiz (1587), the “singeing of the King of Spain’s beard”; the capture of the Portuguese treasure carrack San Felipe off the Azores. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
‘Stop Him Now, and Stop Him Ever!’ — The preparations for the Spanish Armada; Drake’s command role as vice-admiral; the attack on the Armada at Lisbon. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
‘The Sooner We Are Gone, the Better We Shall Be Able to Impeach Them’ — The opening of the Armada campaign (July 1588); the English fleet’s strategy; the battles in the Channel. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
‘It Was Impossible to Come to Hand-Stroke with Them’ — The continued Channel fighting; the fireship attack at Calais; the Battle of Gravelines; the Armada’s flight around Scotland and Ireland. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
‘God Hath Given Us So Good a Day’ — Aftermath of the Armada; analysis of Drake’s tactics and the controversy over his capture of the Rosario; Drake’s role in the victory. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
‘This Will Cause an Evil Summer’ — The England-Portugal expedition (1589), the “Counter-Armada”; the failure at Corunna and Lisbon; the disastrous losses; the decline of Drake’s reputation. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Last Years Ashore — Drake’s remaining years in England (1589–1595); parliamentary service; civic work in Plymouth; financial troubles; the loss of favour at court. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
‘Into a Waste and Desert Wilderness’ — The final voyage of Drake and Hawkins (1595–1596); the failed attack on Puerto Rico; Hawkins’s death; the capture of Nombre de Dios; Drake’s illness and death off Puerto Bello (28 January 1596); his burial at sea in a lead coffin. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Afterword — The aftermath of Drake’s death; the squabble over his will; the Elizabethan privateering tradition that followed him; Drake’s posthumous reputation across four centuries — from legend and children’s literature to the Victorian imperial hero, to twentieth-century revisionism; Drake’s Drum; the use of Drake’s spirit in both World Wars; the famous prayer derived from his 1587 letter to Walsingham. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Postscript — Written for the 2006 edition, this reviews scholarship published in the years since the first edition (c. 1990–2005). Engages critically with Harry Kelsey’s Sir Francis Drake, the Queen’s Pirate (1998), arguing that Kelsey’s vast research is undermined by hostility toward his subject. Discusses recent field research on Drake’s Panama operations (Port Pheasant, the Camino Real), the circumnavigation (Cape Horn, the Oregon landfall, Nova Albion/Drake’s Estero in California), and re-evaluations of the Armada campaign. Notes the persistence of fringe theories (Bawlff’s claim of a secret Northwest voyage). Concludes with a call for a comprehensive, balanced academic biography. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]

Additional Sections

Picture Section — Full-page reproductions of the illustrations listed below
Glossary — Definitions of period nautical, military, and administrative terms (alcalde, arquebus, artillery types, caravel, galleon, etc.)
Bibliography — Full listing of primary and secondary sources
Index — Comprehensive index of persons, places, and ships

Maps (4)

Drake’s Voyage, 1577–1580 — Shows the circumnavigation route
The West Indies and the Spanish Main — The Caribbean theatre of Drake’s operations
The Iberian Peninsula — Spain and Portugal, covering Cadiz, Lisbon, and related operations
The Battles in the Channel, 1588 — The Armada campaign in the English Channel ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]

Illustrations (26)

Bettes (National Portrait Gallery)9Abraham Ortelius’s world map, 1570Shows pre-Drake geography; 1579 edition marked with Drake’s route (British Library)10Philip II of SpainBy Pantoja de la Cruz11Nicola Van Sype’s map of Drake’s voyageProduced ~1583, based on a map given by Drake to the Queen (British Library)12Sir Francis DrakeNicholas Hilliard miniature, 1581 (National Portrait Gallery, London)13Sir Francis DrakeEngraving by Thomas de Leu after Jean Rabel, shortly after circumnavigation14Buckland AbbeyDrake’s country seat (Devon Library Services)15Elizabeth Sydenham (alleged portrait)Before her marriage to Drake (National Maritime Museum, Greenwich)16Combe Sydenham HouseHome of the Sydenhams (Combe Sydenham Hall)17Dom AntonioClaimant to the Portuguese throne (National Maritime Museum, Greenwich)18Robert Dudley, Earl of LeicesterPromoted Drake’s voyages at court (National Portrait Gallery, London)19Drake’s attack on Cartagena, 1586Contemporary map by Baptista Boazia20Charles, Lord Howard of EffinghamLord Admiral in 1588 (National Maritime Museum, Greenwich)21Plymouth FortDrawing of 1602 showing Drake’s fortifications (British Library)22Plymouth about 1590Showing Drake’s Leat bringing fresh water into the town (British Library)23Sir Francis Drake, 1591Portrait attributed to Marcus Gheeraerts (National Maritime Museum, Greenwich)24Terence Morgan as Sir Francis DrakeFrom the 1961–62 television series (ITC Library Sales Ltd)25Boehm’s statue of DrakeReplica erected on Plymouth Hoe in 1884 (Devon Library Services)26The Game of BowlsSeymour Lucas’s 19th-century painting of the legendary story (National Maritime Museum, Greenwich)
^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Sources and Methodology
The book draws on archival research in both English and Spanish repositories, including:

English: Public Record Office, British Library, London Library, University of London Library, Institute of Historical Research, National Portrait Gallery (London); West Country Studies Library and Devonshire Record Office (Exeter); West Devon Record Office, Art Gallery and Public Library (Plymouth); Buckland Abbey (National Trust); National Maritime Museum (Greenwich); Somerset Record Office (Taunton); university libraries of Warwick, Leeds, and Cambridge; Kingston-upon-Hull Public Library
American: Newberry Library, Chicago
Scholarly consultation: Raymond F. Aker (Drake Navigators Guild), Michael Turner, Richard T. Spence

Sugden’s brother Philip contributed significantly to the deciphering of original Elizabethan manuscripts and handled part of the research. ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]
Editions

1990: First edition (Barrie & Jenkins, UK; Henry Holt, US)
1996: First Pimlico edition with a new preface
2006: Revised Pimlico edition with Postscript reviewing recent scholarship ^[source: sugden_drake.txt]

A Journal of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama, 1497–1499
Author: Álvaro Velho (attributed), a soldier on the expedition
Translator/Editor: E. G. Ravenstein, F.R.G.S.
Publisher: Hakluyt Society, London, 1898 (No. XCIX)
Source files: velho_gama_journal.txt (94,500 words), sources/velho-gama-journal-hakluyt/ (336 OCR page files from the original printed edition)
Summary
The sole surviving first-hand account of Vasco da Gama’s historic voyage from Portugal to India around the Cape of Good Hope (1497–1499). Written by a soldier aboard the fleet, the journal covers the departure from Lisbon, the Atlantic crossing, the rounding of the Cape, the East African coast (Mozambique, Mombasa, Malindi), the crossing to Calicut, and the return voyage. Appendices include King Manuel I’s letters announcing the discovery.
Contents
Introduction (pp. xi–xxxv)
Ravenstein’s scholarly preface covering: the importance of Gama’s voyage, Gama’s life, a parallel between Gama and Columbus, authorities on the voyage, the manuscript of the Roteiro (its history and provenance), authorship (attributed to Álvaro Velho), Portuguese editions, French translations, and notes on the present edition.

sources/witsen-scheepsbouw.content:
Aeloude en Hedendaegsche Scheeps-Bouw en Bestier
Author: Nicolaas Witsen (1641–1717), Raad van Amsterdam (Councillor of Amsterdam)
Full title (as printed, 17th-century Dutch orthography): Aeloude en Hedendaegsche Scheeps-Bouw en Bestier: Waer in wijtloopigh wert verhandelt, de wijze van Scheeps-timmeren, by Grieken en Romeynen: Scheeps-oefeningen, Strijden, Tucht, Strafte, Wetten en gewoonten. Beneffens Evenmatige grootheden van Schepen onses tijts, in alle hare deelen: Verschil van bouwen tusschen onzen Landaert: Indische Vaert en uitheemschen: verklaerde Zee-mans spreeck-woorden en benamingen. Doorgaens verciert met vele Kopere Platen.
Place / printer / year: Amsterdam — printed for Casparus Commelijn, Broer en Jan Appelaer, Anno 1671. Issued with a privilege (Octrooy) from the States of Holland and West-Friesland for fifteen years.
Edition: First edition (1671).
Format: HathiTrust scan (ark+=13960=t8z91x30p), 812 page-files.

About the work
Witsen, councillor of Amsterdam, compiled the most comprehensive Dutch treatise on shipbuilding and ship management of the seventeenth century. The work is divided into two parts (Deelen):

Deel I — Scheeps-Bouw (the building of ships), treating the shipwright’s art from antiquity to his own day.
Deel II — Bestier (the governance and management of ships), treating how ships and crews are commanded and administered, again from the ancients to the present.

Witsen’s stated purpose, in his address to the reader (Aen den Leser), is the increase of knowledge in every man and the honour of the Netherlands (het wit dezes werks is vermeerdering van kennis in een yegelijk, roem den Nederlantschen). He observes that Dutch ships are measured and taken apart by foreigners yet never successfully imitated, and defends the publication of Dutch shipbuilding practice against the argument that it might harm the common good.
The author’s preface notes that, the work being already printed, the Duke of Savoy’s books were drawn upon for drawings of ancient ships, gathered originally from marbles and metal remains across Italy, Greece and Egypt by Pyrrhus Licorius, a nobleman of Naples — these are inserted and marked with the letters P.L.

Contents
Front matter:

Engraved title and title page
Privilege (Octrooy) of the States of Holland and West-Friesland, 15 years
Dedication and commendatory verses (Honori Nicolai Witsenii)
Aen den Leser (Address to the reader)
Inhoudt der Hooft-stucken (Table of the principal chapters)

DEEL I — SCHEEPS-BOUW (the construction of ships). Principal chapters (Hooftstucken) include:

Who first built ships, and in general the shipbuilding of the ancients
The earliest shipbuilding of the Greeks and Romans, for war and for trade; the seating of rowers
The different kinds of ancient ships
Ships noted for their uncommon use
That great fleets were fitted out and distant voyages undertaken from ancient times
What the ancients observed in building, rigging and adorning their ships
How shipbuilding stood after the fall of the Roman empire, and how ships were built in these regions a century and a half ago
How ships are built in our own time
The proportional size of all parts of a ship of about 150 feet long, with certain ship measures
Anchors, weight, the standing of rigging and sails, and how best to set them to catch the wind, mathematically demonstrated
How ship parts are successively joined together
Measures (measures or certificates) of various kinds of sea-going ships of different form and use, beginning with the long ship
Inland-water vessels; oddly built craft; the nature of timber and the tools used in building
Galleys
French and English shipbuilding art
Indian ships
Mathematical demonstration of how much water presses against the ship’s side

DEEL II — BESTIER (the governance of ships), beginning at the running head TWEEDE DEEL: Behelzende het bestier der Schepen, zoo van outs, als te dezer tijdt (containing the governance of ships, both of old and in our own time). Its first Hooftstuck treats the management of ships and ship’s company in former times by Greeks and Romans; later chapters carry the treatment down to the present, including provisions of ships, the offices of the admiralty, and the manning of ships in Witsen’s day.
Back matter:

Bladt-Wyzer (Index), an alphabetical subject index running A–W (e.g. Achtersteven, Ankers, Galleyen, Holte van ‘t schip, Hout, Yzerwerck, Welzeilende schepen, etc.)


Scan completeness
The scan is complete. All 812 numbered page-files (00000000.txt–00000811.txt) are present with no gaps; the first and last files are blank front/back leaves. The text runs continuously from the engraved title through the front matter, both parts, and the closing index. OCR quality is good: the seventeenth-century blackletter and long-s text is rendered with high legibility throughout (e.g. running heads Scheeps-bouw en bestier, Aen den Leser, Inhoudt der Hooft-stucken, Bladt-Wyzer are all clearly readable).

Notes

The raw text is stored at wiki/raw/witsen-scheepsbouw.txt (~2.4 MB, 84,381 lines, 812 pages joined with form-feeds).
Author’s initials P.L. mark plates drawn from Pyrrhus Licorius’s collection of ancient ship depictions.
The work is a contemporary source for Dutch shipbuilding practice, ship types (galleys, inland vessels, Indian ships), naval administration, and the Dutch view of foreign (French, English, Portuguese, Spanish, Indian) shipbuilding in 1671.
